questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The marked structure serves as a surface landmark for which anatomical structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stem of the lateral sulcus

The marked structure indicates the pterion and it serves as a landmark for the stem of the lateral sulcus.

The frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones meet at the pterion. It is a landmark for the stem of the lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure), the most prominent sulcus of the cerebral hemisphere. It separates the frontal lobe from the temporal lobe. Deep to the lateral sulcus lies the insular cortex.

Pterion marks as a surface landmark for the following structures:

• Middle meningeal artery and vein: fractures in this area can rupture the middle meningeal artery, leading to an epidural hematoma.
• Broca’s area: Located in the dominant hemisphere (usually left) in the inferior frontal gyrus, it lies in proximity to the pterion
• The insular cortex and parts of the basal ganglia, such as the putamen, are located deep to the pterion, beneath the lateral sulcus.
• Stem of the lateral sulcus, also called the Sylvian fissure. It houses the middle cerebral artery and its branches, playing a crucial role in brain vascularization and cortical organization.

During surgeries, the pterion is a common site for trephining (making a hole in the skull).

Other Options:

Option A: The pineal gland is located in the posterior aspect of the cranial fossa in the brain. It is located deep in the brain, near the midline.

Option B: Wenicke's area is in the superior temporal gyrus in the dominant cerebral hemisphere. It is found in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus.

Option D: The internal carotid artery siphon is a part of the internal carotid artery's course. Characterized by its S-shaped curvature as it traverses the cavernous sinus and enters the cranial cavity. This configuration helps dissipate pulsatile energy, reducing stress on cerebral vessels, and allows adaptability to cranial movements while maintaining cerebral perfusion.
questions.learning: Stem of the lateral sulcus — The marked structure indicates the pterion and it serves as a landmark for the stem of the lateral sulcus. The frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones meet at the pterion.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 72-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital for treatment of unstable angina. Cardiac catheterization shows occlusion that has caused a 50% reduction in the diameter of the left circumflex artery. Resistance to blood flow in this vessel has increased by what factor relative to a vessel with no occlusion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 16

According to Poiseuille’s law, vascular resistance (R) is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the vessel radius (r):

If the diameter is reduced by 50%, the radius also becomes half of the original.

Thus, resistance increases 16-fold.

Small decreases in vessel radius dramatically increase resistance, which significantly reduces blood flow.
questions.learning: 16 According to Poiseuille’s law, vascular resistance (R) is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the vessel radius (r): If the diameter is reduced by 50%, the radius also becomes half of the original.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: The friend and victim had alcohol and got into an argument over a common girlfriend, following which the friend kills the victim by sitting on his chest and covering his nose and mouth. This is an example of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Burking

The given scenario is an example of burking.

Burking is a method of homicidal smothering and traumatic asphyxia where the assaulter kneels or sits on the chest (traumatic asphyxia) and close the nose and mouth with his hands (smothering). This was the method of killing performed by William Burke and William Hare.

Image shows burking

Other options:

Option B: Smothering is a form of asphyxia that is caused by closing the external respiratory orifices either by the hand or by other means or blocking up the cavities of the nose and mouth by a foreign substance, such as mud, paper, cloth, etc.

Below image shows smothering

Option C: Traumatic asphyxia results from respiratory arrest due to mechanical fixation of the chest, by a heavy substance or object. The normal movements of the chest wall are prevented. There is a gross compression of the chest and usually abdomen by a powerful force, due to which chest expansion and diaphragmatic lowering are prevented. For example stampede deaths, crushing by falls of the earth in coal mines, or earthquakes.

Option D: Overlaying or compression suffocation results due to compression of the chest, so as to prevent breathing. It occurs when an intoxicated parent or other person shares a bed with an infant. The thoracic movements are limited and respiratory exchange is either reduced or completely prevented which leads to death. It is always accidental.

Below image below shows overlaying.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to IMNCI, a 6-month-old child is said to have pneumonia if the child has fast breathing with a respiratory rate more than:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 50

Three key clinical signs are used to assess a sick child with cough or difficult breathing:

• Respiratory rate (RR): distinguishes children who have pneumonia from those who do not. Children are classified as pneumonia if:

• > 50/min RR for infants 2 months to 12 months
• > 40/min RR for children 12 months to 5 years of age

• Lower chest wall indrawing indicates severe pneumonia
• Stridor indicates those with severe pneumonia requiring hospital admission.

The following image gives the IMNCI classification for cough/difficulty in breathing in children.

Signs of severe pneumonia are :

• Not able to drink
• Persistent vomiting
• Convulsions
• Lethargic or unconscious
• Stridor in a calm child
• Severe malnutrition

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 9-month-old infant is brought to the pediatric clinic with a history of sudden jerky movements of the head, trunk, and limbs occurring in clusters. EEG shows a chaotic high-amplitude background with multifocal spikes, consistent with hypsarrhythmia. What is the treatment of choice in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ACTH

The clinical scenario of infantile spasms along with hypsarrythmia in EEG is highly suggestive of West syndrome. Therefore, the drug of choice would be adreno-corticotropic hormone (ACTH).

West syndrome is severe generalized epilepsy that begins between the ages of 2 and 12 months. It is characterized by a triad of:

* Infantile epileptic spasms

* Developmental regression

* Hypsarrhythmia on electroencephalogram (EEG)

Hypsarrhythmia refers to a high voltage, slow, chaotic background with multifocal spikes as shown below.

West syndrome has been known by many names like infantile spasms, salaam attacks, salaam convulsions infantile spastic epilepsy, and jackknife convulsion syndrome. During an attack babies typically attain complete heaving of the head forward towards their knees, and then immediately relax into the upright position.

The image given below illustrates infantile spasms in a child.

Diagnosis is confirmed by EEG which typically shows hypsarrythmia.

The treatment of choice in West syndrome is either adreno-corticotropic hormone (ACTH) or corticosteroids. An antiseizure medication, mainly vigabatrin can be used when associated with tuberous sclerosis.

questions.text: A mother brought her 6 month old infant baby to an Anganwadi worker Lata for advice regarding the vaccination of her child. The last vaccines he had received were OPV3, PENTA 3, IPV2, and ROTA3 at 14 weeks of age. BCG and Hep B were given at birth. When is the next vaccination due?
options: MR vaccine at left arm intramuscularly and Vitamin A drops at the end of 9 months
MR vaccine at right arm subcutaneously and Vitamin A drops at the end of 8 months
MR vaccine at left arm intramuscularly and Vitamin A drops at the end of 8 months
MR vaccine at right arm subcutaneously and Vitamin A drops at the end of 9 months
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. MR vaccine at right arm subcutaneously and Vitamin A drops at the end of 9 months

According to the National Immunization Schedule, the Measles/MR vaccine is given at 9 completed months (1st dose), and a second dose is given at 16-24 months. Measles vaccine can be given till 5 years of age. A dose of 0.5 mL is administered subcutaneously in the right upper arm.

Vitamin A schedule in the National Immunisation Schedule(NIS)

• 1 lakh IU at 9 completed months along with the Measles-Rubella vaccine
• 2 lakh IU is administered bi-annually for children between 1-5 years of age

Total number of doses administered- 9 doses,17 lakhs IU

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Vitamin K supplementation is given to neonates to prevent ___.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hemorrhagic disease of newborn

Intramuscular injection of 0.5-1 mg of phytonadione(Vitamin K)  is given to all newborn infants to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

Hemorrhagic disease of the newborn is caused by a transient deficiency of vitamin K–dependent factors, factors II, VII, IX, and X.

Causes include:

* Lack of free vitamin K from the mother

* Absence of the bacterial intestinal flora normally responsible for the synthesis of vitamin K.

It is responsive to and prevented by vitamin K therapy (0.5-1 mg of phytonadione).

However, for newborns with vitamin K deficiency, the dose of vitamin K administered is 1–5 mg intravenously.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the minimum external pressure that leads to the formation of pressure sores?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 30

The minimum external pressure that leads to the formation of pressure sores is 30 mm of Hg.

Pressure sores also known as bedsores, pressure ulcers, or decubitus ulcers are defined as tissue necrosis with ulceration due to prolonged pressure. When the external pressure exceeds the capillary occlusive pressure, blood flow ceases leading to tissue anoxia, necrosis, and ulceration. Thus an external pressure of >30mmHg leads to the formation of pressure sores.

The common sites of pressure sores in decreasing frequency are:

* Ischium

* Greater Trochanter

* Sacrum

* Heel

* Malleolus (lateral followed by medial)

* Occiput

A staging system for the description of pressure sores is:

Stage 1 - Non-blanchable erythema without a breach in the epidermis
Stage 2 - Partial-thickness skin loss involving the epidermis and dermis
Stage 3 - Full-thickness skin loss extending into the subcutaneous tissue but not through underlying fascia
Stage 4 - Full-thickness skin loss through fascia with extensive tissue destruction, maybe involving muscle, bone, tendon, or joint

Prevention is the best treatment for pressure sores. It can be done through good skincare, the use of air-fluidised beds, special pressure dispersion cushions, or foams. The position of the bedridden patients should be changed once every 2 hours, and wheelchair-bound patients should be taught to get out of their chairs for 10 seconds every 10 minutes.

Surgical treatment of pressure sores mainly involves wound management. The pressure sores should be adequately debrided and vacuum-assisted closure (VAC).VAC is done by applying intermittent negative pressure of approximately -125mmHg to hasten debridement and promote granulation tissue formation in chronic wounds and ulcers. Negative pressure decreases edema, removes interstitial fluid, and increases blood flow. This decreases bacterial growth and increases cell proliferation.

Large skin flaps that have muscle with sensory innervation are best for reconstruction(example-extensor fascia lata flap with the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh). Faecal or urinary diversion can be considered in special cases depending on the site of the ulcer, being prone to urine or faecal contamination.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is deficient in a patient with features as shown below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tryptophan

The image provided is characteristic of Casal's necklace, seen in pellagra, and indicates a deficiency of Tryptophan.

Pellagra can occur due to:

• Vitamin B3 (niacin)

• Niacin is derived from tryptophan and needs B2 and B6 for its synthesis.

• Hartnup's disease (tryptophan malabsorption)
• Malignant carcinoid syndrome (↑ tryptophan metabolism)
• Isoniazid (↓ vitamin B6)

In Hartnup's disease, defective membrane transport of tryptophan across PCT and enterocytes leads to malabsorption of tryptophan. This causes a deficiency of tryptophan.

As a result, the production of niacin from tryptophan is reduced and this manifests as pellagra with dermatitis, diarrhea and dementia (3D's) and glossitis. A characteristic skin rash called the Casal’s necklace may also be seen.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following phases of a clinical trial is also referred to as efficacy trial?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phase 2

Efficacy and appropriate dose range is the main aim of phase 2 of clinical trials. It is evaluated on a small group of patients with the target disease.

Phase II of clinical trials involve a small group of patients (50-500). Most of the new drugs will be administered for the first time in patients with the target disease. The study is designed to obtain proof of concept (potential of the drug to treat the disease) and dose-ranging study (provides input for choosing the most appropriate dose for phase 3 studies).

Phase 3 studies are also known as pivotal studies as they establish treatment benefits.
questions.learning: Phase 2 Efficacy and appropriate dose range is the main aim of phase 2 of clinical trials. It is evaluated on a small group of patients with the target disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 23-year-old woman presents with a one-week history of fever. Her cardiac monitor shows a specific rhythm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The ECG strip shows classic features of Atrial Fibrillation (AF): Key features visible: 1. 1. Irregularly irregular R-R intervals : no two consecutive R-R intervals are equal 2. 2. Absent P waves : replaced by chaotic, fibrillatory baseline (wavy/undulating baseline) 3. 3. Narrow QRS complexes : normal ventricular conduction 4. 4. No organized atrial activity visible Clinical context: 28-year-old woman with 1-week fever history — likely cause is myocarditis or rheumatic fever triggering AF. Why other options are wrong: (B) Atrial Flutter : Shows a classic sawtooth pattern of regular flutter waves at ~300 bpm with regular ventricular response (usually 2:1, 3:1 block). This ECG shows irregular rhythm with no sawtooth : rules out flutter. (C) Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT) : SVT shows a rapid but perfectly regular narrow complex tachycardia, usually 150–250 bpm with P waves often hidden in T waves. The irregularity here rules out SVT. (D) Ventricular Tachyarrhythmia : VT shows broad/wide QRS complexes (>0.12s) with rapid rate. The QRS complexes here are narrow : completely rules out VT

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: An intrauterine scan at the 13th week of pregnancy showed a fetus with multiple long bone fractures. What is commonly associated with this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Osteogenesis imperfecta

Osteogenesis imperfecta is commonly associated with this multiple long bone fractures.

Osteogenesis imperfecta is a connective tissue disorder that occurs due to abnormal type 1 collagen production. The main features are joints that are vulnerable to fracture, scleral alterations, dentinogenesis imperfecta, and deafness. Multiple bone fractures are a consequence of bone fragility. It is classified into four types based on scleral involvement, natural history, and mode of inheritance.

Protrusio acetabuli, wormian bones, and proximal femoral ‘shepherd’s crook’ deformities of the femurs are the common radiological findings that are observed. Management comprises the use of bisphosphonates, along with physiotherapy and walking aids.

The images below show blue sclera and wormian bones in osteogenesis imperfecta:

Other options:

Option A: Achondroplasia is an autosomal dominant skeletal dysplasia with disproportionately short limbs, sleep apnea, and kyphoscoliosis. Facial features include button nose, frontal bossing, macrocephaly, etc.

The images below show the features of achondroplasia:

(a) Prominent forehead and body asymmetry, (b) a low nasal bridge, (c) trident hands, (d) scoliosis

Option C: Cretinism occurs due to iodine deficiency. Its clinical features are deaf-mutism, squint, mental retardation, and spastic or rigid neuromotor disorder.

Option D: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder. The affected persons will be tall with long limbs and digits. Spontaneous pneumothorax, aortic dissection, and lens dislocation are also seen. An early diastolic murmur is heard on auscultation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman presents with bleeding after menopause. What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic investigation to evaluate the cause of her symptoms?
questions.explanation: A 55-year-old woman with postmenopausal bleeding (PMB) must always be evaluated for endometrial carcinoma. In exam settings, the most appropriate initial diagnostic investigation is considered to be an endometrial biopsy, because it provides definitive histopathological diagnosis. Endometrial biopsy is: 1. Minimally invasive 2. Can be done as an outpatient procedure 3. Highly effective in detecting endometrial hyperplasia or malignancy Although transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) is often used as a first step in clinical practice to measure endometrial thickness, it is only a screening tool. A thickness >4–5 mm requires biopsy confirmation. Therefore, in exams where ruling out cancer is emphasized, biopsy is preferred as the initial definitive test. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Ultrasound → Screening tool, not diagnostic (C) Fractional curettage → More invasive, used if biopsy inconclusive (D) CA-125 → Not suitable for diagnosis of PMB

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which menstrual cycle length is considered abnormal?
questions.explanation: A normal menstrual cycle typically ranges from 21 to 35 days in length. Cycles falling within this range, such as 28 days (Option A), 30 days (Option B), and 35 days (Option C), are considered physiologically normal variations. A cycle length of 38 days (Option D) exceeds the standard threshold and is classified as oligomenorrhea. Oligomenorrhea can be caused by various factors, including polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), thyroid dysfunction, hyperprolactinemia, or significant physical or emotional stress. While occasional variations in cycle length can occur, persistent cycles longer than 35 days warrant clinical investigation to determine the underlying cause and assess ovulatory function. Understanding the normal parameters of the menstrual cycle is fundamental for diagnosing reproductive disorders and monitoring female health throughout the reproductive years. Therefore, any cycle length greater than 35 days is clinically identified as abnormal
questions.learning: A normal menstrual cycle typically ranges from 21 to 35 days in length. Cycles falling within this range, such as 28 days (Option A), 30 days (Option B), and 35 days (Option C), are considered physiologically normal variations.

questions.text: A 6-year-old child presents with recurrent infections and defective complement activation. Investigations reveal impaired function of proteins localized to cholesterol- and sphingolipid-rich microdomains of the plasma membrane (lipid rafts). Which of the following types of proteins is most characteristically associated with these membrane rafts?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. GPI-anchored proteins

Lipid rafts are cholesterol- and sphingolipid-rich microdomains of the plasma membrane that preferentially contain GPI-anchored proteins, which play key roles in immune signaling and complement regulation.

• Lipid rafts act as platforms for cell signaling and immune responses
• Important examples: CD55 (DAF) and CD59 → complement regulation
• Defects can lead to complement-mediated damage (e.g., PNH)

Differentiation:

A. Mannose-binding protein → soluble protein (not membrane raft–bound)

B. GTP-binding proteins → intracellular signaling (cytosolic)

D. Ion channels → not specifically enriched in lipid rafts

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A young patient presents with nasal polyps and rhinosinusitis. X-ray and clinical images are as below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Kartagener's syndrome

The given clinical scenario along with an X-ray showing dextrocardia, CT showing maxillary polyp, and endoscopy showing nasal polyp is suggestive of Kartagener's syndrome.

Primary ciliary dyskinesia (also called immotile cilia syndrome) is an autosomal recessive disorder affecting ciliary motility. When a patient has bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis, and situs inversus triad, he is known to have Kartagener syndrome. It occurs due to the absence of protein dynein in the A tubules of the respiratory mucosa.

The disease is usually diagnosed based on the clinical picture and should be evaluated in later stages when a child presents with recurrent lower and upper respiratory tract infections. Other features of primary ciliary dyskinesia include congenital heart diseases and neonatal hydrocephalus. Male patients with this condition tend to be infertile, due to asthenospermia (immotile spermatozoa due to impaired sperm flagella function).

Transmission electron microscopy is the gold standard investigation to analyze cilia. There is no specific treatment for this condition and is managed according to the symptoms.

Other options:

Option A: Churg Strauss syndrome clinically presents with asthma, fever and eosinophilia.

Option C: Young's syndrome clinically presents with infertility (azoospermia) and bronchiectasis.

Option D: Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive condition due to a mutation of the CFTR gene on chromosome 7. Clinical features include recurrent sinopulmonary infection, intestinal obstruction, pancreatic insufficiency, and male infertility. Diagnosis is made by elevated sweat chloride levels, abnormal nasal potential difference, and genetic testing for CFTR mutation.
questions.learning: Kartagener's syndrome — The given clinical scenario along with an X-ray showing dextrocardia, CT showing maxillary polyp, and endoscopy showing nasal polyp is suggestive of Kartagener's syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 20-year-old medical student went for a screening health test and was injected with PPD intradermally. Identify the immune cell in the skin that picks up the PPD to present it to T cells.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Langerhans cells

Langerhans cells are specialized dendritic antigen-presenting cells located in the epidermis. They capture antigens entering through the skin and migrate to regional lymph nodes to present antigen via MHC II to T lymphocytes, initiating a cell-mediated immune response.

In the PPD (Mantoux) test, tuberculin protein is injected intradermally. Langerhans cells capture the antigen and present it to sensitized T cells, resulting in a type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction mediated by Th1 cells.

Why not the other options:

A. Langhans cells: Multinucleated giant cells seen in granulomas (e.g., tuberculosis); not antigen-presenting cells in the epidermis.

B. Follicular dendritic cells: Located in germinal centers of lymph nodes and spleen; present antigen to B cells, not involved in skin antigen capture.

D. Natural killer cells: Part of innate immunity, responsible for killing virus-infected or tumor cells, not antigen presentation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements about primary dysmennorhea is true?
options: Pain begins after few hours after onset of periods and can last up to 48 hours
It is dependent on psychological factors
Pain begins 3 days prior to the onset of periods and is present upto the second day of the period
GnRH antagonists are the first line of treatment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is dependent on psychological factors

Primary dysmenorrhea is dependent on psychological factors is the true statement.

Dysmenorrhea is defined as cramping pain that occurs during menstruation.  Low social support, alexithymia, neuroticism trait, long menstrual bleeding, family history of dysmenorrhea, and high-caffeine diet are important risk factors for women with primary dysmenorrhea. It can be classified as:

A. Etiological:

• Primary dysmenorrhea is a type of dysmenorrhoea that is not associated with any pelvic pathology. It affects women in the age group of 18 to 25 years, with ovulatory cycles. It begins just before or with the onset of menstruation. (Not a few hours after as in Option A or not 3 days prior as in option C)
• Secondary (Acquired) dysmenorrhea is associated with the presence of pelvic pathologies such as fibroids, adenomyosis, pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), and endometriosis.

B.  Clinical:

• Spasmodic dysmenorrhea is the most common and is characterized by cramping pain on the first and second days of menstruation.
• Congestive dysmenorrhea presents as worsening pelvic discomfort and pelvic pain, a few days before the onset of menses followed by relief of the symptoms. This is seen in PID, IUCD users, varicosities of pelvic veins, pelvic endometriosis, and fibroids.
• Membranous dysmenorrhea is rare and is characterized by crampy pain that occurs with the passage of the endometrium as a cast at the time of menstruation.

Primary dysmenorrhea can be managed with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), combined oral contraceptive pills,(Option D), and progestin-only pills. GnRH agonists and androgens are also useful. Surgical management includes hysterectomy and is indicated if not responding to medical management. In secondary dysmenorrhea, treating the cause is needed.
questions.learning: It is dependent on psychological factors Primary dysmenorrhea is dependent on psychological factors is the true statement. Dysmenorrhea is defined as cramping pain that occurs during menstruation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with dilation of veins as shown in the image. Which vein is involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Great Saphenous Vein

The image shows prominent, tortuous, dilated veins(varicosities) on the medial aspect of the leg and thigh, which is the characteristic course of the Great Saphenous Vein (GSV). The dorsum of the foot, at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch, medial aspect of the leg and thigh forms the surface marking of the great saphenous vein.

The surface marking for it is marked by joining the following points from foot to thigh:

* On the dorsum of the foot, at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch.

* On the anterior surface of the medial malleolus.

* On the medial border of the tibia at the junction of the upper 2/3rd and lower 1/3rd of the leg.

* At the adductor tubercle

* Just below the centre of the saphenous opening.

Varicose veins are subcutaneous dilated, tortuous veins 3mm or more in diameter. They commonly present with a sensation of dragging pain, heaviness, itching or burning over the affected area or the whole limb, and swelling of the feet. These symptoms increase throughout the day or with prolonged standing and are relieved by elevation or compression hosiery.

Risk factors:

* Female gender

* Increasing age

* Increasing body mass and height

* Pregnancy

* Family history

* Smoking

* Occupations involving prolonged standing

Management of varicose veins

Incompetence
Management

Great saphenous vein (GSV) and saphenofemoral (SFJ)

• Endothermal ablation (gold standard treatment for varicose veins). It includes:

• Endovenous laser ablation (EVLA)
• Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)

• Trendelenburg procedure (Flush Ligation of Saphenofemoral Junction (SFJ) after ligation of 6 tributaries) ± stripping (retrogradely up to the knee, to prevent saphenous nerve injury.)

Short saphenous vein (SSJ) and saphenopopliteal (SPJ)

• Flush ligation of SPJ (Stripping is not done to prevent sural nerve injury)
• Endothermal ablation:

• Endovenous laser ablation (EVLA)
• Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)

Perforator

• Dodd and Crockett surgery - Multiple subfascial ligations
• Subfascial endoscopic perforator surgery (SEPS) - smaller incision, so cosmetically better
• Endothermal ablation:

• Endovenous laser ablation (EVLA)
• Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)

New treatment modalities:

* Foam sclerotherapy - The Tessari method is a widely used method to prepare foam for sclerotherapy. Sclerosant: air ratio taken is 1:3 or 1:4.

* Endovenous glue therapy - endoluminal application of cyanoacrylate adhesive

* TriVex - Transilluminated powered phlebectomy

Other options:

Option B: The small saphenous vein courses from the lateral of the dorsal venous arch to the center of popliteal fossa.

Option C: The femoral vein runs upward in the thigh, accompanying the femoral artery within the femoral sheath and it is a deep vein.

Option D: Perforators: Connect superficial veins to deep veins. They may become incompetent, causing varicose veins, but the main visible dilated vein here is the GSV.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with diabetes mellitus develops painful vesicular lesions involving a unilateral dermatome in the axillary region (herpes zoster) after starting antidiabetic therapy. Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sitagliptin

DPP-4 (dipeptidyl peptidase-4) is identical to CD26, a surface glycoprotein on T lymphocytes that functions as a T-cell costimulatory molecule. Inhibiting DPP-4 with sitagliptin therefore has an immunomodulatory effect, blunting T-cell activation — and because varicella-zoster reactivation is controlled by cell-mediated (T-cell) immunity, gliptins are associated with an increased risk of infections, including herpes zoster, nasopharyngitis and upper respiratory tract infections.

Other gliptin adverse effects: acute pancreatitis, bullous pemphigoid, severe arthralgia, and (with saxagliptin/alogliptin) hospitalization for heart failure.

Other options:

• A. Metformin → GI upset, B₁₂ deficiency, lactic acidosis. No immune effect.
• C. Pioglitazone → fluid retention, CHF, weight gain, fractures, bladder cancer.
• D. Glibenclamide → hypoglycemia, weight gain.

Management: Antiviral — acyclovir/valacyclovir/famciclovir, started within 72 h.

Pearl: DPP-4 = CD26 = T-cell marker → gliptins ↑ infection risk.
questions.learning: Sitagliptin DPP-4 (dipeptidyl peptidase-4) is identical to CD26, a surface glycoprotein on T lymphocytes that functions as a T-cell costimulatory molecule.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A biostatistician is analyzing a small dataset of serum potassium values collected from 10 patients. One value appears suspiciously high compared to the rest. To determine whether this extreme value should be statistically rejected as an outlier, the most appropriate test to apply is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dixon’s Q-test

When dealing with a small sample size (typically n ≤ 30, especially n < 10–12) and one suspected extreme value, the most appropriate statistical test to assess whether it is an outlier is Dixon’s Q-test.

• Designed specifically for small datasets
• Used when there is only one suspected outlier
• Commonly applied in laboratory and clinical measurements
• Compares the gap between the suspicious value and its nearest neighbor relative to the range of the dataset

A. Grubbs’ test ❌

→ Also for outliers, but more appropriate for larger samples (n ≥ 20–30).

questions.text: A patient comes with a history of clean-cut injury which is not lacerated. He says that he received his last dose of tetanus vaccination about 10 years ago. What should be given next?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Single dose tetanus toxoid

A single dose of tetanus toxoid is given as the wound is clean and the last dose was received more than 10 years ago.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with a low-grade fever lasting one week, accompanied by loss of appetite and weight loss. A barium meal follow- through study has been performed, and the image is provided. Based on the clinical features and radiological findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of constitutional symptoms, including mild fever, weight loss, and anorexia in a young adult, combined with the radiographic finding of a distorted ileocaecal region, strongly suggests abdominal tuberculosis. The barium meal follow-through reveals a "pulled-up" caecum and an obtuse ileocaecal angle, which are classic signs of ileocaecal TB (Stierlin's sign or Fleischner's sign). Ulcerative colitis (Option B) typically presents with bloody diarrhea and predominantly affects the rectum and distal colon, showing a "lead pipe" appearance on imaging. Crohn's disease (Option C) can mimic tuberculosis but often presents with a more sectoral distribution and different radiographic features like the "string sign" of Kantor. Carcinoma of the caecum (Option D) usually presents in older age groups and would show a constant filling defect rather than the fibrotic retraction seen here. Given the high prevalence in endemic regions and the specific anatomical distortions observed, ileocaecal tuberculosis is the most probable diagnosis for this young female patient
questions.learning: The clinical history of constitutional symptoms, including mild fever, weight loss, and anorexia in a young adult, combined with the radiographic finding of a distorted ileocaecal region, strongly suggests abdominal tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old man diagnosed with Addison’s disease presents with typical features of adrenal hormone deficiency but also reports an unexpected rise in blood glucose levels. Considering the usual clinical presentation of Addison’s disease, which of the following features is not commonly associated with this condition?
questions.explanation: Addison’s disease, or primary adrenal insufficiency, results from the destruction of the adrenal cortex, leading to a deficiency in cortisol and aldosterone. Cortisol is a "stress hormone" that increases blood glucose; therefore, a deficiency characteristically leads to hypoglycemia rather than hyperglycemia. The aldosterone deficiency causes the kidneys to lose sodium and retain potassium, leading to the hallmark electrolyte abnormalities of hyponatremia (Option B) and hyperkalemia (Option C). Chronic mineralocorticoid deficiency also results in reduced blood volume and hypotension (Option D). The patient’s report of hyperglycemia is contradictory to the pathophysiology of the disease. Other common symptoms include skin hyperpigmentation (due to elevated ACTH) and profound fatigue. A diagnosis of Addison's is confirmed with a low morning cortisol level and a failure to respond to the ACTH stimulation test
questions.learning: Addison’s disease, or primary adrenal insufficiency, results from the destruction of the adrenal cortex, leading to a deficiency in cortisol and aldosterone.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida undergoing cesarean section for placenta previa begins to bleed after placental delivery. The uterus is atonic, and oxytocin along with other uterotonics have already been administered. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intrauterine balloon tamponade

In a primigravida with atonic PPH (Postpartum haemorrhage) unresponsive to initial measures such as oxytocin and other uterotonics, the next best step in management is intrauterine balloon tamponade as it reduces PPH by stimulating uterine contraction and exerting direct tamponade effect.

For balloon tamponade, Foley catheter, Bakri balloon, Condom catheter or Sengstaken-Blakemore tube is inserted into the uterine cavity and the balloon is inflated with normal saline (200-500 mL). It reduces PPH by stimulating uterine contraction and exerting direct hemostatic pressure (tamponade effect) to the open uterine sinuses. It is kept for 4-6 hours. This can avoid hysterectomy in most cases.

The given image shows Bakri balloon tamponade:

The following are the steps used in controlling postpartum haemorrhage:

* Feel the uterus to know the cause of the haemorrhage. If the uterus feels flabby, bleeding is likely to be due to atonicity. If it is firm and contracted, it is likely to be traumatic in origin.

* In case of an atonic uterus, massage the uterus and start the patient on oxytocin drips or methergine.

* If the uterus remains atonic, manual exploration of the uterus is done for removing any retained placental fragments. Blood transfusion is started and oxytocin drips are continued. Other uterotonic agents can also be given.

* Uterine massage and bimanual compression

* Uterine tamponade using a hydrostatic balloon catheter (balloon tamponade)

* Surgical methods to control PPH are outlined as stepwise uterine devascularization procedures:

* Compression sutures: B-Lynch suture (Option D)

* Ligation of uterine arteries (Option A)

* Ligation of ovarian and uterine anastomosis

* Ligation of internal iliac artery (Option B)

* Angiographic embolization of the bleeding vessel

*

*  Hysterectomy

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old male patient presented with complaints of a gradually progressive swelling around his wrist joint for 3 months. Given below is the image of the swelling and the X-ray film. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Osteoclastoma

The clinical presentation and the X-ray showing an eccentric expansile lesion with a soap bubble appearance are suggestive of osteoclastoma or giant cell tumor(GCT).

Osteoclastoma usually affects young adults in the age group of 20-40 years. The most common location of the tumor is the distal femur followed by the proximal tibia. Involvement of the distal end of the radius is also seen and the tumor is more aggressive in this location.

Radiographic findings in GCT:

* A solitary, possibly loculated, lytic lesion in the epiphysis

* Eccentric location, most often subchondral

* Expansion of the overlying cortex

* Soap bubble appearance - The tumor is homogeneously lytic with trabeculae of the remnants of bone traversing it, giving it a loculated appearance called soap bubble appearance

* No calcification within the tumor

* No or minimal reactive sclerosis around the tumor.

Treatment :

* Extended curettage and bone grafting.

* En-bloc wide resection and reconstruction are done for advanced stages, local recurrence, and tumors not responding to other methods.

* Resection without reconstruction is done for lesions in expandable bones like distal ulna, clavicle, etc.

* Irradiation and/or embolization are used for inoperable lesions in the spine and pelvis.

* Bisphosphonates have been shown to reduce the proliferation of osteoclasts and hence have been shown to stabilize local and metastatic disease.

* Denosumab is approved for use in unresectable tumors in skeletally mature patients.

Other options:

Ewing's sarcoma:

It is a primary malignant tumor of the bone commonly involving the age group of 4-25 years. It commonly involves the diaphysis of the long bones like the femur, tibia, fibula, and humerus.

Radiographic findings: Onion-peel appearance due to deposition of periosteal reaction in layers is the typical finding.

Osteosarcoma:

It is the most common non-hematologic primary malignancy of bone. It occurs most commonly in the second decade of life. It is typically metaphyseal. The distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus are the common sites.

Radiographic findings: The periosteal reaction is the typical finding and it may take the form of a Codman's triangle or it may have a sunburst (sunray) appearance on X-ray.

Osteochondroma:

Osteochondromas are common benign bone tumors. The lesions consist of a bony mass, often in the form of a stalk, produced by endochondral ossification of a growing cartilaginous cap. The common sites of involvement are the distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida presents to the emergency room in the early stage of labor with adequate uterine contractions. On per vaginal examination, a gynecoid pelvis is felt, the membranes are ruptured, and the vertex is felt in the right occipito-posterior position. How will you manage this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Normal vaginal delivery

The given features of right occipito-posterior presentation with the favorable pelvis (gynecoid) and adequate uterine contractions can be managed by normal vaginal delivery.

Right occipito-posterior position (ROP) is the most common malposition, which occurs when the occiput is situated posteriorly over the sacroiliac joint, or directly over the sacrum. It is associated with the risk of delayed engagement of the head, prolonged labor due to transverse arrest, and the need for cesarean sections.

Features of occipito-posterior position include infra-umbilical flattening and fetal heart sounds localized to the flank. The fetal parts are more prominently felt near the midline. The head engages through the right oblique diameter in ROP and the engaging AP diameter is occipitofrontal or suboccipito-frontal. In 90% of circumstances with a favorable pelvis and strong uterine contractions without any complications, it undergoes the mechanism like that of normal labor. Hence, we can wait and watch for the progress of normal vaginal delivery.

In some cases, it undergoes non-rotation resulting in oblique posterior arrest. If it undergoes malrotation (anterior rotation of the sinciput), it can cause a persistent occipito-posterior position. Spontaneous delivery can occur as face to pubis. If an arrest occurs in this position, it is termed an occipito-sacral arrest. Incomplete forward rotation leads to a deep transverse arrest.

Indications of cesarean section in occipito-posterior position include the arrest of labor, inadequate uterine contractions, fetal distress, and other obstetrical complications.

During the second stage of labor, if the anterior rotation of the occiput is completed, delivery occurs spontaneously or may require the application of ventouse or low forceps.
questions.learning: Normal vaginal delivery — The given features of right occipito-posterior presentation with the favorable pelvis (gynecoid) and adequate uterine contractions can be managed by normal vaginal delivery.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman comes to the clinic. She already has twins by normal delivery. Which of the following is the correct representation of her obstetric score?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. G2P1

The obstetric score of a pregnant woman who previously delivered twins would be G2P1.

The obstetric score is used to summarize the past obstetric history as follows:

• G - Gravidity, denoting the total number of pregnancies, including the present one. It is irrespective of the period of gestation.
• P - Parity, denoting the total number of previous pregnancies crossing the period of viability, which is 28 weeks in India.

• This includes both live births and stillbirths
• The current pregnancy is not included

• A - Abortus or the number of pregnancies that were lost for any reason, including induced abortions or miscarriages.
• L - Living children

Both Gravida and para are the numbers of pregnancies rather than babies.

Terminology

• Nulligravida: One who is not and has never been pregnant
• Primigravida: One who is pregnant for the first time
• Multigravida: One who has previously been pregnant
• Nullipara: One who has never completed a pregnancy to the stage of viability
• Primipara: One who has delivered only once (fetuses born alive or dead after becoming viable)
• Multipara: One with 2 or more pregnancies to the stage of viability or more
• Parturient: A woman in labor
questions.learning: G2P1 — The obstetric score of a pregnant woman who previously delivered twins would be G2P1. The obstetric score is used to summarize the past obstetric history as follows: • G - Gravidity, denoting the total number of pregnancies, including the present one.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-month-old infant is brought to the outpatient department with a deformity visible in the accompanying image. Based on this clinical presentation, what would be the appropriate line of management for this child?
questions.explanation: The image displays Congenital Talipes Equinovarus (CTEV), also known as clubfoot. The gold standard for initial management of CTEV, especially in an infant as young as 6 months old, is the Ponseti method. This involves gentle serial manipulation and casting (Option A) started ideally within the first few weeks of life to progressively correct the four components of the deformity: cavus, adductus, varus, and equinus. If the child is already 6 months old and has not been treated, Ponseti casting remains the primary first-line therapy. Surgical options like posteromedial soft tissue release (Option B) are now reserved for cases that fail conservative casting. Evan’s procedure (Option D) is used for children between 4 and 8 years of age. Triple arthrodesis (Option C) is a radical corrective surgery for skeletal maturity, typically performed after 10–12 years of age. Therefore, conservative manipulation and casting is the definitive starting point
questions.learning: The image displays Congenital Talipes Equinovarus (CTEV), also known as clubfoot. The gold standard for initial management of CTEV, especially in an infant as young as 6 months old, is the Ponseti method.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presents with a one- week history of creamy white vaginal discharge accompanied by a fishy odor, particularly noticeable after intercourse. Microscopic examination of a vaginal swab is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with creamy white vaginal discharge and a fishy odor, especially after intercourse—classic features of bacterial vaginosis (BV). The odor is due to amine release (positive whiff test with KOH). The microscopy image shows clue cells, which are vaginal epithelial cells coated with bacteria, giving a granular, indistinct border appearance. This is a key diagnostic feature of BV and forms part of Amsel’s criteria. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Trichomoniasis: Characterized by greenish-yellow, frothy discharge and motile organisms on microscopy, not clue cells. (B) Candidiasis: Presents with thick, curdy discharge and itching; microscopy shows budding yeast/pseudohyphae, not clue cells. (D) Gonorrhoea: Produces purulent discharge with intracellular diplococci; no fishy odor or clue cells are seen
questions.learning: The patient presents with creamy white vaginal discharge and a fishy odor, especially after intercourse—classic features of bacterial vaginosis (BV). The odor is due to amine release (positive whiff test with KOH).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Radioactive isotope used for teletherapy?
questions.explanation: Teletherapy refers to external beam radiation therapy where the radiation source is located at a distance from the patient. Cobalt-60 is the standard radioactive isotope used for teletherapy in many centers (specifically in Cobalt units). It emits high-energy gamma rays and has a half-life of 5.27 years. Iridium-192 (Option A) and Iodine-125 (Option B) are characteristically used for brachytherapy, where the radioactive source is placed inside or very close to the tumor. Iodine-131 (Option D) is an unsealed isotope used for the diagnosis and treatment of thyroid diseases, not for external teletherapy. While linear accelerators (LINACs) have largely replaced cobalt units in high-resource settings, Cobalt-60 remains a vital isotope for teletherapy globally due to its reliability and simpler maintenance. Understanding the differences between teletherapy and brachytherapy isotopes is a core concept in clinical oncology and radiotherapy
questions.learning: Teletherapy refers to external beam radiation therapy where the radiation source is located at a distance from the patient. Cobalt-60 is the standard radioactive isotope used for teletherapy in many centers (specifically in Cobalt units).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 39-year-old male patient presented with complaints of fever and cough. His chest radiograph shows air bronchogram sign. The probable diagnosis is :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Consolidation

The radiograph shows air bronchogram sign in a lung with consolidation, seen in pneumonia, which is supported by the clinical history of this patient.

An air bronchogram is a tubular outline of an airway made visible when there is filling of the surrounding alveoli by fluid or inflammatory exudates.

The causes of air bronchogram are as follows:

• Lung consolidation
• Pulmonary edema
• Nonobstructive pulmonary atelectasis
• Severe interstitial disease
• Neoplasm
• Normal expiration

Pleural effusion is seen as a homogenous opacity on chest radiograph.

The given radiograph shows peribronchial thickening and air bronchogram sign:
questions.learning: Consolidation — The radiograph shows air bronchogram sign in a lung with consolidation, seen in pneumonia, which is supported by the clinical history of this patient.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The best method to obtain tissue for the diagnosis of pancreatic carcinoma is:
options: Transgastric FNAC guided by endoscopic ultrasound
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Transgastric FNAC guided by endoscopic ultrasound

Accurate diagnosis of pancreatic carcinoma requires histologic confirmation (especially before starting chemotherapy/radiation or when the tumor is unresectable/borderline resectable). The preferred method for obtaining tissue is one that provides high diagnostic yield with the lowest risk of complications, particularly tumor seeding.

Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)-guided transgastric fine-needle aspiration/biopsy (FNAC/FNB) is the best method because it:

• Allows real-time high-resolution visualization of pancreatic masses
• Enables precise needle placement into the lesion
• Has high sensitivity and specificity
• Minimizes risk of peritoneal tumor seeding compared with percutaneous approaches
• Also permits sampling of regional lymph nodes

Percutaneous transperitoneal biopsy has a higher risk of needle tract/peritoneal seeding, and percutaneous transhepatic routes are technically limited and not preferred. Laparoscopic biopsy is invasive and reserved when less invasive options fail or staging laparoscopy is required.
questions.learning: Transgastric FNAC guided by endoscopic ultrasound Accurate diagnosis of pancreatic carcinoma requires histologic confirmation (especially before starting chemotherapy/radiation or when the tumor is unresectable/borderline resectable).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A deep-sea diver develops euphoria, impaired judgment, and altered consciousness at increased depth due to exposure to an inert gas under high pressure. This phenomenon is known as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nitrogen narcosis

At greater diving depths, the partial pressure of nitrogen increases in the breathing gas mixture. Nitrogen dissolves in neuronal lipid membranes and depresses central nervous system activity, producing effects similar to alcohol intoxication. Clinical features of nitrogen narcosis:

• Euphoria
• Impaired judgment
• Slowed reaction time
• Confusion and altered consciousness

These symptoms usually occur at depths >30 meters (≈100 ft) and resolve when the diver ascends and nitrogen partial pressure decreases.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Helium narcosis: Helium is used in deep diving precisely because it does not cause narcosis like nitrogen.

B. Oxygen toxicity: Occurs at very high oxygen partial pressures, causing seizures or lung injury.

D. Decompression sickness: Caused by nitrogen bubble formation during rapid ascent, leading to joint pain (“the bends”), neurologic deficits, and embolic phenomena.
questions.learning: Nitrogen narcosis At greater diving depths, the partial pressure of nitrogen increases in the breathing gas mixture. Nitrogen dissolves in neuronal lipid membranes and depresses central nervous system activity, producing effects similar to alcohol…

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which deficiency is most likely in a patient with delayed wound healing and alopecia?
questions.explanation: The combination of delayed wound healing and alopecia (hair loss) is a hallmark clinical presentation of zinc deficiency. Zinc is a critical component of numerous metalloenzymes involved in DNA synthesis, cell division, and protein synthesis, all of which are essential for tissue repair and hair follicle maintenance. Severe deficiency can also lead to dermatitis, particularly acrodermatitis enteropathica. Regarding the distractors, copper deficiency (Option B) primarily manifests as microcytic anemia and neutropenia rather than alopecia. Calcium deficiency (Option C) is associated with tetany and skeletal issues, while Vitamin D deficiency (Option D) leads to rickets or osteomalacia. None of these typically cause the specific integumentary issues seen with low zinc. Thus, given the role of zinc in collagen synthesis and rapidly dividing skin cells, it is the most likely deficient nutrient
questions.learning: The combination of delayed wound healing and alopecia (hair loss) is a hallmark clinical presentation of zinc deficiency. Zinc is a critical component of numerous metalloenzymes involved in DNA synthesis, cell division, and protein synthesis, all of which…

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text:
A 40-year-old woman presents with mild, progressive, bilateral hearing loss. A PTA showed the following findings. What is the most likely clinical finding in this patient?

PTA - Pure Tone Audiogram
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Schwartze sign

The clinical scenario describes a 40-year-old female patient with mild, progressive, bilateral hearing loss, and a PTA showing Carhart's notch (dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz) are all suggestive of Otosclerosis and the classical sign seen here is Schwartze sign.

The presence of a reddish hue on the promontory through the tympanic membrane, known as the Schwartze sign, suggests an active focus.

Otosclerosis is caused by bony overgrowth involving the enchondral layer of the bony otic capsule. It presents with bilateral progressive conductive hearing loss and tinnitus. It has an autosomal dominant inheritance and can worsen with stress and hormonal changes like during pregnancy and menopause.

Stapedial otosclerosis is the most common type of otosclerosis. Here the lesion starts just in front of the oval window in an area called fistula ante fenestrae.

PTA shows loss of air conduction with air-bone gap, more for lower frequencies and Carhart's notch may be seen. Tympanometry shows an As type of tympanogram in which there is reduced compliance at or near the ambient air pressure.

Medical management with sodium fluoride is used in the active stage. Definitive treatment is stapedectomy/stapedotomy with the placement of a prosthesis. Carhart notch usually disappears after a successful stapedectomy.

Other options:

Option A: Hennebert sign is pressure-induced dizziness seen in patients with Superior semicircular canal dehiscence syndrome, congenital syphilis, and Méniére’s disease.

Option B: Compression of the facial nerve due to acoustic neuroma will result in hypoesthesia of the posterior wall of the external auditory canal. This is called the Hitzelberger sign.

Option D: The gurgling sound produced on pressing the swelling in the laryngocele is known as Bryce's sign.
questions.learning: Schwartze sign — The clinical scenario describes a 40-year-old female patient with mild, progressive, bilateral hearing loss, and a PTA showing Carhart's notch (dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz) are all suggestive of Otosclerosis and the classical sign…

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the type of hearing loss.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mixed hearing loss

The given audiogram is suggestive of left-sided mixed hearing loss.

Interpretation of the audiogram:

• Blue colour indicates the left ear.
• > indicates bone conduction (BC), and the threshold is >25 dB. Hence, BC is abnormal, which implies that the abnormality is in the sensorineural pathway.
• × indicates air conduction (AC), and the threshold is >15 dB. Hence, AC is abnormal.
• Both AC and BC are abnormal. It indicates sensorineural hearing loss.
• In addition, the air-bone gap is present, which implies conductive hearing loss.
• Hence, the interpretation is left-mixed hearing loss.

A mixed type of hearing loss presents with defects in both conductive and sensorineural pathways. This type of hearing loss is seen in chronic suppurative otitis media and otosclerosis.

questions.text: Which of the following positions of the appendix is likely to present with suprapubic pain in a patient with acute appendicitis? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Subcaecal

The subcaecal position is most likely to cause suprapubic pain among the given options. When the appendix is positioned below the cecum, it can extend inferiorly toward the pelvic brim. Inflammation in this position may spread downward, causing irritation to pelvic structures and resulting in suprapubic discomfort. This anatomical relationship explains why subcaecal appendicitis can present with symptoms similar to pelvic appendicitis.

questions.text: A 32-year-old male presents with a long history of nasal obstruction, which is worse during inspiration. On anterior rhinoscopy, no obvious growth is noted. During examination, when the cheek is pulled laterally, the obstruction improves and the patient breathes comfortably through the affected nostril. Which of the following forms the lateral boundary of the site of obstruction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Upper lateral cartilage

The above clinical scenario of a 32-year-old male, with nasal obstruction on normal anterior rhinoscopy, and a positive Cottle's Test (when the cheek is pulled laterally, the obstruction improves and the patient breathes comfortably through the affected nostril), which indicated that the site of obstruction was Internal nasal valve, the lateral boundary of this area is formed by the upper lateral cartilage.

The Internal Nasal valve is the narrowest portion of the nasal passage. It is bounded medially by the nasal septum, superiorly and laterally by the caudal margin of the upper lateral cartilage, and inferiorly by the floor of the piriform aperture. The nasal valve is the specific slit-like segment between the caudal margin of the upper lateral cartilage and the septum.

Conditions with a positive Cottle's test:

* Deviated nasal septum

* Collapsed nasal valve - causes snoring and sleep apnoea

* Valve stenosis

* Laterally: Lower border of upper lateral cartilage and fibrofatty tissue and anterior end of inferior turbinate

* Medially: Cartilaginous nasal septum

* Caudally: Floor of the pyriform aperture

The nasal valve is the narrowest part and offers maximum resistance to airflow

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: For a population of 10,000, what does a sex ratio of more than 1000 mean?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Males are less than 5000

For a population of 10000, if the sex ratio is more than 1000, it means males are less than 5000 i.e., less than half the population.

The sex ratio refers to the number of females per 1000 males. An ideal sex ratio would be 1000 which indicates the population comprises an equal number of males and females.

Sex ratio >1000 indicates that there are more females than males in a population. Sex ratio <1000 indicates that there are fewer females compared to males in the population.

Pearl PF0985: Sex Ratio

* It is the number of females per 1000 males.

* According to a census in 2011, the sex ratio in India was 940 females per 1000 males.

* Kerala currently holds a favorable sex ratio with values of 1084 females per 1000 men.

* The sex composition of the population is affected by the differentials in mortality conditions of males and females, sex-selective migration and the sex ratio at birth.

* A very low sex ratio indicates male-child favoritism.

questions.text: A 6-year-old boy presents with lower abdominal pain and diarrhoea. Stool examination reveals the findings shown below. Which organism is the most likely cause of this infection?
questions.explanation: The image displays an Entamoeba histolytica trophozoite, characterized by its distinctive central nucleus and potentially ingested red blood cells. This parasite is the causative agent of amoebic dysentery, which classically presents with lower abdominal pain, diarrhea, and bloody stools. Trophozoites cause significant tissue destruction in the colon, leading to characteristic "flask-shaped" ulcerations. Giardia lamblia (Option A) presents with non-bloody, greasy stools and has a "pear-shaped" trophozoite with two nuclei. Shigella dysenteriae (Option B) and Campylobacter jejuni (Option D) are bacterial causes of dysentery; while they present with similar symptoms, they would not show these characteristic large protozoal trophozoites on microscopic stool examination. Therefore, based on the specific protozoal morphology shown, Entamoeba histolytica is the definitive diagnosis

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During measurement of a rifled barrel weapon, the caliber depends on?
questions.explanation: In forensic ballistics, the caliber of a rifled firearm is defined as the internal diameter of the barrel. Specifically, for a rifled weapon, it is measured as the distance between two opposite lands (the raised portions of the rifling). The grooves (Option B) are the recessed portions; the distance between them would be slightly larger than the true caliber. The number of lead pellets (Option C) relates to the "gauge" or "bore" of a smooth-bore shotgun, not a rifled weapon. Mass and velocity (Option D) determine the kinetic energy and wounding potential of the projectile but do not define the weapon's caliber. Accurate caliber determination is essential for matching a fired bullet to a suspect firearm. Each firearm leaves unique land and groove impressions on the bullet, acting as a "ballistic fingerprint" that allows forensic experts to link evidence from a crime scene to a specific weapon

questions.text: Spanish windlass is a type of which strangulation method?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Garrotting

Spanish windlass is an improvised version of garrotting, and it involves tightening an iron collar (Spanish windlass) around the neck and forcing a spike against the neck into the spinal cord.

This was a form of judicial execution once employed in Spain. The rod-like object used to tighten the ligature is called a Spanish windlass; this may be a ruler, stick, or screwdriver.

Garrotting involves attacking the victim from behind using a ligature. The ligature is thrown over the victim’s neck and then tightened by twisting with a lever.

The image given below shows garrotting.

Option A: Squeezing to death using sticks is called bansdola. The neck or the chest is squeezed between two sticks, one placed in front, and one behind. The neck may also be squeezed with a single stick in front if the victim is lying down.

Option C: Squeezing the neck with the arm and forearm is called mugging. The image below shows mugging.

Option D: Throttling or manual strangulation occurs due to compression of the neck by humans leading to asphyxia. Thumb impression and finger marks may be seen over the victim's neck.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 30-year-old patient was brought to the emergency room by his relatives in a state of agitation, impaired judgment, and combativeness. His spot blood glucose level was 45 mg/dL. Yesterday, the patient went to the gym directly after work, following which he attended a party where he only consumed alcoholic beverages and skipped his meals. Which of the following is the likely cause of hypoglycemia in this patient?
options: Decreased NADH/NAD+ ratio leads to hypoglycemia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alcohol inhibits gluconeogenesis

The given clinical scenario of a patient who had a history of alcohol intake presenting with hypoglycemia is suggestive of alcohol (ethanol) intoxication that inhibits the process of gluconeogenesis.

Alcohol is metabolized in the liver via the enzymes alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase. These reactions convert ethanol to acetaldehyde and then to acetate, using NAD⁺ as a cofactor and producing NADH. The excess NADH shifts the balance of metabolic processes, diverting key substrates (like pyruvate and oxaloacetate) away from gluconeogenesis, thus impairing the liver's ability to produce glucose.

The patient skipped meals at the party, reducing dietary glucose intake, and making them reliant on the liver to maintain blood glucose levels via gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis.

His gym workout would have used up muscle glycogen, further increasing the body’s dependence on hepatic gluconeogenesis for glucose production. Since alcohol inhibits this process, it would exacerbate the hypoglycemia.

Other options:

Option A: Thiamine deficiency is not a cause of hypoglycemia but is responsible for causing Wernicke's encephalopathy as well as Korsakoff syndrome in alcoholics. It presents with ophthalmoplegia, confusion, and cerebellar ataxia.

Option C: The HMP shunt is an alternative pathway to glycolysis and is used to produce ribose-5-phosphate and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH). It doesn't cause hypoglycemia

Option D: Alcoholics tend to have an increased NADH/NAD ratio.

Correct answer: C. Anterior cerebral artery and anterior communicating artery

Blood is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery and anterior communicating artery as the marked structure is the anterior part of the corpus callosum.

Corpus callosum is the largest fibre pathway of the brain. The parts of the corpus callosum are the rostrum, genu, trunk or body, and splenium.

The anterior cerebral and anterior communicating artery give rise to anteromedial group which supplies the rostrum of the corpus callosum.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 20-year-old female patient presented to OPD with the given presentation. On examination, it seems gelatinous in consistency. She reports fluctuation in size, mild numbness in hand and occasional pain. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ganglion cyst

The history and image are suggestive of a patient with a ganglion cyst.

Ganglion cyst arises from the leakage of synovial fluid from a joint or tendon sheath and thus contains a glary, viscous fluid.

It can appear anywhere in the wrist but the most common area is the dorsal surface of the scapholunate ligament.

Patients usually present with painless, well-defined, cystic, transillumination-positive, and non-tender swelling. If there is an impingement on a nearby nerve or structure it can cause pain.

It disappears spontaneously, but the aspiration of the swelling or operative removal can be done for reassurance or when there is pressure on the nerve. Even if treatment is done, the rates of recurrence are high.

Other Options:

Option B: Lipomas are benign tumors of adipose tissue. It can occur anywhere and at any depth. It can be encapsulated or diffuse, superficial or deep. On examination, they are nontender and non-pulsatile. Because of the soft consistency, they may appear to be fluctuant but they are not. The slip sign is positive.

Option C: Dermoid Cyst presents as asymptomatic, slowly enlarging, painless, superficial localized swellings over the volar aspect of the hand, especially the distal portion of the digits.

Option D: An extremity hematoma is a localized collection of blood in the soft tissues of an extremity, typically occurring after trauma, surgery, or in patients with bleeding disorders. The hematoma can develop in various tissue planes: subcutaneous, intramuscular, or subfascial compartments.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Regarding the procedure done with the needle shown below, which of the following is false?
options: To be done in lateral recumbent position
The bevel should face upwards while inserting the needle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Coagulopathy is not a contraindication

The given image shows a Quincke-type lumbar puncture needle. Coagulopathy is a contraindication to perform lumbar puncture (LP).

Contraindications for LP include:

• Patients receiving anticoagulant or antiplatelet medications and those with coagulation defects
• Possible raised intracranial pressure
• Suspected spinal epidural abscess
• Infection at the site of puncture

Before performing an LP, it is important to assess the patient's bleeding risk by checking their platelet count, international normalized ratio (INR), and partial thromboplastin time (PTT). LP is considered contraindicated if the platelet count is less than 20,000/μL, and some institutions recommend a platelet count of greater than 40,000/μL before proceeding with the procedure.

Proper positioning of the patient is crucial for an LP. The patient should lie on their side away from the examiner, with their knees bent and pulled up toward the abdomen (lateral decubitus). The neck should be gently bent forward, and the shoulders and pelvis should be aligned vertically. LP is typically performed at or below the L3-L4 interspace, which can be identified by palpating the spinous processes and using a line drawn between the posterior superior iliac crests as a guide.

Alternatively, the LP can be done with the patient seated upright, leaning forward to flex the back. This position is suitable for obese patients.

After sterile preparation of the insertion site and the injection of a local anesthetic, the LP needle is inserted midline between two spinous processes, with the bevel parallel to the dural fibers facing upwards. The needle is advanced until the subarachnoid space (SAS) is reached indicated by a loss of resistance. Once the SAS is reached, the opening pressure is measured, and CSF is allowed to drip into collection tubes for analysis.

A traumatic tap may cause a bloody tap, which can be differentiated from subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) by examining the supernatant after centrifugation. Prior to needle removal, the stylet is reinserted to prevent nerve entrapment and the development of a dural CSF leak. There is no need for prolonged recumbency after the procedure to prevent post-LP headache.

Neuroimaging is recommended before performing an LP in patients who have an altered level of consciousness, focal neurological deficits, new-onset seizures, or papilledema. This is because these patients are at a higher risk of developing cerebellar or tentorial herniation, a rare but potentially fatal complication. Imaging studies should also include the spine in patients with symptoms suggestive of spinal cord compression, such as back pain, leg weakness, urinary retention, or incontinence. In cases where acute meningitis is suspected and neuroimaging is necessary before the LP, it is recommended to administer antibiotics, preferably after blood culture, before conducting the imaging study.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old chronic alcoholic man presents with altered consciousness, disorientation and severe agitation. He reports his last alcohol intake was 48 hours ago. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Delirium tremens

The clinical scenario of a 45-year-old chronic alcoholic man with altered consciousness, disorientation and severe agitation and his last alcohol consumption 48 hours ago points to delirium tremens.

Delirium tremens is a medical emergency that occurs during alcohol withdrawal. It is an acute condition and usually develops within 72 hours after the last drink. It has symptoms of both delirium and alcohol withdrawal. The clinical features of delirium tremens are:

* Altered sensorium with disorientation

* Perceptual distortions, most frequently tactile or visual hallucinations

* Autonomic hyperactivity with tachycardia, fever, anxiety, insomnia, and hypertension. And sweating

* Fluctuating levels of psychomotor activity, ranging from agitation to lethargy
Altered sleep-wake cycle

Wernicke’s encephalopathy (alcoholic encephalopathy) is associated with thiamine deficiency. Alcohol abuse may lead to thiamine deficiency because of poor nutritional habits or malabsorption. It is an acute neurological disorder characterised by:

* Global confusion

* Ocular abnormalities like horizontal nystagmus, gaze palsy, anisocoria, and sluggish pupillary reflex

* Ataxia—mainly affecting the gait

* Vestibular dysfunction

It may resolve with thiamine therapy or progress to Korsakoff's syndrome.

Other options:

Option B: Alcohol-induced psychosis is a severe mental condition triggered by excessive alcohol use, leading to hallucinations, delusions, and confusion. It typically occurs during withdrawal or chronic alcohol abuse and requires immediate medical intervention.

Option C: Opioid withdrawal can cause symptoms like drug craving, feelings of temperature change, musculoskeletal pain, and GI distress. Signs of opioid withdrawal include confusion, drowsiness, vomiting, and diarrhoea. It is not typically life-threatening, especially compared to alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, which can lead to seizures or delirium tremens. Hence, opioid withdrawal is rarely fatal.

Option D: Alcohol-induced hallucinations occur due to excessive alcohol use or withdrawal, causing false visual, auditory, or tactile perceptions. They are distinct from delirium tremens and can persist even with clear consciousness.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following stages of modern sewage treatment plants: 1. Use of Grit chamber 2. Use of Primary sedimentation tank 3. Screening 4. Use of Sludge digester What would be the correct sequence of the above stages?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3 → 1 → 2 → 4

Sewage treatment is the process of removing physical, chemical, and biological impurities from wastewater before its safe disposal or reuse. A modern sewage treatment plant follows a definite sequence of treatment steps: Screening → Grit Chamber → Primary Sedimentation Tank → Sludge Digester

• Stage 3: Screening

• Removes large floating materials such as rags, sticks, paper, plastics, and leaves using coarse and fine screens.

• Stage 1: Grit Chamber

• Removes heavy inorganic particles like sand, gravel, grit, and broken glass that could damage pumps and machinery.

• Stage 2: Primary Sedimentation Tank

• Allows suspended organic solids to settle as primary sludge, while scum floats and is removed.

• Stage 4: Sludge Digester

• Anaerobic digestion of sludge produces biogas (mainly methane) and stabilizes the sludge for safe disposal.
questions.learning: 3 → 1 → 2 → 4 Sewage treatment is the process of removing physical, chemical, and biological impurities from wastewater before its safe disposal or reuse.

questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 5-year- old child who presents with abdominal distension and a soft, fluctuant mass that is mobile perpendicular to the line of mesenteric attachment?
questions.explanation: The clinical sign described—a soft, fluctuant abdominal mass that is "mobile in a plane perpendicular to the line of attachment of the mesentery" (from right upper to left lower quadrant)—is pathognomonic for a Mesenteric Cyst, specifically a Chylolymphatic cyst (Option C) . This movement happens because the cyst is located between the layers of the small bowel mesentery. A peritoneal cyst (Option A) would not show this specific directional mobility. A lipoma (Option B) is a solid fatty mass and would not be fluctuant. A pseudocyst (Option D) is usually fixed in the retroperitoneum and follows an episode of pancreatitis, which is rare in a healthy 5-year-old. Chylolymphatic cysts are thin-walled lymphatic malformations that contain milky chyle. While often asymptomatic, they can cause pain or intestinal obstruction due to their size. The definitive treatment is surgical enucleation. Therefore, the characteristic mobility defines this congenital lymphatic anomaly

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following anti-tubercular drugs is associated with visual adverse effects?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ethambutol

Ethambutol is associated with ophthalmic toxicity.

Ethambutol inhibits arabinose transferase III, thereby decreasing arabinogalactan biosynthesis. This results in, disruption in mycobacterial cell wall synthesis. It is primarily excreted unchanged by kidneys and accumulation occurs in renal failure. Ethambutol does not undergo hepatic metabolism and can be safely prescribed for the treatment of TB in patients with hepatitis.

Optic neuritis resulting in decreased visual acuity and loss of ability to differentiate red from green is the most serious adverse effect of ethambutol. It is a dose-dependent adverse effect that can be unilateral or bilateral.

Tests of visual acuity and red-green discrimination before the start of therapy and periodically thereafter are recommended.

Orange urine, sweat, and tears. Flu-like symptoms with intermittent dosing.

The most hepatotoxic drug. It also causes hyperuricemia.

Optic neuritis and hence, not preferred in children.

Mechanism of resistance
