questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A virus exploits the neuron's intracellular transport machinery to travel from a peripheral nerve terminal back to the cell body, moving at approximately 200 mm/day along microtubules. Which motor protein mediates this movement, and which direction does it represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dynein — retrograde transport

Retrograde axonal transport carries materials from the nerve terminal back to the neuronal cell body along microtubules and is mediated by the motor protein dynein. This transport pathway is exploited by several neurotropic viruses, including Rabies, to reach the central nervous system after entering peripheral nerves.

Why not the other options?

• A. Kinesin — orthograde transport: Kinesin mediates anterograde (cell body → axon terminal) transport.
• C. Kinesin — retrograde transport: Kinesin does not mediate retrograde movement.
• D. Myosin — orthograde transport: Myosin functions primarily on actin filaments, not microtubule-based long-distance axonal transport.
questions.learning: Dynein — retrograde transport Retrograde axonal transport carries materials from the nerve terminal back to the neuronal cell body along microtubules and is mediated by the motor protein dynein.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presents with hyperthermia, autonomic instability, confusion, hyperreflexia, muscle rigidity, and dilated pupils. The patient takes sertraline and was recently prescribed amitryptiline and sumatriptan for depression and migraines, respectively. Which medication is most likely to be effective in treating this patient's current condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cyproheptadine

This patient with a history of depression treated with sertraline and now amitryptiline most likely has developed serotonin syndrome. Serotonin syndrome is treated with cyproheptadine (5-HT2 receptor antagonist). Cyproheptadine can effectively treat serotonin syndrome by blocking the effects of excess serotonin.

Serotonin syndrome is characterized by a triad of:

• Autonomic instability - hyperthermia, hypertension, tachycardia, diaphoresis, vomiting, diarrhea.
• Altered mental status - agitation, confusion, delirium.
• Neuromuscular hyperactivity - tremor, hyperreflexia, myoclonus.

Serotonin syndrome rarely occurs with a single serotonergic drug used at therapeutic doses. More commonly, it occurs due to the combined side effects with any drug that increases serum serotonin levels like MAOIs (monoamine oxidase inhibitors), SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors), SNRIs (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors), TCAs (tricyclic antidepressants), tramadol, ondansetron, triptans, linezolid, MDMA (amphetamine), dextromethorphan, etc.
questions.learning: Cyproheptadine — This patient with a history of depression treated with sertraline and now amitryptiline most likely has developed serotonin syndrome. Serotonin syndrome is treated with cyproheptadine (5-HT2 receptor antagonist).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A woman presents with fever after returning from a forest trip. On examination, a black eschar is seen on the abdomen/trunk. What is the drug of choice in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Doxycycline

In the above clinical scenario, a history of a forest trip followed by the development of a characteristic eschar at the bite site along with fever suggests a diagnosis of scrub typhus, which is treated with doxycycline.

Humans are infected when they are bitten by the mite larvae known as chiggers. The incubation period is 1-3 weeks. Patients develop a characteristic eschar at the site of the mite bite, along with regional lymphadenopathy and maculopapular rash. It can be associated with fever, headache, and conjunctival injection. Meningoencephalitis, myocarditis, and pneumonia can be seen in severe cases.

Oral doxycycline is given in uncomplicated scrub typhus. In pregnancy, oral azithromycin is preferred.

In scrub typhus, both the adult and nymphal stages of mites are free-living in nature; hence, they do not feed on vertebrate hosts. The larval stage (chigger) feeds on the vertebrate host and picks up the rickettsiae. Rodents are the mammalian reservoir for scrub typhus. Eschar can be seen in the image below:

Serologic assays are used for diagnosis. The Weil-Felix reaction is a heterophile agglutination reaction used for diagnosis, wherein the sera are tested for agglutinins to the O antigens of certain Proteus strains, OX19, OX2, and OXK. OXK is agglutinated only in scrub typhus.

Scrub typhus:

* Most widespread Rickettsial disease

* A mite is a vector

* Vector – Trombiculid Mite

* Causative agent – Rickettsia tsutsugamushi

* Incubation period – 10–12 days

* Typical clinical feature – Eschar

* Weil-Felix reaction is strongly positive with Proteus strain OXK

* Treatment – Tetracycline

Renal involvement is a common systemic manifestation of scrub typhus. The severity of renal involvement can range from minor urinary abnormalities such as albuminuria and active urinary sediments such as cellular casts, pyuria, and hematuria to acute kidney injury (AKI), necessitating the immediate initiation of renal replacement therapies.
questions.learning: Doxycycline — In the above clinical scenario, a history of a forest trip followed by the development of a characteristic eschar at the bite site along with fever suggests a diagnosis of scrub typhus, which is treated with doxycycline.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 7-month-old boy presented with a two-day history of fever and abscess over the neck. The mother reveals that the child had similar recurrent infections in the past. The dihydrorhodamine test (DHR) was found to be positive. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chronic granulomatous disease

The given clinical history of fever,abscess and recurrent infections in the past and positive dihydrorhodamine test (DHR) most likely suggests chronic granulomatous disease.

Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is an X-linked recessive disorder due to the deficiency in NADPH oxidase which is important in respiratory or oxidative bursts. In CGD, there is an increased risk of catalase-positive species (Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, Aspergillus spp, etc.) leading to granulomas. The condition usually manifests in the first year of life with recurrent pyogenic infections with catalase-positive organisms.

Patients have recurrent bacterial and fungal infections. The symptoms begin within the first two years of life, affecting the pulmonary, gastrointestinal, skin, and lymphatic drainage of these organs.

Nitroblue tetrazolium is used as a diagnostic test. The yellow-coloured Nitroblue tetrazolium dye is converted to a purple insoluble substance (positive) in the presence of oxidative burst by the free oxygen radicals so formed. A negative test (yellow color remains) is seen in CGD.

Individuals with CGD will exhibit diminished or absent fluorescence in the DHR test, indicating impaired ROS production by phagocytes. This result confirms the diagnosis of CGD and aids in distinguishing it from other conditions with similar symptoms. It can also assess the effectiveness of treatments like bone marrow transplantation or gene therapy in restoring normal phagocyte function.

Other options:

Option A) Chediak-Higashi syndrome is a primary immunodeficiency due to a disorder of the phagolysosome function of leukocytes, leading to delayed microbial clearance. In addition, there is a disorder of melanin (albinism), nerve defects, and bleeding disorders.

Option C) Severe combined immunodeficiency is a primary immunodeficiency with a disorder of both cellular and humoral immunity. Persons with SCID are susceptible to recurrent severe infections caused by a wide variety of pathogens and usually do not survive beyond the first year of life without a stem cell transplant.

Option D) Tuberculosis is a bacterial disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and is characterized by the formation of granulomas as an immune response to contain the infection. Tuberculosis presents with cavitary lesions in the upper lobes of the lungs. Histopathology reveals caseous necrosis with multinucleated giant cells. Common manifestations include fever, night sweats, anorexia, weakness, and weight loss. Blood investigations may reveal anemia with leukopenia, lymphopenia, neutrophilic leukocytosis, leukemoid reactions, and polycythemia.
questions.learning: Chronic granulomatous disease — The given clinical history of fever,abscess and recurrent infections in the past and positive dihydrorhodamine test (DHR) most likely suggests chronic granulomatous disease.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman with a history of two pregnancies—one delivered by cesarean section and one managed with dilation and curettage— presents with severe abdominal pain, hypotension, and tachycardia. On examination, fetal parts are palpable through the abdomen, and the fetal heart sounds are faint. Based on these clinical findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Uterine rupture is a catastrophic obstetric emergency. The patient has significant risk factors: a "previous Cesarean section" and "D&C" history, which weaken the uterine wall. The presentation of sudden severe abdominal pain, maternal shock (hypotension and tachycardia), and the pathognomonic finding of "palpable fetal parts in the abdomen" (outside the uterus) is diagnostic. Amniotic fluid embolization (Option A) usually presents with sudden cardiovascular collapse and coagulopathy, but not palpable fetal parts in the abdomen. Placental abruption (Option B) causes painful bleeding and uterine rigidity, but the fetus remains within the intact uterus. Local anesthesia anaphylaxis (Option D) is a systemic reaction occurring immediately after drug administration, unrelated to the physical findings described. Uterine rupture requires immediate resuscitative measures and emergency laparotomy to deliver the fetus and repair the uterus or perform a hysterectomy. The prognosis depends on the speed of intervention, as fetal mortality is high and maternal life is at grave risk
questions.learning: Uterine rupture is a catastrophic obstetric emergency. The patient has significant risk factors: a "previous Cesarean section" and "D&C" history, which weaken the uterine wall.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Consider the following statements about sympathetic, parasympathetic, and motor nerves. Which of the following statements are true?

1. Sympathetic efferents are distributed all over the body/ extensively whereas parasympathetic distribution is limited.
2. Sympathetic fibers travel long distances after leaving the sympathetic chain, before finally synapsing and then a shorter distance to effector organs.
3. Parasympathetic fibers travel a shorter distance to their respective ganglia which are located close to the target organs.
4. Motor neurons are located in the ventral horn of the spinal cord from where the axons come out and divide into several branches, each of which supplies an individual muscle fiber.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1,4

The true statements are 1,4.

Sympathetic efferents are distributed extensively all over the body whereas parasympathetic distribution is limited to head, neck, and trunk regions.

Sympathetic fibers travel short distances to the sympathetic ganglionic chain, before finally synapsing and then have a long course to supply the target organs. Parasympathetic fibers travel a longer distance to their respective ganglia which are located close to the target organs.

Motor neurons are located in the ventral horn of the spinal cord from where the axons come out and divide into several branches, each of which supplies an individual muscle fiber. A motor unit comprises a motor neuron and a group of skeletal muscle fibers it innervates.
questions.learning: Sympathetic efferents are distributed extensively all over the body whereas parasympathetic distribution is limited to head, neck, and trunk regions. Sympathetic fibers travel short distances to the sympathetic ganglionic chain, before finally synapsing…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A group of hostel boys consumed hamburgers from a local street food shop following which they developed abdominal pain, diarrhoea, vomiting, and fever. They were diagnosed with hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). Escherichia coli O157:H7 was detected in the stool samples and the ham. What does H represent in H7?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Flagella

H in E coli O157:H7 represents flagellar antigen.

O represents somatic antigen.

E. Coli O157:H7 is an enterohemorrhagic bacterial strain that causes hemorrhagic diarrhoea and cramping in the abdomen. It is transmitted through the fecal-oral route after consumption of contaminated, undercooked liquids and foods.

E. Coli O157:H7 uses the fimbriae to adhere to the microvilli of intestinal epithelial cells. When bacteria attach to an epithelial layer, they rearrange the cytoskeletal actin, which flattens the microvilli and interferes with normal intestinal cell function. This is known as an effacing lesion.

Three days after exposure to the contaminated food specimen, diarrhoea—often the hemorrhagic kind- occurs due to exposure to the Shiga toxin. The patients will experience bloody diarrhoea after three days of symptoms. After seven days, the symptoms of hemorrhagic diarrhoea usually go away on their own for 85% of patients; the remaining 15%, who are usually children, will experience systemic manifestations, most commonly HUS.

EHEC are gram-negative bacilli which are lactose fermenting. Unlike most other E. coli serotypes, O157: H7 does not use sorbitol and produces clear colonies on the Sorbitol MacConkey agar, whereas other serotypes produce pink colonies. O157: H7 is a strain of E.coli called enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) which produces verocytotoxin or Shiga-like-toxin. Shiga toxin acts by inactivating the 60s ribosomal subunit thereby inhibiting protein synthesis. It is absorbed from the inflamed gastrointestinal mucosa into the circulation and causes endothelial dysfunction, and causes platelet activation and aggregation. Children and older adults are at the highest risk. It causes mild non-bloody diarrhea to hemorrhagic colitis, or a severe form of dysentery, with hemolytic uremic syndrome, a disease resulting in acute renal failure, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia.
questions.learning: Flagella H in E coli O157:H7 represents flagellar antigen. Coli O157:H7 is an enterohemorrhagic bacterial strain that causes hemorrhagic diarrhoea and cramping in the abdomen.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the sequence of muscles forming the posterior abdominal wall from medial to lateral.
options: Psoas major, Psoas minor, Transversus abdominis, Quadratus lumborum
Psoas major, Psoas minor, Quadratus lumborum, Transversus abdominis
Psoas major, Quadratus lumborum, Transversus abdominis, Psoas minor
Psoas minor, Psoas major, Quadratus lumborum, Transversus abdominis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Psoas minor, Psoas major, Quadratus lumborum, Transversus abdominis

The posterior abdominal wall muscles, arranged from medial to lateral, are psoas minor (when present), psoas major, quadratus lumborum, and transversus abdominis. This anatomical relationship is important for interpreting cross-sectional imaging, understanding the spread of retroperitoneal infections, and performing retroperitoneal surgical approaches.

FMGE/NEET PG Pearl

• Medial → Lateral: Psoas minor → Psoas major → Quadratus lumborum → Transversus abdominis.
• Psoas minor is absent in \~40–60% of individuals and is a weak trunk flexor.
• Psoas major is the chief flexor of the hip and is innervated by L1–L3.
• Quadratus lumborum laterally flexes the trunk and fixes the 12th rib during respiration.
questions.learning: Psoas minor, Psoas major, Quadratus lumborum, Transversus abdominis The posterior abdominal wall muscles, arranged from medial to lateral, are psoas minor (when present), psoas major, quadratus lumborum, and transversus abdominis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
Serologic findings of a patient with hepatitis are given below.

HBsAg positive
Anti-HBc IgG positive
Anti-HDV IgM positive
Titer of HBV DNA - 7.4 X 108
Titer of HDV DNA - 4.1 X 104

Which of the following is most useful in diagnosing HDV superinfection over coinfection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anti-HBc IgG positivity

As anti-HBc IgG antibodies are representative of a chronic hepatitis B infection, their presence may be indicative of an HBV/HDV (hepatitis B/hepatitis D) superinfection.

HDV superinfection occurs when a person who is already chronically infected with HBV acquires HDV. The infection of HDV on chronic hepatitis B can accelerate the progression to severe disease in all ages. HDV superinfection accelerates progression to cirrhosis almost a decade earlier than HBV mono-infected persons.

HBV/HDV coinfection occurs when a person simultaneously becomes infected with both HBV and HDV. In acute hepatitis, simultaneous infection with HBV and HDV can lead to mild-to-severe hepatitis. The signs and symptoms typically appear 3–7 weeks after the initial infection and include fever, fatigue, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, dark urine, pale stools, jaundice (yellow eyes), and even fulminant hepatitis. However, recovery is usually complete.

Diagnosis of HDV infection is by detecting high levels of anti-HDV immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM). It is confirmed by the detection of HDV RNA in serum, and their levels are not helpful in differentiating between acute and chronic infections. There is no specific treatment for HDV infection. Pegylated interferon alpha may be used (with limited efficacy).

Anti-HBc IgM and anti-HBs IgM are indicative of acute phases of hepatitis B and, therefore, more likely to be associated with coinfection of HDV.
questions.learning: Anti-HBc IgG positivity As anti-HBc IgG antibodies are representative of a chronic hepatitis B infection, their presence may be indicative of an HBV/HDV (hepatitis B/hepatitis D) superinfection.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Regarding the speed of axonal transport, All of the following statements are correct except:
options: Fast anterograde (orthograde) transport occurs at a speed of approximately 200–400 mm/day
Retrograde axonal transport occurs at a speed of approximately 100–300 mm/day
Slow anterograde axonal transport occurs at a speed of approximately 1–5 mm/day
Retrograde axonal transport is slower than slow anterograde transport
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Retrograde axonal transport is slower than slow anterograde transport

Axonal transport moves materials between the neuronal cell body and axon terminals along microtubules using motor proteins.

Types of axonal transport:

●  Fast anterograde (orthograde) transport:

• Speed: \~200–400 mm/day
• Motor protein: Kinesin
• Carries synaptic vesicles, mitochondria, enzymes

● Retrograde transport:

• Speed: \~100–300 mm/day
• Motor protein: Dynein
• Carries endocytosed materials, growth factors, toxins, viruses back to the cell body

● Slow anterograde transport:

• Speed: \~1–5 mm/day
• Carries cytoskeletal proteins (actin, tubulin) Statement D is incorrect because retrograde transport is faster than slow anterograde transport.
questions.learning: Retrograde axonal transport is slower than slow anterograde transport Axonal transport moves materials between the neuronal cell body and axon terminals along microtubules using motor proteins.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 54-year-old man with resistant hypertension is started on an experimental drug that lowers blood pressure without affecting heart rate or cardiac output. It acts by selectively activating potassium channels in vascular smooth muscle, causing membrane hyperpolarization and relaxation. Chronic use leads to fluid retention and hypertrichosis. Which drug is responsible for these findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Minoxidil

Why: This vignette describes the classic pharmacologic profile of Minoxidil:

Mechanism: Minoxidil is a prodrug converted by hepatic sulfotransferase to minoxidil sulfate, its active form. Minoxidil sulfate opens ATP-sensitive potassium (K⁺-ATP) channels in vascular smooth muscle (predominantly arteriolar). This causes:

• K⁺ efflux → membrane hyperpolarization
• Hyperpolarization closes voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels → decreased intracellular Ca²⁺
• Result: smooth muscle relaxation → arteriolar vasodilation → ↓ BP

Key distinguishing features in this vignette:

• Hypertrichosis — a well-known, distinctive side effect of minoxidil (in fact, topical minoxidil is used clinically to treat androgenetic alopecia because of this very effect)
• Fluid/salt retention — occurs due to reflex activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) secondary to vasodilation, requiring co-administration with a diuretic
• Used for resistant/severe hypertension — minoxidil is a potent vasodilator reserved for refractory cases

Why not the others:

• A. Hydralazine — Also an arteriolar vasodilator causing reflex tachycardia and fluid retention, but its mechanism is not via K⁺ channels (more related to NO release/cGMP and interference with IP3-mediated Ca²⁺ release); classically causes a lupus-like syndrome, not hypertrichosis.
• C. Diazoxide — Also a K⁺-ATP channel opener causing vasodilation (used in hypertensive emergencies and as a treatment for hypoglycemia due to insulinoma via inhibition of insulin release), but it is not associated with hypertrichosis; more notably causes hyperglycemia.
• D. Nicorandil — A K⁺-ATP channel opener and nitric oxide donor, used for angina (not primarily hypertension); no hypertrichosis association.

High-yield takeaway:

• K⁺-ATP channel opener + hypertrichosis + fluid retention + used in resistant hypertension = Minoxidil. (Contrast with Diazoxide, which shares the mechanism but is used for hypertensive emergencies/hypoglycemia and lacks the hair growth side effect.)
questions.learning: Minoxidil Why: — This vignette describes the classic pharmacologic profile of Minoxidil: Mechanism: Minoxidil is a prodrug converted by hepatic sulfotransferase to minoxidil sulfate, its active form.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: An epidemiologist is studying changes in the population of a country with time. This process is called the demographic cycle. Which of the following options best defines the correct sequence of the phases of the demographic cycle?
options: High expanding→ Early stationary → Late expanding → Low stationary → Declining
High stationary → Early expanding → Late expanding → Low stationary → Declining
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. High stationary → Early expanding → Late expanding → Low stationary → Declining

The correct sequence of the phases of the demographic cycle is High stationary → Early expanding → Late expanding → Low stationary → Declining.

The demographic cycle is comprised of five stages and is as described below:

Stage 1: High stationary population - There is a high birth rate and a high death rate that cancel each other and the population remains stationary.

Stage 2: Early expanding population - There is a decline in the death rate that begins but the birth rate stays constant. Ex: Many countries in South Asia, and Africa are in this phase.

Stage 3: Late expanding population - There is a further fall in the death rate, with the birth rate beginning to fall. The population is still increasing due to a net increase in births. India has entered this phase.

Stage 4: Low stationary population - There is a low birth and low death rate, and this can result in a stationary population. It can also result in zero population growth like in Austria (1980-85). Other examples: the UK, Denmark, Sweden, Belgium recorded a growth rate of 0.1 in 1980-85. It has occurred in most industrialized countries as a demographic transition shifting from high birth and high death rates to low birth and low death rates.

Stage 5: Contracting population - The birth rate is lower than the death rate, causing population decline. Ex: East European countries like Germany, and Hungary.

India is currently in the "late expanding" stage which is the third stage in the demographic cycle where declining death rates and declining birth rates are seen.

Another important concept of the demographic cycle is the demographic gap which is the difference between birth rate and death rate. The demographic gap is maximum in the early-expanding phase, characterized by a high birth rate and low death rate. As the demography of the country transitions to the late-expanding phase, both birth rate and death rate falls causing a decreasing demographic gap. Although the birth rate is falling in the late-expanding phase, it is still higher than the death rate, which causes the population to increase.

Pearl PF2298: Demographic Process and Cycle

Stages of the demographic cycle include:

* Stage 1 - High stationary

* High birth rates and high death rates render the population stationary

* Narrow demographic gap

* Stage 2 - Early expanding

* The death rate declines and the birth rate remains unchanged

* The demographic gap starts increasing and becomes maximum

* Stage 3 - Late expanding

* Death rate declines further and birth rate falls

* India is in this stage, currently

* The demographic gap starts declining

* Stage 4 - Low stationary

* Low birth rate and low death rate renders the population stationary

* Narrow demographic gap

* Stage 5 - Declining

* The population begins to decline as the birth rate is lower than the death rate

* The demographic gap is negative
questions.learning: High stationary → Early expanding → Late expanding → Low stationary → Declining The correct sequence of the phases of the demographic cycle is High stationary → Early expanding → Late expanding → Low stationary → Declining.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Of the following, all are findings of the condition in the below chest x-ray except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Right atrial enlargement

The given chest x-ray shows an egg-on-string appearance seen in the transposition of great arteries (TGA). Enlargement of the left atrium is seen in TGA, not the right atrium.

The reason for left atrial enlargement is due to increased pulmonary blood flow.

TGA is characterized by the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle. This abnormal configuration leads to a narrow vascular pedicle.

As pulmonary vascular resistance drops during the first few days of life, blood flow through the pulmonary vasculature is increased. There is also elevated pulmonary venous pressure seen in TGA, especially in infants with an intact interventricular septum.

The globular (egg) appearance of the heart due to abnormal convexity of the right atrial border and left atrial enlargement, and the narrow superior mediastinum (string) result in the classical egg-on-string appearance.

TGA is the most specific heart disease in infants of diabetic mothers.

Early management includes an immediate infusion of prostaglandin E1 which keeps the ductus arteriosus patent for improving oxygenation. Rashkind balloon atrial septostomy is a palliative catheter-based intervention that can be done to improve the hypoxic state before definitive surgery. The procedure creates an opening in the atrial septum which allows better inter-circulatory mixing of the blood. Jatene arterial switch procedure is the definitive surgery.

Most infants with TGA do not survive till adulthood without corrective surgery.
questions.learning: Right atrial enlargement — The given chest x-ray shows an egg-on-string appearance seen in the transposition of great arteries (TGA). Enlargement of the left atrium is seen in TGA, not the right atrium.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: All are the symptoms of Gaisböck syndrome except?
questions.explanation: Gaisböck syndrome, also known as stress polycythemia or relative polycythemia, is a condition characterized by a pseudo-elevation in the hematocrit. Unlike Polycythemia Vera, the total red cell mass is actually normal; however, the "plasma volume" is significantly reduced, leading to hemoconcentration and a high hematocrit (erythrocytosis, Option B). This syndrome is typically seen in middle-aged, hard-driving, anxious men who are "obese" (Option D) and have a history of smoking and "hypertension." Therefore, hypotension (low blood pressure) is NOT a feature; in fact, hypertension is a defining characteristic of Gaisböck syndrome. The leukocyte counts (Option C) and platelet counts are typically normal, which helps distinguish it from true myeloproliferative disorders like Polycythemia Vera where these are often elevated. Management primarily involves addressing the underlying lifestyle factors, such as weight loss, smoking cessation, and blood pressure control, rather than phlebotomy. Thus, hypertension, not hypotension, is the hallmark clinical finding

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl presents in OPD with complaints of cyclical pain in abdomen. On examination, a suprapubic bulge can be seen in the pelvic area. PR examination reveals a swelling in the anterior aspect. On genital examination (if performed), a bluish bulging hymenal membrane is seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Transverse vaginal septum above the vagina
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Imperforate hymen

Cyclical pain with outflow obstruction and suprapubic bulge plus PR swelling along the anterior wall indicate hematocolpos due to imperforate hymen (cryptomenorrhea). Transverse septum and vaginal atresia present differently and do not show a tense bulging hymen. It is the most common obstructive anomaly of the female genital tract. Normally the hymen perforates before birth.

In imperforate hymen:

Hymenal membrane fails to perforate

↓

Menstrual blood cannot exit

↓

Blood accumulates in vagina

↓

Hematocolpos

| Feature | Reason

| ------- | ------

| Primary amenorrhea | Menstrual blood cannot exit

| Cyclical abdominal pain | Uterine contractions during menses

| Suprapubic mass | Accumulated blood

| Bluish bulging hymen | Blood behind hymen

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Prolonged exposure to high partial pressure of oxygen causes pulmonary capillary endothelial damage, leading to alveolar inflammation and edema. This phenomenon is known as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lorrain–Smith effect

Lorrain–Smith effect refers to pulmonary oxygen toxicity caused by prolonged exposure to high partial pressures of oxygen (hyperoxia).

• Excess oxygen leads to formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS).
• ROS cause damage to pulmonary capillary endothelium and alveolar epithelium.
• This results in alveolar inflammation, pulmonary edema, and decreased lung compliance.

Clinical settings:

• Prolonged oxygen therapy
• Hyperbaric oxygen exposure
• Diving or high-pressure environments

Other effects:

A. Paul Bert effect: CNS oxygen toxicity → seizures due to high oxygen pressure.

C. Bohr effect: Effect of CO₂ and pH on hemoglobin oxygen affinity.

D. Haldane effect: Oxygenation of hemoglobin reduces CO₂ carrying capacity.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A middle-aged man with diabetes presents with progressive visual impairment. Fluorescein angiography findings are available for evaluation. Based on the typical angiographic features seen in such cases, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) is the advanced stage of diabetic eye disease. The hallmark of PDR is "neovascularization"—the growth of new, fragile blood vessels from the retina into the vitreous. On fluorescein angiography (FA), these new vessels are identified by an intense, late-phase leakage of fluorescein dye because they lack a proper blood-retinal barrier. Options A and B (NPDR) are characterized by microaneurysms, hemorrhages, and exudates but not the growth of new vessels. Option C (Birdshot choroidopathy) is a rare autoimmune uveitis with different clinical features. PDR is caused by widespread retinal ischemia, which triggers the release of Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF). These new vessels can lead to vitreous hemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment, resulting in severe vision loss. Treatment involves Pan-Retinal Photocoagulation (PRP) or anti-VEGF injections to induce regression of the neovascularization and prevent blindness
questions.learning: Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) is the advanced stage of diabetic eye disease. The hallmark of PDR is "neovascularization"—the growth of new, fragile blood vessels from the retina into the vitreous.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A surgeon sees a necrotic bowel when operating on a child for an inguinal hernia. What is true about the resection and anastomosis of the bowel?
options: The surgeon must use chromic catgut
The surgeon must not include the submucosa in the sutures
The surgeon must use the single-layer, extramucosal suture technique
The surgeon must use the single-layer seromuscular suture technique
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The surgeon must use the single-layer, extramucosal suture technique

The standard technique used currently for resection anastomosis of the bowel is a one-layer extra mucosal suture technique since it causes the least tissue necrosis and luminal narrowing. Interrupted and continuous single-layer suture techniques are adequate and safe.

The extra mucosal suture must also include the submucosa because this layer has a high collagen content and it is the most stable suture layer in all sections of the gastrointestinal tract.

Catgut has now been replaced with absorbable synthetic polymers. Stapling devices can be used when speed is required.
questions.learning: The surgeon must use the single-layer, extramucosal suture technique The standard technique used currently for resection anastomosis of the bowel is a one-layer extra mucosal suture technique since it causes the least tissue necrosis and luminal narrowing.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In an experiment, a value of 39 was mistakenly recorded as 93. Which of the following statistical measures is most likely to be affected by this error?
options: Mean will remain same, median will increase
Mean and median both will increase
Mean will increase, median will remain same
Both mean and median will decrease
questions.explanation: In biostatistics, the mean is highly sensitive to extreme values (outliers) because it is calculated by summing all values and dividing by the total number. Recording 93 instead of 39 significantly increases the total sum, which directly causes the mean to increase. Conversely, the median is a "robust" measure of central tendency representing the middle value in a sorted data set. As long as both 39 and 93 are positioned on the same side of the middle value (e.g., both are larger than the median), replacing one with the other does not change the central rank; thus, the median remains the same. Option B is incorrect because the median is rarely affected by single errors at the extreme ends. Options A and D are mathematically incorrect based on these properties. This concept is critical for researchers, emphasizing why the median is often a better measure of central tendency for skewed data sets containing outliers or recording errors
questions.learning: In biostatistics, the mean is highly sensitive to extreme values (outliers) because it is calculated by summing all values and dividing by the total number.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with pain along the lateral aspect of the thigh. What is the root value of this nerve?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. L2-L3

Pain along the lateral aspect of the thigh with sensory symptoms indicates involvement of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.

This nerve arises from L2–L3 roots, passes under the inguinal ligament near ASIS, and is commonly compressed causing meralgia paresthetica.

It is a purely sensory nerve, with no motor deficit, helping distinguish it from femoral or obturator nerve lesions.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the grip in the image given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pawlik grip

Leopold's third maneuver (also called the Pawlik’s grip) is performed by grasping with the thumb and fingers, the lower portion of the maternal abdomen just above the symphysis pubis. If the presenting part is not engaged, a movable mass will be felt.

Abdominal palpation- Leopold maneuvers:

In the abdominal examination, the mother is made to lie supine and comfortably positioned with her abdomen barred. Leopold maneuvers can be performed throughout the latter months of pregnancy and during and between the contractions of labor.

Leopold's maneuvers may be difficult if not impossible to perform and interpret if the patient is obese, if the amnionic fluid volume is excessive, or if the placenta is anteriorly implanted.

With experience, it is possible to estimate the size of the fetus.

1. 1st Leopold (fundal grip): identifies which fetal pole (cephalic or podalic) occupies the uterine fundus. The fetal head is hard and round and is more mobile and ballotable whereas the breech is felt as a large, soft and irregular mass.
2. 2nd Leopold (lateral/umbilical grip): palms are placed on either side of the abdomen and gentle, but deep pressure is exerted. The back is felt as a hard and resistant structure. The fetal limbs are felt as numerous, small, irregular parts. By noting whether the back is directed anteriorly, transversely or posteriorly, the fetal orientation can be determined.
3. 3rd Leopold (pawlik's grip): it aids in confirmation of fetal presentation. In transverse lie, pawlik's grip is empty.
4. 4th Leopold (pelvic grip): it helps to determine the degree of descent.
questions.learning: Pawlik grip Leopold's third maneuver (also called the Pawlik’s grip) is performed by grasping with the thumb and fingers, the lower portion of the maternal abdomen just above the symphysis pubis.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: The mask given below works on which of the following principles?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bernoulli principle

The given image shows a Venturi mask and it works using the Bernoulli principle in delivering a predetermined and fixed concentration of oxygen to the patient.

In the Venturi mask ,the size of the constriction present in the device determines the final concentration of oxygen for a given gas flow. This is achieved in spite of the patient's respiratory pattern by providing a higher gas flow than the peak inspiratory flow rate.

Patients with COPD require greater FiO2 than those provided by low-flow devices and are ideal candidates for the use of a Venturi mask.

In the Venturi mask system, oxygen inflow is connected to a specific color-coded entrainment device at the base of the mask that provides a set Fio2 at a set oxygen inflow rate. Various entrainment devices can provide a Fio2 of 0.24 to 0.5, with an oxygen inflow of 4 to 15 l/min and a delivered total flow of 35 to 45 l/min.
questions.learning: Bernoulli principle — The given image shows a Venturi mask and it works using the Bernoulli principle in delivering a predetermined and fixed concentration of oxygen to the patient.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient with CSOM presented to the OPD with seizures, headache, vomiting and photophobia. On eye examination, homonymous hemianopia was noted. CT brain showed the following findings. Identify the condition. Chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Temporal lobe abscess

The clinical vignette depicting features of seizures, headache, vomiting, and photophobia in a patient with a chronic ear infection and the CT image showing a ring-enhancing lesion point to a diagnosis of a temporal lobe abscess.

Temporal lobe abscess is an intracranial complication that can arise from chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM).

Brain abscess typically progresses through 4 stages.

* The first stage is the stage of invasion (initial encephalitis), which often goes unnoticed. Symptoms such as headache, malaise, low-grade fever, and drowsiness may be present.

* The second stage is the stage of localization (latent abscess), during which a capsule forms around the abscess, effectively localizing the pus.

* The third stage is the stage of enlargement (manifest abscess). The abscess enlarges, leading to increased intracranial pressure (ICP) and the development of edema surrounding the abscess. As a result, symptoms worsen.

* The final stage is the stage of termination (rupture of abscess). At this point, the abscess expands and eventually ruptures into the ventricle or subarachnoid space, which can result in potentially fatal meningitis.

Characteristic findings associated with temporal lobe abscess include nominal aphasia, homonymous hemianopia, seizures, contralateral motor paralysis, pupillary changes, and oculomotor palsy. Signs of raised ICP like headache, nausea, vomiting, lethargy, drowsiness, confusion, papilledema, and coma may also be seen.

The preferred diagnostic imaging modality for temporal lobe abscess is a CT scan of the brain. This imaging study reveals a ring-enhancing lesion indicative of a brain abscess.

Medical treatment involves initiating intravenous antibiotics, typically metronidazole. Raised ICP can be addressed using dexamethasone or mannitol. Surgical intervention is the definitive management and involves drainage of the abscess followed by radical mastoidectomy to address the underlying CSOM.

Other options:

Option B: Cerebellar abscess is a form of brain abscess and is usually associated with an otogenic source of infection. It can occur as a direct extension through Trautmann's triangle or via retrograde thrombophlebitis.

An MRI image showing cerebellar abscess is given below:

Option C: Subdural abscess refers to the focal collection of purulent material between the dura mater and the arachnoid mater.

An MRI image showing subdural abscess is given below:

Option D: Meningitis is the inflammation of the leptomeninges which includes the arachnoid mater and pia mater. It can be due to an infectious or noninfectious etiology. It presents with fever, vomiting, neck stiffness, and signs of meningeal irritation. Ring-enhancing lesion on neuroimaging is not a feature of meningitis.
questions.learning: Temporal lobe abscess — The clinical vignette depicting features of seizures, headache, vomiting, and photophobia in a patient with a chronic ear infection and the CT image showing a ring-enhancing lesion point to a diagnosis of a temporal lobe abscess.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the type of ulcer shown in the image below:
questions.explanation: The image depicts a characteristic trophic ulcer, also known as a pressure or neurotrophic ulcer, typically located on weight-bearing areas such as the heel or the ball of the foot. These ulcers result from repeated trauma to a denervated or insensitive limb, commonly seen in patients with peripheral neuropathy due to diabetes mellitus or leprosy. Trophic ulcers are characterized by a punched-out appearance with a thickened, hyperkeratotic rim of skin. While diabetic patients often develop these (Option D), "trophic ulcer" is the specific clinical term for the lesion's pathophysiology regarding nerve loss. Arterial ulcers (Option A) usually occur on distal points like toes and are extremely painful with "dry" gangrene. Venous ulcers (Option B) typically appear in the "gaiter area" above the medial malleolus and are associated with hyperpigmentation and edema. Because this lesion is specifically situated on the pressure-bearing heel with callous formation, it is best classified as a trophic ulcer

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following laryngeal cartilages is least likely to be calcified?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Epiglottis

Epiglottis is unlikely to be calcified as it is made up of elastic cartilage.

Only hyaline cartilages can undergo ossification (calcifications on x-ray). It between the ages of 25-65y. These calcifications may be confused with foreign bodies of esophagus or larynx on x-rays.

The hyaline laryngeal cartilages are:

* Thyroid

* Cricoid

* Most of arytenoid.

The elastic laryngeal cartilages are:

* Epiglottis

* Corniculate

* Cuneiform

* Tip of arytenoid.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the surest sign of wound dehiscence?
questions.explanation: Abdominal wound dehiscence, or "burst abdomen," is a serious surgical complication where the fascial closure fails. As discussed in Q.199, the surest clinical sign of impending or actual dehiscence is the sudden, profuse discharge of pinkish, serosanguinous fluid from the wound. This "salmon-pink" drainage represents peritoneal fluid leaking through a compromised fascial layer and is often described by patients as a feeling that "something gave way" during coughing or straining. Infection (Option B) is a risk factor for dehiscence but not a diagnostic sign of the dehiscence itself. Hypotension (Option C) and rebound tenderness (Option D) are signs of systemic sepsis or peritonitis, which can complicate but do not define the mechanical failure of the wound. Recognizing serosanguinous discharge is vital, as it often precedes the physical evisceration of bowel loops. Treatment involves immediate protection of the wound with sterile saline-soaked dressings followed by an urgent return to the operating room for a formal re-closure, typically using non-absorbable tension sutures

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A resident is evaluating a patient, who presented with acute onset of chest pain and dyspnea, for pulmonary embolism. Which of the following imaging test should be performed to confirm this diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CT pulmonary angiography

CT pulmonary angiography should be performed as it is the principal imaging test for the diagnosis of pulmonary embolism (PE).

Option A: Most patients with acute PE have normal echocardiograms. However, echocardiography is a very useful diagnostic tool for detecting conditions that may mimic PE, such as acute myocardial infarction, pericardial tamponade, and aortic dissection.

Option C: Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan is now considered a second-line test for diagnosing PE. It is mainly used when CT findings are inconclusive or the patient cannot receive intravenous contrast.

Option D: MR pulmonary angiography may detect large proximal PE but is not reliable for smaller segmental and subsegmental PE. It is used when neither CT angiography nor ventilation-perfusion scan can be done.

The images below demonstrate a pulmonary embolus (marked by arrows). The image of the gross specimen shows saddle thromboembolism.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Myosin ceases to be in contact with actin filaments as a result of:
options: Cessation of calcium release from sarcoplasm
Attachment of ATP to myosin head
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Attachment of ATP to myosin head

Myosin ceases to be in contact with actin filaments as a result of the attachment of ATP to the myosin head.

Muscle contraction occurs by sliding of thin filament over thick filament. The sequence of events are as follows:

•  Troponin I is bound to actin and tropomyosin and covers the sites where actin interacts with myosin heads in a resting muscle. The myosin head contains tightly bound adenosine phosphate (ADP) and inorganic phosphate (Pi).
• Following an action potential, cytosolic Ca2+ is increased due to the Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.  Simultaneously Ca2+ influx happens through voltage-gated Ca2+ channels too.
• The free Ca2+ binds with troponin C. This binding will weaken the troponin I interaction with actin and exposes the actin-binding site for myosin.
• This results in the formation of myosin-actin cross-bridges.
• The cross-bridge between the head of the myosin and the active site of the actin causes a conformational change in the head and the power stroke occurs, moving the thin filament relative to the thick filament.
• Once the head of the cross-bridge tilts, the ADP and phosphate ion that were previously attached to the head are released and a new ATP molecule can bind in that place.
• The binding of the new ATP molecule to the free site on the myosin causes detachment of the head of the myosin from the actin.
• ATP is hydrolyzed and Pi released, causing a re-cocking of the myosin head and completing the cycle.
questions.learning: Attachment of ATP to myosin head Myosin ceases to be in contact with actin filaments as a result of the attachment of ATP to the myosin head. Muscle contraction occurs by sliding of thin filament over thick filament.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: True statement regarding Ayushman Bharat scheme?
options: Rs 5 lakh/per family per year is given
Rs 10 lakh/per family per year is given
Rs 6 lakh/per family per year is given
Rs 2 lakh/per family per year is given
questions.explanation: The Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY) is the world's largest government-funded healthcare program. Its primary feature is providing a health cover of Rs 5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary care hospitalization. This benefit is available to over 12 crore poor and vulnerable families based on Socio-Economic Caste Census (SECC) data. Options B (10 lakh), C (6 lakh), and D (2 lakh) are incorrect amounts for the standard annual coverage. The scheme is "portable," meaning a beneficiary can receive treatment in any empaneled public or private hospital across India. It covers pre-hospitalization, medicines, and post-hospitalization expenses. The program aims to reduce catastrophic out-of-pocket expenditure that often pushes families into poverty. By providing cashless and paperless access to services, Ayushman Bharat is a critical step toward achieving Universal Health Coverage in India, specifically targeting the bottom 40% of the population
questions.learning: The Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY) is the world's largest government-funded healthcare program. Its primary feature is providing a health cover of Rs 5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary care hospitalization.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman with a history of lower segment cesarean section (LSCS) presents with her fetus in the occiput posterior (OP) position. What is the most appropriate management strategy in this case?
questions.explanation: A woman with a previous lower segment cesarean section (LSCS) can be offered a trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC) if there are no contraindications. The presence of a fetus in the occiput posterior (OP) position is not an absolute indication for cesarean section. OP position is relatively common during labor, and in many cases, the fetal head rotates spontaneously to occiput anterior, allowing successful vaginal delivery. Although OP position may be associated with prolonged labor, back pain, and increased need for assistance, it does not preclude a trial of vaginal birth. Continuous fetal monitoring and careful observation for scar integrity are essential due to the history of LSCS. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Cesarean section: Reserved for complications like fetal distress, failed labor, or scar dehiscence, not just OP position. (C) External cephalic version: Used for breech presentation, not for OP position. (D) Vacuum-assisted delivery: Considered only in the second stage of labor if descent is inadequate, not as an initial approach. Thus, trial of normal vaginal delivery is the most appropriate management
questions.learning: A woman with a previous lower segment cesarean section (LSCS) can be offered a trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC) if there are no contraindications.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A woman presented with confusion, constipation, and headache. Serum calcium was 13.1mg/dL and ALP was elevated. She was diagnosed with primary hyperparathyroidism. Which of the following is the imaging of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sestamibi scan

Sestamibi scan is the imaging of choice to delineate parathyroid abnormalities.

Sestamibi is a monovalent lipophilic cation. It shows passive diffusion across cell membranes and accumulates in mitochondria. Because of its accumulation in the mitochondria, there is a difference in the rate at which it gets washed out depending upon the number of mitochondria in each tissue.

In parathyroid adenomas, there is a high concentration of oxyphilic cells with high mitochondrial content. The three protocols for sestamibi scanning are:

• Single-isotope dual-phase scan
• Dual-isotope subtraction imaging
• Single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT).

SPECT is commonly used because of its improved spatial resolution. Sestamibi combined with CT can be used to detect smaller parathyroid tissues.

Other imaging modalities for parathyroid localization:

• Ultrasonography:

• It is inexpensive and noninvasive
• Mediastinal parathyroid tissue cannot be detected because USG cannot penetrate the sternum or clavicles.

• Four-dimensional CT:

• It has a very high sensitivity
• Increased radiation exposure than other routine modalities is a potential disadvantage

• Selective venous sampling for PTH can be used for the exact localization of adenomas
questions.learning: Sestamibi scan Sestamibi scan is the imaging of choice to delineate parathyroid abnormalities. Sestamibi is a monovalent lipophilic cation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old man is evaluated for abdominal pain. Contrast-enhanced CT imaging reveals an abnormal finding marked by an arrow. Based on this radiological feature, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The axial Contrast-Enhanced Computed Tomography (CECT) scan shows renal tissue crossing the midline anterior to the aorta and vertebral column, connecting the lower poles of both kidneys. This "isthmus" of tissue is the definitive diagnostic feature of a Horseshoe Kidney (Option B). Appendicitis (Option A) would show a thickened, blind-ending tubular structure in the right iliac fossa, not renal tissue crossing the aorta. Wilms Tumor (Option C) is a large, distorted renal mass primarily seen in children, not a symmetrical fusion anomaly. An abdominal aortic aneurysm (Option D) would show an enlarged, dilated aorta often with mural thrombus, which is unrelated to renal fusion. Although often asymptomatic, horseshoe kidneys can cause abdominal pain if there is associated hydronephrosis or stone formation. Therefore, the anatomical bridge of renal parenchyma across the great vessels identifies this fused renal state
questions.learning: The axial Contrast-Enhanced Computed Tomography (CECT) scan shows renal tissue crossing the midline anterior to the aorta and vertebral column, connecting the lower poles of both kidneys.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A woman presents to the gynecology OPD with foul-smelling frothy vaginal discharge, severe itching, and a strawberry cervix on examination. Which statement regarding the causative organism is incorrect?
options: It exists in cyst and trophozoite form
The gold standard for diagnosis is culture on CPLM or PEM
The treatment of choice is metronidazole
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of frothy vaginal discharge and a "strawberry cervix" is pathognomonic for trichomoniasis, caused by the flagellated protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis. A key biological characteristic of T. vaginalis is that it exists ONLY in the trophozoite form and does not have a cyst stage. It is an obligate parasite (Option B) that cannot survive long outside the human body. The gold standard for definitive diagnosis remains culture on specialized media such as Diamond's, CPLM, or PEM (Option C). The treatment of choice is indeed Metronidazole (Option D), and it is essential to treat sexual partners simultaneously. Therefore, the statement regarding a cyst form is incorrect as it applies to other protozoa like Entamoeba or Giardia, but not to Trichomonas
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of frothy vaginal discharge and a "strawberry cervix" is pathognomonic for trichomoniasis, caused by the flagellated protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Anti-nuclear antibodies are required for the diagnosis of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Systemic lupus erythematosus

Antinuclear antibodies (ANAs) are required for the diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus.

ANAs are autoantibodies that bind to the contents of the cell nucleus. They are present in > 95% of patients with SLE. A positive antinuclear antibody ( ANA ) test with a titer of at least 1:80 is the obligatory entry criterion along with the additive criteria in 7 clinical and 3 immunologic domains. If a total of >10 points achieved, it is indicative of SLE according to 2019 EULAR/ACR Classification Criteria for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)

Most sensitive antibody for SLE: ANA

Most specific antibody for SLE: Anti smith > Anti dsDNA
ANA may also be positive in the other options but it is not a criterion for diagnosis of these conditions.

The following antibodies are specific for their respective autoimmune conditions.

• Scleroderma (option A): Anti-topoisomerase I(Scl-70) and anti-centromere antibodies highly specific for Systemic sclerosis.
• Rheumatoid arthritis (option C): RF and anti-CCP antibodies
• Sjogren syndrome (option D): Anti-Ro, Anti-La
questions.learning: Systemic lupus erythematosus Antinuclear antibodies (ANAs) are required for the diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus. ANAs are autoantibodies that bind to the contents of the cell nucleus.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements with regard to Ice-Lined Refrigerator (ILR) employed for storing vaccines at the sub-district level: I. These types of refrigerators are top-opening. II. Based on the temperature zone, the inside of ILRs can be divided into 3 parts. III. The upper part of ILR is cooler compared to the lower part. IV. Vaccines should never be kept directly on the floor of the ILR as they can get damaged. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I and IV

An Ice-Lined Refrigerator (ILR) is the standard vaccine storage equipment used at Primary Health Centres (PHCs), Community Health Centres (CHCs), and sub-district health facilities under the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP). It maintains a temperature of +2°C to +8°C to preserve vaccine potency.

Why are I and IV correct?

• I. ILRs are top-opening refrigerators: Cold air is retained when the lid is opened, minimizing temperature fluctuations.
• IV. Vaccines should never be kept directly on the floor of the ILR: The floor is the coldest part due to the ice lining, and freeze-sensitive vaccines may be damaged if placed directly on it. Vaccines should always be stored in baskets.

Why are II and III incorrect?

• II. The inside of an ILR can be divided into 3 temperature zones: ILRs are generally considered to have two temperature zones (colder bottom and relatively warmer upper portion), not three.
• III. The upper part of the ILR is cooler than the lower part: The lower part is colder, while the upper part is relatively warmer because the ice lining is present along the walls and bottom.
questions.learning: I and IV — An Ice-Lined Refrigerator (ILR) is the standard vaccine storage equipment used at Primary Health Centres (PHCs), Community Health Centres (CHCs), and sub-district health facilities under the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A female patient presents with severe restlessness, palpitations, and tremors to the emergency department. She is a known case of bronchial asthma. On examination, the neck looks swollen. Blood pressure is elevated, and tachycardia is noted. ECG shows atrial fibrillation. Which of the following drugs is used for immediate management in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Diltiazem

The given clinical scenario suggests the diagnosis of thyroid storm/thyroid crisis presenting with atrial fibrillation, and the immediate management in this patient is to rate control the arrhythmia with diltiazem (calcium channel blocker).

Thyroid storm/Thyrotoxic crisis is a rare but severe life-threatening complication of hyperthyroidism induced by the release of excessive thyroid hormones.

It is caused by abrupt cessation of antithyroid medications, infection, inadequately prepared hyperthyroid patient for thyroidectomy, amiodarone administration, exposure to iodinated contrast agents, and following radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy.

Features:

• Fever and severe dehydration
• Cardiovascular: Circulatory collapse, palpitations, tachycardia, cardiac arrhythmias, and cardiac failure
• GI symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice
• Neurological symptoms: Restlessness, irritability, delirium, tremor, convulsions, and coma

Treatment:

• If the patient presents with atrial fibrillation, the first step in the management is to do rate control using beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin, or amiodarone. Since this patient is a known asthmatic, beta-blockers (propranolol and esmolol) are contraindicated. So, a calcium channel blocker (diltiazem) is the preferred drug for immediate management in this patient.
• Supportive measures – rehydration by proper fluid therapy, tepid sponging, and cooling blankets.
• Thionamides like propylthiouracil (PTU) or methimazole or carbimazole can be used. PTU (Option D) is the drug of choice in thyroid storm, but it is given only after controlling atrial fibrillation.
• Lugol’s iodide is given one hour after intake of thionamides. They inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis by Wolff- Chaikoff effect.
• Glucocorticoids – reduce the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 and controls the shock.
• Digoxin and cardiac monitoring are crucial.

Other options:

Options B & C: Beta-blockers like propranolol and esmolol are contraindicated in bronchial asthma patients.
questions.learning: Diltiazem — The given clinical scenario suggests the diagnosis of thyroid storm/thyroid crisis presenting with atrial fibrillation, and the immediate management in this patient is to rate control the arrhythmia with diltiazem (calcium channel blocker).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following accurately represents Bormann's classification for gastric carcinoma?
options: Type I: Polypoid tumor with a small ulcerated component
Type II: Ulcerated tumor with raised margins
Type III: Diffusely infiltrative tumor with linitis plastica appearance
Type IV: Mucinous carcinoma with extensive peritoneal metastases
questions.explanation: Bormann’s classification describes the gross morphological types of advanced gastric carcinoma. 1. Type I is a polypoid or fungating mass projecting into the lumen and is not typically defined by ulceration, so option (A) is inaccurate. 2. Type II is characterized by an ulcerated lesion with well-defined, raised margins, which matches option (B) correctly. 3. Type III refers to an ulceroinfiltrative tumor with poorly defined margins that infiltrates deeply into the gastric wall, not a diffusely infiltrative pattern, so option (C) is incorrect. 4. Type IV represents a diffuse infiltrative carcinoma, leading to linitis plastica (leather bottle stomach) due to widespread thickening of the stomach wall. It is not specifically defined as mucinous carcinoma with peritoneal metastasis, making option (D) incorrect. Thus, only option (B) correctly matches the Bormann classification
questions.learning: Bormann’s classification describes the gross morphological types of advanced gastric carcinoma. Type I is a polypoid or fungating mass projecting into the lumen and is not typically defined by ulceration, so option (A) is inaccurate.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a study about the age of a small population, the highest value 36 was mistakenly recorded as 63. What will happen to the mean and median of the data?
options: Median will increase, mean will remain the same
Mean will increase, median will remain the same
Both mean and median will increase
Neither mean nor median will increase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mean will increase, median will remain the same

When the highest recorded value is replaced by a bigger value, mean will increase while median will be unaffected.

Median

* The median is the central element in a distribution when all the elements are arranged in order.

* In a distribution that has an odd number of elements, the median is the middle value.

* In a distribution that has an even number of elements, the median is the average of the middle values, i.e., the arithmetic mean of the two middle values.

* The median is not sensitive to extreme values, i.e., outliers and thus it is preferred measure of location for very skewed distributions.

* The drawback of the median is that it doesn’t respond to the actual values of the elements but only to the number of values above or below

* The median is the same as the 50th centile.

* It is sometimes symbolized by Mdn.

* The median can be arrived at in ordinal, interval and ratio data scales.

Pearl PF1749: The Mean (Arithmetic) in Biostatistics

* The mean is also called the average or arithmetic mean.

* It is the sum of all elements in the distribution divided by the number of all the elements in it.

* It is usually denoted by μ in a population and by x̄ (x-bar) in a sample.

* The formula for sample mean is given as:

where the sigma sign denotes summation and n is the total number of elements.

* The arithmetic mean responds to the exact value of every element in the distribution.

* This makes it over-sensitive to extreme values, i.e., outliers thus making it an inappropriate measure for skewed distributions.

* The advantage of the arithmetic mean is that if repeated samples are taken from the same populations, they will have very similar means, i.e., the measure of central tendency that best resists the influence of fluctuation between samples is the mean.

* The mean can be calculated only on quantitative data on an interval or a ratio scale.
questions.learning: Mean will increase, median will remain the same When the highest recorded value is replaced by a bigger value, mean will increase while median will be unaffected.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 6-month-old infant presents with protuberant abdomen, doll-like facies, and recurrent episodes of hypoglycemia. On examination, there is marked hepatomegaly. Laboratory evaluation suggests Von Gierke disease. What is the primary mechanism responsible for the enlarged liver in this condition?
options: Excess deposition of glycogen within hepatocytes
Accumulation of glucose-6-phosphate due to enzymatic block
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Excess deposition of glycogen within hepatocytes

• Core pathology = impaired conversion of G6P → glucose
• This leads to shunting into glycogen synthesis → hepatomegaly
• So although G6P accumulates, clinical enlargement is due to glycogen deposition

Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (Glycogen Storage Disease Type I – Von Gierke disease) prevents the conversion of glucose-6-phosphate to free glucose in the liver. Because glucose cannot be released into the blood, glucose-6-phosphate accumulates and is diverted toward glycogen synthesis, leading to excess glycogen deposition in hepatocytes. This excessive glycogen storage causes hepatic enlargement (hepatomegaly).

Hepatomegaly in glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency occurs due to accumulation of glycogen in the liver.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Accumulation of glucose-6-phosphate: Although it increases, it primarily drives other pathways (glycogen synthesis, glycolysis, lipogenesis) and is not the direct structural cause of hepatomegaly.
• Accumulation of glucose-1-phosphate: Not the main metabolite accumulating in this condition.
• Accumulation of glycogenin: Glycogenin only acts as a primer for glycogen formation and does not accumulate to cause liver enlargement.
questions.learning: Excess deposition of glycogen within hepatocytes • Core pathology = impaired conversion of G6P → glucose • This leads to shunting into glycogen synthesis → hepatomegaly • So although G6P accumulates, clinical enlargement is due to glycogen deposition…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient was suspected to have acute brucellosis. A serum sample was sent for a standard agglutination test. It came out to be negative initially but after serial dilutions of the serum sample, the test turned out to be positive. Which of the following is responsible for the initial negative test?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Prozone phenomenon

The initial negative test is explained by the prozone phenomenon. The standard agglutination test is a tube agglutination test that mainly identifies IgM antibodies. It is used in establishing a diagnosis of acute brucellosis.

Prozone phenomenon refers to the failure of a visible precipitation reaction due to inhibition of lattice formation by the presence of excessive antibodies. This gives rise to a false-negative test. This excess in antibodies can be overcome by diluting the serum sample, leading to an increase in the antigen-antibody interactions, eventually giving rise to a positive result.

Lattice hypothesis:

The lattice hypothesis explains precipitation reactions. The amount of precipitate formed is greatly influenced by the relative proportions of antigens and antibodies.

• Prozone phenomenon: Caused by excessive antibodies in the test system. (weak/absent precipitation- false-negative test)
• Zone of equivalence: Antigens and antibodies are in optimum proportions and maximum precipitation occurs.
• Post–zone phenomenon: (Option-D) Due to the presence of excessive antigen in the test system. (weaker/absent precipitation)

Standard agglutination test identifies mainly IgM antibodies, hence it is useful in acute brucellosis. Following 7-10 days of infection, both IgM and IgG antibodies appear. The IgM antibodies then gradually fall and only IgG antibodies persist in chronic brucellosis. The complement fixation test (Option-B) is more useful in chronic cases as it detects the IgG antibody also.

Brucellosis/ Undulant fever:

Brucellosis is a zoonotic disease caused by gram-negative, capnophilic coccobacilli. The most important species that are pathologic to humans are B.melitensis, B. suis, and B.abortus. It is transmitted to humans from contact with or consumption of contaminated products.

These bacteria proliferate within the reticuloendothelial system, which accounts for its resistance to simple antimicrobial therapy.

Patients with acute infection may present with undulant fever, arthralgia, muscular pain, sweating, loss of weight, and appetite. CNS symptoms such as fatigue, irritability, and depression might also occur. Chronic infection tends to be episodic with non-specific symptoms.

Laboratory diagnosis of brucellosis includes:

• Polymerase chain reaction
• Blood culture with Castaneda method
• Serological methods include standard agglutination test (SAT), complement fixation test, Coomb’s antiglobulin test, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA).
• Tests for animals and animal products: Milk ring tests and Rose Bengal card tests.

• Milk ring test- A sample of milk is mixed with stained brucella antigen and incubated. If the sample contains antibodies, agglutination occurs seen as a blue ring.

Treatment includes antimicrobial therapy with IM streptomycin and oral doxycycline. Prevention of brucellosis can be achieved by pasteurization of milk and milk products.

The images below show the Casteneda's medium and the milk ring test respectively.
questions.learning: Prozone phenomenon — The initial negative test is explained by the prozone phenomenon. The standard agglutination test is a tube agglutination test that mainly identifies IgM antibodies.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following conditions can cause euvolaemic hyponatraemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypothyroidism

Euvolemic hyponatremia is characterized by low serum sodium with normal extracellular fluid volume, without clinical evidence of edema or dehydration. It is most commonly caused by syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), but hypothyroidism and secondary adrenal insufficiency are important endocrine causes that must always be excluded.

• Hypothyroidism can cause euvolemic hyponatremia by:

• Decreasing cardiac output and GFR
• Increasing ADH secretion
• Reducing free water clearance

• The resulting water retention dilutes serum sodium without causing significant edema.

Why not the other options?

• A. Adrenocortical failure: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) usually causes hypovolemic hyponatremia due to aldosterone deficiency causing sodium loss. (Secondary adrenal insufficiency may present with euvolemic hyponatremia.)
• C. Nephrotic syndrome: Causes hypervolemic hyponatremia due to edema and water retention.
• D. Burns: Cause hypovolemic hyponatremia because of fluid and sodium losses.
questions.learning: Hypothyroidism Euvolemic hyponatremia is characterized by low serum sodium with normal extracellular fluid volume, without clinical evidence of edema or dehydration.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 40-year-old man with a known case of chronic pancreatitis presents to the OPD with complaint of skin pigmentation over the abdomen. The patient gives a history of chronic use of a hot water bottle to relieve the abdominal discomfort. Which one of the following is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Erythema ab igne

Erythema ab igne (“redness from fire”) is a localized skin condition caused by repeated or prolonged exposure to moderate heat (43–47°C) that is insufficient to cause burns. It classically presents as a reticulated (net-like), brownish hyperpigmented rash over the area of chronic heat exposure.

In patients with chronic pancreatitis, recurrent abdominal pain often leads to repeated use of hot water bottles or heating pads, making erythema ab igne a characteristic clinical finding.

Why not the other options?

• A. Erythema infectiosum: A viral exanthem caused by Parvovirus B19, characterized by a “slapped cheek” rash in children.
• B. Erythema marginatum: One of the major Jones criteria of acute rheumatic fever; presents as evanescent, serpiginous, non-pruritic annular lesions.
• C. Erythema nodosum: Painful, tender erythematous nodules over the anterior shins, associated with conditions such as tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, and streptococcal infections.
questions.learning: Erythema ab igne Erythema ab igne (“redness from fire”) is a localized skin condition caused by repeated or prolonged exposure to moderate heat (43–47°C) that is insufficient to cause burns.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Why do neoplastic cells utilize Warburg metabolism?
options: It decreases glucose utilisation by neoplastic cells
It forms metabolic intermediates which are needed for cell growth and multiplication
It provides more energy in the form of increased ATP production
It prevents apoptosis and makes the cancer cells immortal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It forms metabolic intermediates which are needed for cell growth and multiplication

Neoplastic cells utilize Warburg metabolism for the generation of metabolic intermediates, which are needed for cell growth and multiplication.

The Warburg Effect is a phenomenon in which there is an increase in the rate of glucose uptake and conversion into lactate(fermentation), even in the presence of oxygen. Cancer cells derive energy mainly from glycolysis.

Cancer cells utilize glycolysis (2 ATP) over mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (36 ATP) for glucose metabolism, even though the latter produces more ATP. It is because pure oxidative phosphorylation produces abundant ATP, but also burns glucose to CO2 and H2O, leaving no carbon moieties suitable for use as building blocks for lipids or proteins.

For this reason, rapidly growing cells, by undergoing glycolysis, produce carbon moieties that are needed for growth and cellular maintenance.

The image given below shows the comparison of glucose metabolism in normal cells versus cancer cells.

As a result of decreased ATP production, the main metabolic function of mitochondria in growing cells is not to generate ATP, but to carry
out reactions that generate cellular building blocks. For example, lipid biosynthesis.

Warburg effect is produced by growth factor receptors downstream signalling pathways. These include receptor tyrosine kinase/PI3K/AKT and MYC.

Clinically, cancer cells exhibiting the Warburg effect show a property of glucose hunger. This is used to visualize them via positron emission tomography (PET) scanning.
questions.learning: It forms metabolic intermediates which are needed for cell growth and multiplication Neoplastic cells utilize Warburg metabolism for the generation of metabolic intermediates, which are needed for cell growth and multiplication.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following types of inhibition is depicted in the given Lineweaver-Burk plot?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Competitive inhibition

The given graph shows competitive inhibition, in which the value of Vmax remains constant and the Km value increases.

• Km is the substrate concentration at which velocity is half maximum.
• Vmax is the maximum velocity of a reaction.

Inhibition
