questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A female undergoes a methylene blue 3 swab test and the middle swab is stained with blue. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vesicovaginal fistula

The given clinical scenario with methylene blue swab test showing staining of middle swab is suggestive of vesicovaginal fistula.

Vesicovaginal fistula (VVF) is a type of genital fistula, which is an abnormal communication between the genital tract and the urinary tract. It can be classified as simple or complicated. Their features are given in the table below.

Simple VVF
Complicated VVF

Size ≤ 3 cm
Size > 3 cm

Located near the cuff or supra-trigonal
Located away from the cuff / there is the involvement of trigone

No prior malignancy
Pelvic malignancy present

No prior radiation
Prior radiation therapy

The vaginal length remains normal
Vaginal length shortened

Vesicovaginal fistulae occur mostly due to obstetric injuries such as prolonged labor, and instrumental or manipulative deliveries. Patients present with true incontinence characterized by constant dribbling of urine. The presence of urine in the undergarments is uncomfortable and leads to pruritus and excoriation of the genital area.

Investigations to be performed include

* Urine culture and treatment of infection if required

* Ultrasound of the kidney, ureter, and bladder

* Intravenous pyelography

* Methylene blue - 3 swab test if the fistula is small. Here, methylene blue is injected into the bladder via the catheter, and three sterile swabs are placed into the vaginal cavity.

* The uppermost swab gets wet and not stained - the leak is from the ureter, seen in the ureterovaginal fistula

* The middle swab gets stained - the leak is from the bladder, seen in vesicovaginal fistula

* The lowermost swab gets stained- the leak is from the urethra, seen in the urethrovaginal fistula

* Cystourethroscopy helps in fistula localization, determination of its proximity to the ureteral orifices, inspection for multiple fistula sites, etc.

Vesicovaginal fistula is treated surgically. It can be attempted after 3 months to allow the inflammation to subside and clear the infection. After this, the Latzko procedure can be performed. Here, the vaginal epithelium around the fistula is removed and the edges are approximated. The Chassar Moir technique can also be attempted. Here, the vagina and bladder are separated and sutured into two layers taking care to avoid tension and overlapping suture lines.
questions.learning: Vesicovaginal fistula — The given clinical scenario with methylene blue swab test showing staining of middle swab is suggestive of vesicovaginal fistula.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following changes does not occur in chronic starvation?
questions.explanation: Chronic starvation leads to a series of physiological adaptations designed to conserve energy and preserve essential organ function. One of the primary responses is a significant decrease in the basal metabolic rate (BMR). This results in "hypothermia" (low body temperature), not hyperthermia. The body reduces heat production to minimize caloric expenditure. Exhaustion (Option B) is a classic finding as glycogen and fat stores are depleted. Heart atrophy (Option C) occurs as the body breaks down its own muscle tissue (autophagy) to provide amino acids for essential processes, leading to reduced cardiac mass and output. Hypotension (Option D) is also common due to reduced sympathetic activity and cardiac atrophy. Other changes include bradycardia, dry skin, and edema (if protein stores are severely depleted, as in kwashiorkor). Since hyperthermia (elevated body temperature) would involve increased energy consumption, it is the opposite of what occurs during the body's conservation phase in chronic starvation
questions.learning: Chronic starvation leads to a series of physiological adaptations designed to conserve energy and preserve essential organ function. One of the primary responses is a significant decrease in the basal metabolic rate (BMR).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A child is brought to the hospital with constricted (pinpoint) pupils and respiratory distress after playing at home. What is the most likely substance the child may have accidentally ingested?
questions.explanation: Classic opioid toxicity presents with a hallmark triad: miosis (pinpoint pupils), respiratory depression, and a decreased level of consciousness. In children, accidental ingestion can also lead to flaccid muscles or convulsions. Organophosphate poisoning (Option A) also causes miosis and breathing difficulty, but it is typically accompanied by "SLUDGE" symptoms (salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI upset, and emesis), which are absent here. Atropine ingestion (Option C) results in mydriasis (dilated pupils) and dry skin, the opposite of the signs described. Benzodiazepine overdose (Option D) causes generalized CNS depression and slurred speech but does not typically result in pinpoint pupils. Therefore, the combination of pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression is pathognomonic for an opioid overdose. The emergency antidote for this condition is intravenous Naloxone
questions.learning: Classic opioid toxicity presents with a hallmark triad: miosis (pinpoint pupils), respiratory depression, and a decreased level of consciousness. In children, accidental ingestion can also lead to flaccid muscles or convulsions.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient who was admitted after a road traffic accident is put on mechanical ventilation. He opens his eyes on verbal command and moves all four limbs spontaneously. Calculate his GCS.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Eyes-3, Verbal-NT, Motor-6

The patients GCS is Eyes-3, Verbal-NT, Motor-6.

It is calculated as follows:

• Eye opening: Opening to verbal command - 3
• Verbal response: In the case of endotracheal intubation, the verbal response score is noted as NT (non-testable)
• Motor respone: Movement of all 4 limbs spontaneously - 6

Total GCS score is not recorded since one of the components is non-testable.
questions.learning: Eyes-3, Verbal-NT, Motor-6 — The patients GCS is Eyes-3, Verbal-NT, Motor-6. It is calculated as follows: • Eye opening: Opening to verbal command - 3 • Verbal response: In the case of endotracheal intubation, the verbal response score is noted as NT…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient with a penicillin allergy presents with enterococcal endocarditis. Which of the following drugs can be used safely in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vancomycin

Enterococcal endocarditis is commonly caused by Enterococcus faecalis or Enterococcus faecium. Standard therapy usually involves β-lactam antibiotics (e.g., penicillin or ampicillin) often combined with an aminoglycoside. However, in patients with a penicillin allergy, an alternative drug must be used.

Vancomycin is effective against gram-positive organisms including Enterococcus and is commonly used for:

• Enterococcal endocarditis
• MRSA infections
• Patients with severe β-lactam allergy

Why other options are incorrect

• A. Aztreonam – active mainly against gram-negative bacteria, not Enterococcus.

C. Ceftriaxone – a cephalosporin; may cross-react in penicillin allergy and has limited activity against Enterococcus.

D. Piperacillin – a β-lactam penicillin, contraindicated in penicillin-allergic patients.
questions.learning: Vancomycin Enterococcal endocarditis is commonly caused by Enterococcus faecalis or Enterococcus faecium. Standard therapy usually involves β-lactam antibiotics (e.g., penicillin or ampicillin) often combined with an aminoglycoside.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient develops vomiting, abdominal pain, and chest discomfort after consuming alcohol. On examination, the patient is hypotensive. Which drug is responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The symptoms of vomiting, abdominal/chest pain, and hypotension following alcohol consumption describe a severe disulfiram-like reaction. This reaction occurs when a drug inhibits the enzyme acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, causing toxic levels of acetaldehyde to build up. Cefoperazone, a third-generation cephalosporin, contains a methyltetrazolethiol (MTT) side chain that is specifically known to cause this reaction. Other common drugs include metronidazole and some sulfonylureas. Propranolol (Option B), Calcium channel blockers (Option C), and Pantoprazole (Option D) do not have this metabolic interaction with alcohol. The severity of the reaction can lead to cardiovascular collapse. Clinicians must strictly warn any patient prescribed cefoperazone or metronidazole to avoid all alcohol during and for several days after completing their course. This pharmacological interaction is a classic high-yield topic for preventing serious iatrogenic harm in patients who may consume alcohol socially
questions.learning: The symptoms of vomiting, abdominal/chest pain, and hypotension following alcohol consumption describe a severe disulfiram-like reaction. This reaction occurs when a drug inhibits the enzyme acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, causing toxic levels of acetaldehyde…

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the given histology slide:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pancreas

The above image shows pancreatic islet cells. Islet of Langerhans makes up the endocrine part of the pancreas.

Islets are characterized by secretory cells supported by reticulin fibers, and containing numerous fenestrated capillaries. There is a delicate capsule around each islet. They are paler than the surrounding exocrine cells, as they have less rough endoplasmic reticulum. The image given below shows the histology of the pancreas:

The islets of Langerhans contain four major and two minor cell types:

Four main types are β, α, δ, and PP (pancreatic polypeptide) cells:

* α or A cells- located peripherally and secrete glucagon

* β or B cells- located centrally and produce insulin

* δ or D cells- scattered between beta cells and secrete somatostatin

* PP cells- are present in islets and also in the exocrine pancreas. They secrete a pancreatic polypeptide, which exerts several gastrointestinal effects, such as stimulation of secretion of gastric and intestinal enzymes and inhibition of intestinal motility.

Minor cell types:

* D1 cells secrete vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), a hormone that induces glycogenolysis and hyperglycemia. It also stimulates gastrointestinal fluid secretion and causes secretory diarrhea.

* Enterochromaffin cells synthesize serotonin and are the source of pancreatic tumors that cause carcinoid syndrome.

Other options:

Option A: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs. The structure of lymph nodes consists of an outer cortex and inner medulla. The cortex contains an aggregation of B-lymphocytes (primary follicles) and quiescent secondary follicles with a pale central germinal center.

The inner medulla consists of medullary cords (lymphocytes and plasma cells) and medullary sinuses. Between the cortex and medulla, there is an ill-defined zone called the paracortex, which contains T lymphocytes. The image given below shows the histology of the lymph node:

Option B: Glomerulus is a rounded tuft of anastomosing capillaries. The glomerular capillary wall is the filtering membrane and consists of fenestrated endothelial cells, basement membrane, and visceral epithelial cells called podocytes, which contain foot processes. The image given below shows the histology of the glomerulus:

Option C: Spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ. It contains round white pulp surrounded by red pulp. The white pulp is made up of aggregations of lymphocytes that surround a small artery or arterioles.

The red pulp is a modified lymphoid tissue infiltrated with all the cells of circulating blood. It is like a sponge permeated by spaces (splenic sinusoids) lined by reticular cells. The zone of red pulp immediately surrounding white pulp is the marginal zone. This zone has a rich network of sinusoids. The image given below shows the histology of the spleen:
questions.learning: Pancreas — The above image shows pancreatic islet cells. Islet of Langerhans makes up the endocrine part of the pancreas.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A neonate was brought with yellow sclera and hypoglycemia. He is exclusively breastfed. Urine Benedict's test is positive. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this neonate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase

Features of jaundice and hypoglycemia in a neonate who is breastfed, suggest a diagnosis of Classic Galactosemia, in which there is a deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase.

Classic galactosemia:

* Deficiency of galactose-1-uridyltransferase leads to the accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate and galactitol

* Infants show vomiting, diarrhea, and poor weight gain within 3-4 days of breastfeeding

* Jaundice and liver dysfunction appear in the first or second week of life.

* Proximal renal tubular disease may also manifest as metabolic acidosis, galactosuria, glucosuria, and aminoaciduria

* Most common cause of death is E.coli sepsis

* Acute galactose toxicity is manifested by neurological symptoms

* Diagnosis is made by genetic or mutational analysis. There will be presence of reducing substances in the urine.
questions.learning: Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase Features of jaundice and hypoglycemia in a neonate who is breastfed, suggest a diagnosis of Classic Galactosemia, in which there is a deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 35-year-old chronic hypertensive woman visits the outpatient department for pre-conceptional counseling. Which of the following anti-hypertensives should she discontinue?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors

Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors should be discontinued in pregnancy as they can cause hypoplasia of organs, growth retardation, and fetal loss.

ACE inhibitors cause reduced perfusion and oligohydramnios leading to fetal growth retardation, calvarium maldevelopment, hypoplasia of lungs and kidneys, and limb contractures.

Antihypertensive drugs to be avoided in pregnancy:

• ACE inhibitors and Angiotensin receptor blockers(ARB) - Can cause growth retardation and fetal damage.
• Diuretics - Can decrease uteroplacental perfusion
• Nonselective beta-blockers
• Sodium nitroprusside - It is contraindicated in eclampsia.

Antihypertensive drugs that can be used in pregnancy:

• Labetalol - Combined α + β blocker
• Nifedipine - Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. It is useful in preeclampsia but should be stopped before labor as they weaken the uterine contractions.
• Methyldopa
• Hydralazine

Note:

Thiazide diuretics like hydrochlorothiazide are considered to be safe in pregnancy and are useful in the management of chronic hypertension in pregnant women.
questions.learning: Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors should be discontinued in pregnancy as they can cause hypoplasia of organs, growth retardation, and fetal loss.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old bedridden patient presents with sudden-onset breathlessness and chest pain, and a CTPA has been performed. Which non- invasive investigation would be useful to help confirm the underlying etiology?
questions.explanation: A bedridden patient presenting with sudden dyspnea and chest pain is highly likely to have a Pulmonary Embolism (PE), often originating from a Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT). While CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) is the gold standard for diagnosing PE, a Doppler ultrasound of the legs is an essential non-invasive tool to confirm the etiology by identifying the source thrombus in the deep veins. D-dimer (Option A) is a sensitive screening tool but is often elevated in hospitalized or bedridden patients regardless of PE, making it non-specific. MRI (Option B) and a Coagulogram (Option C) are not the primary diagnostic steps for confirming acute PE or its venous source. Finding a clot on Doppler in this symptomatic patient strongly supports the diagnosis of venous thromboembolism. Immediate treatment involves anticoagulation with heparin or LMWH. Preventing DVT in bedridden patients through mechanical and pharmacological prophylaxis is a fundamental aspect of inpatient clinical care
questions.learning: A bedridden patient presenting with sudden dyspnea and chest pain is highly likely to have a Pulmonary Embolism (PE), often originating from a Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
Match the following genetic disorders with their inheritance patterns:

A. Cystic fibrosis
1. Autosomal dominant

B. Leber optic neuropathy
2. Autosomal recessive

C. Duchenne muscular dystrophy
3. X-Linked recesssive

D. Myotonic dystrophy
4. Mitochondrial
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A2, B4, C3, D1

Genetic disorder
Inheritance pattern

A. Cystic fibrosis
Autosomal recessive

B. Leber optic neuropathy
Mitochondrial

C. Duchenne muscular dystrophy
X-linked recessive

D. Myotonic dystrophy
Autosomal dominant

Cystic fibrosis: Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder; both parents must carry a copy of the mutated gene in order for the child to be affected.

Leber optic neuropathy: Leber optic neuropathy is a mitochondrial genetic disorder. This means that the mutated gene is located on the mitochondrial DNA, which is DNA that is outside of the nucleus of the cell. Mitochondrial DNA is inherited solely from the mother.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked recessive genetic disorder. This means that the mutated gene is located on the X chromosome. Males have only one X chromosome, so if they inherit a mutated copy of the gene, they will be affected. Females have two X chromosomes, so if they inherit one mutated copy of the gene, they will be carriers.

Myotonic dystrophy: Myotonic dystrophy is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder. This means that only one parent needs to carry a copy of the mutated gene in order for their child to be affected.
questions.learning: A2, B4, C3, D1 Genetic disorder Inheritance pattern A. Cystic fibrosis Autosomal recessive B.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 29-year-old male patient presents to the OPD with a 10-year history of coarse facial features and progressive enlargement of the hands and feet. Laboratory evaluation revealed elevated IGF-1 and non-suppressible growth hormone levels after the 75 g glucose challenge test. A diagnosis of acromegaly is made. Which of the following drugs is preferred for the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lanreotide depot formulation

Lanreotide depot formulation is useful in the management of acromegaly.

Acromegaly commonly occurs due to growth hormone-secreting somatotrophic adenoma. Increased secretion of growth hormone (GH) and insulin-like growth factor- 1 (IGF-1) results in acral bone overgrowth. Patients present with frontal bossing, increased hand, and foot size, mandibular enlargement with prognathism, and widened space between the lower incisor teeth. Soft tissue swelling results in increased heel pad thickness, ring tightening, characteristic coarse facial features, and a large fleshy nose.

The cardiovascular system has a significant impact on GH excess characterized by cardiomyopathy with arrhythmias, left ventricular hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, and hypertension.

Other manifestations seen in growth hormone excess are obstructive sleep apnea and diabetes mellitus.

Serum IGF-1 levels and GH suppression test with oral glucose are useful in the diagnosis. The levels of GH do not reduce in response to the oral glucose load.

GH-secreting adenomas are managed with surgery. Transsphenoidal surgical treatment is the preferred surgery. The preferred medical treatments include long-acting injectable somatostatin receptor ligand (SRL) depot formulations of octreotide and lanreotide as well as oral octreotide capsules. Another drug that is useful in acromegaly is pegvisomant. It is a growth hormone receptor antagonist and therefore, antagonizes the actions of GH.

Other options:

Option B: Terlipressin is a vasopressin analogue that acts selectively on V1 receptors and is used in the management of bleeding oesophageal varices and hepatorenal syndrome.

Option C: Ketoconazole is used in the management of Cushing's disease. Ketoconazole inhibits several P450 enzymes and effectively lowers cortisol levels in most patients with Cushing’s disease.

Option D: Leuprolide is a long-acting GnRH agonist. It is used as a palliation of carcinoma prostate, uterine fibroids, endometriosis, and precocious puberty. Side effects include hot flashes, decreased bone mineral density, vaginal dryness, and erectile dysfunction.
questions.learning: Lanreotide depot formulation Lanreotide depot formulation is useful in the management of acromegaly. Acromegaly commonly occurs due to growth hormone-secreting somatotrophic adenoma.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug is most effective for reducing uric acid levels to prevent renal injury in patients with tumor lysis syndrome?
questions.explanation: Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS) is an oncological emergency characterized by the massive release of intracellular contents, including nucleic acids which are metabolized into uric acid. Severe hyperuricemia can cause acute urate nephropathy and renal failure. Rasburicase is a recombinant urate oxidase enzyme that directly converts uric acid into allantoin, a much more soluble metabolite that is easily excreted by the kidneys. It acts rapidly to lower existing high levels of uric acid. Febuxostat (Option D) and Allopurinol are xanthine oxidase inhibitors that prevent the formation of new uric acid but do not clear what is already in the blood. Furosemide (Option A) is a diuretic used to maintain urine flow but doesn't target uric acid. Corticosteroids (Option C) are part of chemotherapy but not a primary treatment for TLS hyperuricemia. Thus, Rasburicase is the most potent and direct agent for managing established hyperuricemia in TLS
questions.learning: Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS) is an oncological emergency characterized by the massive release of intracellular contents, including nucleic acids which are metabolized into uric acid.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presents with lethargy, excessive sleepiness, and weight gain. Laboratory evaluation shows low plasma TSH along with reduced T3 and T4 levels, but TSH levels rise after administration of TRH. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Hyperthyroidism due to disease in the pituitary
Hypothyroidism due to disease in the pituitary
Hypothyroidism due to disease in the hypothalamus
Hyperthyroidism due to disease in the hypothalamus
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms of lethargy and weight gain combined with low T3 and T4 confirm "hypothyroidism". A low or inappropriately normal TSH in the setting of low T4 indicates "central" hypothyroidism (either pituitary or hypothalamic origin). To distinguish between the two, a TRH stimulation test is used. If the TSH level "increases" following TRH administration, it demonstrates that the pituitary gland is healthy and capable of responding, but it was not receiving endogenous TRH from the brain. Therefore, the primary defect lies in the "hypothalamus" (Tertiary Hypothyroidism). If the TSH had failed to increase, the diagnosis would be pituitary disease (Secondary Hypothyroidism, Option B). Options A and D are incorrect because the patient’s labs and clinical picture represent a deficiency (hypo) rather than an excess (hyper) of thyroid hormone. This diagnostic logic is a cornerstone of endocrinology for localizing the exact level of axis failure
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms of lethargy and weight gain combined with low T3 and T4 confirm "hypothyroidism". A low or inappropriately normal TSH in the setting of low T4 indicates "central" hypothyroidism (either pituitary or hypothalamic origin).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is not an example of an aneuploidy disorder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bloom syndrome

Aneuploidy refers to an abnormal number of chromosomes due to gain or loss of whole chromosomes, typically caused by nondisjunction.

• Trisomy 21, Trisomy 13, and Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) are classic examples of aneuploidy
• These conditions involve numerical chromosomal abnormalities

Why Bloom syndrome is not aneuploidy:

• Bloom syndrome is a chromosomal instability disorder caused by mutation in the BLM gene
• It involves defective DNA repair and increased sister chromatid exchanges, not a change in chromosome number

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A radiologist notices significant artefacts on MRI brain images obtained in a newly constructed imaging suite. The biomedical engineer reports that external radiofrequency signals from nearby equipment are interfering with the scanner. To prevent both ingress of external RF signals and containment of RF signals generated by the scanner itself, which shielding system must be installed around the MRI room?
options: Maxwell cage — uses magnetic field cancellation coils arranged around the room
Faraday cage — a conductive enclosure that blocks external electromagnetic fields and contains internal RF emissions
Edison cage — an insulated enclosure that dissipates static electrical charge buildup
Ohm cage — a resistive barrier that attenuates high-frequency electrical noise through impedance matching
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Faraday cage — a conductive enclosure that blocks external electromagnetic fields and contains internal RF emissions

A Faraday cage is a conductive enclosure (typically copper or aluminium lining) that redistributes electromagnetic charges on its surface, effectively cancelling external RF fields inside and preventing internal RF from escaping. MRI rooms require this because the scanner operates at specific radiofrequency ranges (Larmor frequency) and any external EM interference degrades the signal-to-noise ratio of images. The other options are distractors — Maxwell, Edison, and Ohm cages are not real shielding systems used in radiology.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which stages of the demographic cycle are characterized by the same birth rate but differing death rates?
questions.explanation: In the demographic transition model, different stages represent changes in birth and death rates. Stage 1 (High Stationary) is characterized by both high birth rates and high death rates. Stage 2 (Early Expanding) is marked by the same high birth rate, but the death rate begins to decline rapidly due to improved sanitation and medicine. This difference in the death rate while the birth rate remains constant leads to a population explosion. Stage 3 (Late Expanding) involves a declining birth rate (Option B). Stage 4 (Low Stationary) has both low birth and death rates, while Stage 5 (Declining) involves a birth rate that falls below the death rate (Options C and D). Therefore, Stages 1 and 2 are the specific phases where the birth rate remains consistently high while the death rate is the variable factor. This understanding is fundamental for demographers and policy makers to predict population growth trends and plan for future resource needs in developing nations
questions.learning: In the demographic transition model, different stages represent changes in birth and death rates. Stage 1 (High Stationary) is characterized by both high birth rates and high death rates.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following do not represent the corrected refractive error?
questions.explanation: This question focuses on the nature of common visual impairments. Myopia (Option A), Hyperopia (Option B), and Astigmatism (Option D) are true ametropic refractive errors caused by a mismatch between the eye's axial length and its focusing power. Presbyopia, however, is not a refractive error in the traditional sense; it is an age-related loss of accommodative amplitude. It occurs because the natural lens loses its elasticity and the ciliary muscles weaken, making it difficult to focus on near objects. While it is corrected with glasses (like refractive errors), its underlying mechanism is physiological aging rather than a structural refractive mismatch. Myopia involves light focusing in front of the retina, while hyperopia involves light focusing behind it. Astigmatism occurs when the cornea or lens has an irregular curvature. Therefore, while all four impact vision, presbyopia is distinct as a progressive age-related condition of the lens's dynamic focusing ability rather than a static refractive state of the eye
questions.learning: This question focuses on the nature of common visual impairments. Myopia (Option A), Hyperopia (Option B), and Astigmatism (Option D) are true ametropic refractive errors caused by a mismatch between the eye's axial length and its focusing power.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A male patient came with a history of unprotected sexual intercourse around 20 years ago. Now, he complains of neurological symptoms and visual disturbances. Which of the following will be seen on exposure of his pupils to light?
options: Pupils react but do not accommodate.
Pupils accommodate but do not react.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pupils accommodate but do not react.

The patient most likely has acquired syphilis due to unprotected sex and has developed neurological and visual disturbances secondarily as a complication of neurosyphilis. Argyll-Robertson pupils(ARP) are seen associated with neurosyphilis where the pupils accommodate but do not react to light.

Argyll Robertson pupil is attributed to a dorsal midbrain lesion of neurosyphilis that affects the pupillary light pathway but spares the more ventrally placed pupillary near reflex pathway(Accomdation pathway), thereby causing a light-near dissociation.

Features of Argyll Robertson pupil (ARP) include:

• Bilateral small, irregular pupils in dim light
• Accommodation Reflex Present (ARP)- The eye accomdates by constricting the pupil for a near target.
• Light Reflex absent: pupils do not constrict when exposed to bright light.
• Cocaine eye drops(mydriatics) induced mydriasis.

Other clinical features in neurosyphilis:

• Fleeting and repetitive lancinating pains, primarily in the legs
• acute abdominal pain with vomiting(visceral crisis)
• Tabes dorsalis with Ataxia and gait disturbances due to loss of position sense
• Loss of reflexes in the legs
• Paresthesias, bladder disturbances

Other causes of light-near dissociation are:

In unilateral eye

1. Adie pupil
2. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus
3. Aberrant regeneration of the third cranial nerve

In bilateral eyes

1. Neurosyphilis
2. Type 1 diabetes mellitus
3. Myotonic dystrophy

Note: Adie's pupil more commonly manifests in young women with unilateral large regular pupil(Anisocoria) with absent light reflex and sluggish and tonic accomdation reflex.

It is caused by post-ganglionic parasympathetic pupillary supply damage and is usually associated with absent knee jerk.

Adie's pupil constricts with weak pilocarpine (0.1%) drops, while normal pupil and Argyll robertson pupil does not.
questions.learning: Pupils accommodate but do not react. The patient most likely has acquired syphilis due to unprotected sex and has developed neurological and visual disturbances secondarily as a complication of neurosyphilis.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient of anorexia nervosa was eating all her meals according to the prescribed diet chart but there is no change in her weight after 1 week. Which of the following needs to be done?
options: Observe the patient for 2 hours post meal
Ask the psychiatrist to prescribe anti-anxiety medication
Increase the calories from 1500 to 2000 in her diet
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Observe the patient for 2 hours post meal

Observe the patient for 2 hours post-meal because the patient might vomit the food.

Treatment of anorexia nervosa:

• Hospitalization:

• Patients with a weight 20% less than expected weight for height should be considered for hospitalization.
• During a hospitalized treatment program, patients should be weighed daily, early in the morning after emptying the bladder.
• The daily fluid intake and urine output should be recorded.
• If vomiting is occurring, hospital staff members must monitor serum electrolyte levels regularly and watch for the development of hypokalemia.
• Because food is often regurgitated after meals, the staff may be able to control vomiting by making the bathroom inaccessible for at least 2 hours after meals or by having an attendant in the bathroom to prevent the opportunity for vomiting.

• Psychotherapy:

• Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT)
• Dynamic psychotherapy
• Family therapy

• Pharmacotherapy:

• Pharmacological agents are not the first-line treatment but cyproheptadine, amitriptyline, clomipramine, pimozide, and chlorpromazine show some improvement in these patients.
• Trials of fluoxetine have resulted in some reports of weight gain.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the cause of the constriction encountered at the oesophageal junction, approximately 25 cm from the incisors, during endoscopic examination?
questions.explanation: The esophagus has four physiological constrictions where foreign bodies are most likely to lodge and which are important landmarks during endoscopy. These are measured from the upper incisor teeth: 1. At the pharyngoesophageal junction (15 cm), caused by the cricopharyngeus muscle. 2. Where it is crossed by the arch of the aorta (25 cm) (Option B). 3. Where it is crossed by the left main bronchus (not the right, Option C) (28 cm). 4. Where it passes through the diaphragmatic opening (40 cm) (Option D). The inferior vena cava (Option A) does not cross or constrict the esophagus. Therefore, a constriction felt specifically at the 25 cm mark during an endoscopic procedure is anatomically localized to the site where the aortic arch indentates the esophageal wall. Accurate knowledge of these distances is essential for endoscopists to accurately describe the location of lesions or obstructions
questions.learning: The esophagus has four physiological constrictions where foreign bodies are most likely to lodge and which are important landmarks during endoscopy. These are measured from the upper incisor teeth: 1.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A female patient presents with sudden onset of dysphagia, dysarthria, and gait ataxia. MRI of the brain reveals an acute infarct in the right dorsolateral medulla. Based on these findings, what is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Wallenberg syndrome, also known as Lateral Medullary Syndrome, results from an infarct in the dorsolateral medulla, typically due to occlusion of the Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (PICA) or the vertebral artery. The clinical presentation includes the "bulbar" triad of dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) and dysarthria (speech difficulty) due to involvement of the nucleus ambiguus, as well as gait ataxia from cerebellar tract damage. Dejerine's syndrome (Option A) involves the medial medulla, causing contralateral hemiparesis and tongue deviation. Babinski-Nageotte syndrome (Option C) is a more extensive brainstem lesion combining lateral and medial features. Weber syndrome (Option D) involves the midbrain, presenting with oculomotor nerve palsy and contralateral hemiplegia. Because the patient's symptoms perfectly correlate with the specific dorsal and lateral structures of the medulla identified on the MRI, Wallenberg syndrome is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: Wallenberg syndrome, also known as Lateral Medullary Syndrome, results from an infarct in the dorsolateral medulla, typically due to occlusion of the Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (PICA) or the vertebral artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: When does the anterior fontanelle close?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 12-24 months

The anterior fontanelle ideally closes between 18-24 months. However, the closest answer in the given options is 12–24 months of age.

Fontanelle of the skull:

* The anterior fontanelle is present between the two frontal and two parietal bones. It closes at around 18-24 months. The junction is marked by bregma where the coronal and sagittal sutures meet.

* The posterior fontanelle is present between the junction of the sagittal and lambdoid suture and closes at around 2-3 months of birth.

* The sphenoid fontanelle corresponds to the pterion and also closes at around 2-3 months of birth.

* The mastoid fontanelle closes around at the end of the first year.
questions.learning: 12-24 months The anterior fontanelle ideally closes between 18-24 months. However, the closest answer in the given options is 12–24 months of age.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The changes that the malarial parasite undergoes in the mosquito represent which one of the following types of biological transmission?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cyclopropagative

In malaria, the parasite undergoes both:

• Development → sexual and developmental changes occur inside the mosquito.
• No multiplication of the parasite in the mosquito vector in the sense relevant to this classification? Actually, the parasite undergoes multiplication as well as development, making malaria transmission cyclopropagative.

Therefore, the correct answer is C. Cyclopropagative.

Exam Pearl:

Types of Transmission in Vectors

1. Propagative

• Example: Plague bacilli in rat fleas, YF in Aedes

2. Cyclo-propagative

• Example: Malarial parasites in Anopheles

3. Cyclo-developmental

• Example: Microfilaria in Culex

4. Transovarial

• Example: Rickettsia rickettsii in ticks, Mite in scrub typhus

5. Transstadial

• Example: Borrelia burgdorferi, Indian tick typhus
questions.learning: Cyclopropagative — In malaria, the parasite undergoes both: • Development → sexual and developmental changes occur inside the mosquito. • No multiplication of the parasite in the mosquito vector in the sense relevant to this classification?

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a blood pressure of 230/110 mmHg, severe headache, blurred vision, and signs of end-organ damage. Which is the drug of choice for immediate blood pressure reduction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sodium nitroprusside

Hypertensive emergency is defined as severe hypertension (usually ≥180/120 mmHg) associated with acute target-organ damage (e.g., hypertensive encephalopathy, stroke, acute heart failure, aortic dissection, acute kidney injury). It requires immediate but controlled reduction of blood pressure using intravenous antihypertensive agents. Sodium nitroprusside is a rapid-acting arterial and venous vasodilator that is classically used for rapid BP reduction in hypertensive emergencies because of its immediate onset and short duration of action.

Why not the other options?

• A. Hydrochlorothiazide: Oral thiazide diuretic used for chronic hypertension, not emergencies.
• B. Amlodipine: Oral calcium channel blocker with a slow onset of action; unsuitable for acute BP reduction.
• D. Losartan: Oral angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB) used for long-term hypertension management, not hypertensive emergencies.
questions.learning: Sodium nitroprusside Hypertensive emergency is defined as severe hypertension (usually ≥180/120 mmHg) associated with acute target-organ damage (e.g., hypertensive encephalopathy, stroke, acute heart failure, aortic dissection, acute kidney injury).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In which of the following conditions is ovarian drilling commonly indicated?
questions.explanation: Laparoscopic Ovarian Drilling (LOD) is a specialized surgical procedure indicated for women with Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS) who suffer from infertility and have not responded to medical treatments like clomiphene citrate. The procedure involves using heat or a laser to destroy small portions of the ovarian stroma. This reduces the production of excessive androgens, which often restores regular ovulation and improves pregnancy rates. Ovarian tumors (Option A) require resection or staging surgery, not drilling. Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (Option C) is a medical complication of IVF that requires fluid management, as surgery can be dangerous. Endometriosis (Option D) is treated via laparoscopic ablation of implants or cystectomy for endometriomas, not stromal drilling. Therefore, ovarian drilling is a specific second-line treatment for the management of anovulatory infertility in PCOS patients
questions.learning: Laparoscopic Ovarian Drilling (LOD) is a specialized surgical procedure indicated for women with Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS) who suffer from infertility and have not responded to medical treatments like clomiphene citrate.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman in her second trimester of pregnancy presents with multiple symmetrical hypopigmented skin lesions, diffuse peripheral nerve thickening, and a positive slit-skin smear for Mycobacterium leprae. She is diagnosed with multibacillary leprosy. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Standard multidrug therapy (MDT)

Pregnancy is not a contraindication to the treatment of leprosy. Patients with multibacillary (MB) leprosy should receive the standard WHO multidrug therapy (MDT) regimen during pregnancy. Early treatment reduces bacterial load, prevents nerve damage and disability, and decreases the risk of disease progression and lepra reactions.

The standard MB-MDT consists of:

• Rifampicin (monthly supervised)
• Clofazimine (monthly supervised + daily)
• Dapsone (daily)

These drugs are generally considered safe during pregnancy. Clofazimine may cause reversible skin discoloration in the mother and infant but is not a reason to withhold treatment.

Why not the other options?

• A. Postpone treatment until after childbirth: Incorrect. Delaying therapy increases the risk of irreversible nerve damage, deformities, and disease progression.
• B. Rifampicin monotherapy: Incorrect. Monotherapy promotes drug resistance and is never recommended for leprosy.
• D. Dapsone monotherapy: Incorrect. Dapsone monotherapy was abandoned because of widespread resistance; combination MDT is the standard of care.

High-yield pearl

• Leprosy in pregnancy → Treat with standard WHO MDT; do not delay therapy.
• Never use monotherapy for leprosy because of the high risk of developing resistant M. leprae.
questions.learning: Standard multidrug therapy (MDT) Pregnancy is not a contraindication to the treatment of leprosy. Patients with multibacillary (MB) leprosy should receive the standard WHO multidrug therapy (MDT) regimen during pregnancy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl presents with progressive pallor, fatigue, and mild jaundice. Peripheral smear suggests hemolytic anemia, and an autoimmune etiology is suspected. A direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is performed. A positive direct Coombs test indicates which of the following?
options: Free circulating antibodies against red blood cells are present in the patient's serum
Red blood cells are coated with immunoglobulins and/or complement components
Donor red blood cells carrying foreign antigens are present in the circulation
Red blood cells have increased osmotic fragility
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Red blood cells are coated with immunoglobulins and/or complement components

The Direct Coombs (Direct Antiglobulin Test, DAT) detects IgG antibodies and/or complement (C3) that are already bound to the patient's red blood cells in vivo.

A positive test is characteristic of:

• Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA)
• Hemolytic disease of the newborn
• Hemolytic transfusion reactions
• Drug-induced immune hemolysis

The patient's RBCs are washed and then mixed with Coombs (antihuman globulin) reagent. Agglutination indicates that immunoglobulin and/or complement is attached to the RBC surface.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Free circulating antibodies against red blood cells are present in the patient's serum – This is detected by the Indirect Coombs test, which identifies free circulating anti-RBC antibodies.
• C. Donor red blood cells carrying foreign antigens are present in the circulation – The Direct Coombs test does not detect foreign RBCs; it detects antibodies or complement bound to the patient's own RBCs.
• D. Red blood cells have increased osmotic fragility – This is assessed by tests such as the osmotic fragility test, used in hereditary spherocytosis, and is unrelated to the Coombs test.

High-yield pearl

| Test | Detects | Common use

| ---- | ------- | ----------

| Direct Coombs (DAT) | IgG and/or C3 bound to patient RBCs | Autoimmune hemolytic anemia, hemolytic disease of the newborn, transfusion reactions

| Indirect Coombs (IAT) | Free anti-RBC antibodies in serum | Antenatal antibody screening and pre-transfusion compatibility testing
questions.learning: Red blood cells are coated with immunoglobulins and/or complement components The Direct Coombs (Direct Antiglobulin Test, DAT) detects IgG antibodies and/or complement (C3) that are already bound to the patient's red blood cells in vivo.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In treatment, the V-Y procedure is employed for which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: The V-Y plasty is a fundamental reconstructive technique used in plastic and oculoplastic surgery, particularly for correcting cicatricial (scar-related) ectropion. Ectropion is a condition where the eyelid margins turn outward, exposing the bulbar conjunctiva. Cicatricial ectropion occurs when skin shortening or scarring pulls the eyelid away from the globe. The V-Y procedure involves making a V-shaped incision and closing it in a Y-shape; this effectively increases the length of the skin in the direction of the vertical stem of the Y, relieving the tension pulling the eyelid down. Option A (Entropion) is the inward turning of the lid, usually requiring different surgical procedures. Option C (Blepharophimosis) and Option D (Ptosis) are congenital or myogenic conditions involving lid drooping, requiring surgeries like levator resection or frontalis slings. The V-Y plasty is highly effective for localized skin deficiency and is a classic solution for lid malpositions caused by facial burns or trauma
questions.learning: The V-Y plasty is a fundamental reconstructive technique used in plastic and oculoplastic surgery, particularly for correcting cicatricial (scar-related) ectropion.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 28-year-old trekker ascends rapidly from sea level to a high-altitude base camp at 4,500 meters. Over the next several days, his body undergoes physiological acclimatization. Which of the following changes is most directly responsible for the early rightward compensation that helps maintain tissue oxygen delivery despite a falling arterial PO2?
options: Decreased 2,3-BPG levels, increasing hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen
Hyperventilation-driven respiratory alkalosis, causing a leftward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, followed by renal compensation
Increased renal erythropoietin secretion, causing an immediate rise in hemoglobin concentration within hours
Decreased 2,3-BPG levels and a leftward-shifted curve, improving oxygen loading in the lungs at the cost of tissue unloading
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hyperventilation-driven respiratory alkalosis, causing a leftward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, followed by renal compensation

• The earliest acclimatization response to high altitude hypoxia is hyperventilation, triggered by peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies) sensing the fall in arterial PO2. This hyperventilation causes a respiratory alkalosis (low PaCO2, high pH), which initially shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the left (increasing hemoglobin's affinity for O2, favoring better loading in the relatively hypoxic alveoli) — though this transiently impairs O2 unloading at the tissues.
• Over subsequent days, renal compensation (bicarbonate excretion) corrects the pH, while a separate, slightly delayed adaptation occurs: increased red cell 2,3-BPG production, which shifts the curve back to the right, restoring better tissue oxygen unloading despite low PaO2.
• Option A (Decreased 2,3-BPG levels, increasing hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen) and Option D (Decreased 2,3-BPG levels and a leftward-shifted curve, improving oxygen loading in the lungs at the cost of tissue unloading) incorrectly state that 2,3-BPG decreases with altitude (it actually increases).
• Option C (Increased renal erythropoietin secretion, causing an immediate rise in hemoglobin concentration within hours) is incorrect because erythropoietin-driven increases in red cell mass/hemoglobin take days to weeks to manifest significantly, not hours — making it a later, not early, compensatory mechanism.

Quick reference — Time course of high-altitude acclimatization:

| Mechanism | Onset | Effect

| --------- | ----- | ------

| Hyperventilation (chemoreceptor-driven) | Minutes–hours | ↓ PaCO2, respiratory alkalosis, ↑ PaO2

| Renal bicarbonate excretion | Days | Corrects pH toward normal, permits further hyperventilation

| ↑ 2,3-BPG in RBCs | Days | Rightward shift of O2-Hb curve, improves tissue O2 unloading

| ↑ Erythropoietin → ↑RBC mass | Days to weeks | ↑ Hemoglobin concentration, ↑O2-carrying capacity

| ↑ Pulmonary vasoconstriction (hypoxic) | Hours–days | Can contribute to high-altitude pulmonary edema if excessive

| ↑ 2,3-DPG, ↑capillary density, ↑ mitochondria (chronic) | Weeks–months | Long-term tissue-level adaptation
questions.learning: Hyperventilation-driven respiratory alkalosis, causing a leftward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, followed by renal compensation • The earliest acclimatization response to high altitude hypoxia is hyperventilation, triggered by…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the structure marked with the yellow arrow in the intraoperative image of spermatic cord of a patient with a congenital inguinal hernia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Testicular vein

The given clinical image is an open inguinal hernia repair of a child with a structure marked as the spermatic cord whose content includes the testicular vein.

Normally the funicular process of the peritoneum becomes obliterated after the testis has reached the scrotum. The scrotal part of the process remains patent and acquires the name 'tunica vaginalis'. In case of congenital hernia, the whole process remains patent. With the increase in abdominal pressure, abdominal contents come out through the patent peritoneal process. So it reaches the bottom of the scrotum very quickly. It may so happen that the funicular process remains patent up to the top of the testis. So the hernia stops at the top of the testis and is known as a congenital funicular hernia.

Indirect hernia comprises more than 80% of inguinal hernias which are common in women and children. It occurs earlier than a direct hernia and is often complete. The two forms often seen under indirect are congenital and acquired. Unlike congenital, acquired hernias do not become complete at once. They progress gradually. Clinically a congenital hernia may present at a later period.

The pearls attached below describe the inguinal canal and the differences between direct and indirect inguinal hernia.

Other options are not the contents of the spermatic cord. Contents are mentioned in the pearl below.
questions.learning: Testicular vein — The given clinical image is an open inguinal hernia repair of a child with a structure marked as the spermatic cord whose content includes the testicular vein.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
Match the cytokines with the effector cells .

1. IL-4
A. Eosinophils

2. IL-5
B. Mast cells

3. IL-9
C. B cells

4. IL-13
D. Dendritic cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1-C;2-A;3-B;4-D

The correct answer is option B:

1. IL4
C. B cells

2. IL5
A. Eosinophils

3. IL9
B. Mast cells

4. IL13
D. Dendritic cells

Cytokines are proteins produced by many cell types (principally activated lymphocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells, but also endothelial, epithelial, and connective tissue cells) that mediate and regulate immune and inflammatory reactions.

Three subsets of CD4+ T cells secrete different types of cytokines and elicit different types of inflammation.

TH1 cells - activate macrophages by the classical pathway by secreting IFNγ.

TH2 cells - recruit and activate eosinophils and are responsible for the alternative pathway of macrophage activation by secreting IL4, IL5, and IL13.

• IL4 acts on B cells to stimulate class switching to IgE and promotes the development of additional TH2 cells.
• IL5 is involved in the development and activation of eosinophils, which are essential effectors of type I hypersensitivity
(discussed later).
• IL13 enhances IgE production and acts on epithelial cells to stimulate mucus secretion. In addition, TH2 cells (as well as mast cells and epithelial cells) produce chemokines that attract more TH2 cells, as well as other leukocytes, to the reaction site. It also shares some functional similarities to IL-4 and can thus induce differentiation in dendritic cells.

TH17 cells secrete IL17 and other cytokines responsible for neutrophils and monocyte recruitment.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with recurrent kidney stones. Microscopic examination finding of the urine specimen is shown below. Which of the following is not seen in the urine of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Histidine

The image shows hexagonal, translucent and white crystals suggestive of cystinuria. Histidine is not seen in the urine of this patient.

Cystinuria is an autosomal-recessive disease due to a defect in renal PCT & intestinal amino acid transporter that is essential for reabsorptive transport of Cystine and the dibasic amino acids Ornithine, Lysine, and Arginine (COLA).

Diagnosis of cystinuria is by the cyanide–nitroprusside test. Initial treatment is with adequate hydration, alkalization of the urine with citrate supplementation or acetazolamide, and dietary modification to reduce salt and protein intake. If this fails then patients are usually started on chelation therapy with penicillamine.
questions.learning: Histidine — The image shows hexagonal, translucent and white crystals suggestive of cystinuria. Histidine is not seen in the urine of this patient.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the procedure being done.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intrauterine balloon tamponade

The given image shows an intrauterine balloon tamponade.

A Bakri postpartum balloon may be inserted and inflated to tamponade the endometrial cavity and stop bleeding. It is used to manage refractory uterine atony.

The insertion process requires two or three team members. First-person to perform abdominal sonography during the procedure. Another to place the deflated balloon into the uterus and stabilize it. The third person instills normal saline to inflate the balloon, rapid infusion of at least 150 mL followed by further instillation over a few minutes for a total of 300 to 500 mL to arrest hemorrhage. Once the bleeding subsides, the catheter is generally removed after 12 to 24 hours.

Segstaken Blakemore, Rusch, and ebb balloons, Foley's catheter, and condom catheters can also be used instead.

In the technique where Foley's catheter is utilized, a 24F-30F size of the catheter with 30ml balloon is used, the tip is guided into the uterine cavity and filled with 60-80ml of saline. In some cases, if the balloon ruptures, a 34F with 60ml balloon can be used. Once the bleeding subsides, the catheter can be removed after 12 -24 hours.

Types of PPH:

Primary/early PPH: Hemorrhage occurring within 24 hours of childbirth. Causes include:

* Atony: Primi, grand multipara, over distended uterus, hydramnios, precipitate labor, prolonged labor, uterine malformations, fibroid uterus

* Trauma: Instrumental deliveries, episiotomy, precipitate labor, macrosomia

* Retained tissues: retained placenta, blood clots

* Bleeding disorders: Sepsis, Intrauterine death, HELLP syndrome.

Secondary/ late PPH: Hemorrhage occurring after 24 hours and up to 12 weeks postpartum. Causes include:

* Placental polyp: Retained products undergo necrosis with fibrin deposition and eventually form a placental polyp, which on detachment from the myometrium causes brisk hemorrhage.

* Abnormal involution of the placental site.

* Retention of placental cotyledon or products of conception.

* Uterine artery pseudoaneurysm.

* Endometritis

* Coagulopathy
questions.learning: Intrauterine balloon tamponade — The given image shows an intrauterine balloon tamponade. A Bakri postpartum balloon may be inserted and inflated to tamponade the endometrial cavity and stop bleeding.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An unvaccinated child from a migrant worker's family presents with fever, sore throat, a characteristic red blotchy skin rash, and a Bitot's spot in the right eye. What would be the appropriate management in this situation?
options: Isolate in the institution along with Vitamin A treatment
Home isolation of the child along with Vitamin A supplementation
Give MR vaccine, isolate the child and vitamin A treatment
Only Vitamin A supplement, no action needed for the rash
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Isolate in the institution along with Vitamin A treatment

The given clinical scenario of an unvaccinated child from a migrant worker's family presenting with fever, sore throat, a characteristic red blotchy skin rash which suggests measles, and a Bitot's spot in the right eye suggests deficiency of VItamin A. The appropriate management in this situation would be to isolate in the institution along with vitamin A treatment.

Vitamin A deficiency arises primarily due to inadequate amounts of vitamin A in the diet. It can present as night blindness, conjunctival xerosis, Bitot's spots, and keratomalacia. In later stages, it can lead to xerophthalmia. It also increases the risk of developing measles, diarrhea, and dysentery. Hence, vitamin A therapy is indicated in all patients with measles.

Treatment of Vitamin A deficiency in measles:

Age
< 6 months
6-12 months
> 1 year

Dose

50,000 IU P.O for 2 doses

100,000 IU P.O for 2 doses

200,000 IU P.O for 2 doses

Vitamin A routine supplementation dosage schedule: A total dose of 17 lakh IU is given as per the following schedule:

* 100,000 IU is given with measles at 9 months.

* 200,000 IU is given with a DPT booster at 15–18 months.

* 200,000 IU is given every 6 months (till 5 years of age).

Red blotchy rash of measles and Koplik spots:

Bitot's Spot seen in Vitamin A deficiency seen in the figure:

Other options :

Option B : Home isolation of the child along with Vitamin A supplementation is not enough as Measles is a highly contagious and potentially life-threatening illness, especially for young children, pregnant women, and people with weakened immune systems.  We need to isolate the patient in institution because Measles can lead to serious complications, such as pneumonia, bronchitis, laryngitis, and encephalitis .

Option C : Administeration of MR vaccine has no role in treatment once the symptoms have appeared.

Option D : Treatment with only Vitamin A supplementation is not enough as Measles has a SAR of >90% and hence Isolation of the patient in institution is necessary to prevent its spread and complications.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A guy was playing in a garden. Suddenly, he collapsed and was rushed to the hospital. His friend who played with him in the garden informed the doctors that he ate one of the fruits in the garden post which he seemed to have developed these symptoms. He also had irritability, restlessness, dry hot skin, and was unable to pass urine and stools. Identify the poison and its appropriate antidote.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Datura, Physostigmine

The clinical vignette in the question is suggestive of Datura poisoning for which the appropriate antidote is physostigmine, a reversible acetylcholine esterase antagonist. It is an effective treatment for severe anticholinergic poisoning.

Datura poisoning:

The common names include thorn apple, Jimson weed, and Devil's trumpet. The active ingredients include the anticholinergic alkaloids atropine, scopolamine, and hyoscyamine. The seeds or other parts of the plant can be ingested or smoked.

Toxic manifestations of Datura:

• Mnemonic: "hot as a hare, blind as a bat, dry as a bone, red as a beet, and mad as a hatter"
• Also, remember the D's of Datura

• Dry hot skin (Temp rises up to 42 C, a scarlet rash may also be appreciated).
• Dilatation of pupils along with loss of accommodation
• Diplopia
• Dryness of the mouth and throat, unquenchable thirst
• Dysphagia
• Dilatation of cutaneous blood vessels
• Dysarthria (Difficulty in talking)
• Drunken gait
• Delirium
• Drowsiness
• Death due to respiratory or cardiac failure

Treatment

• Gastric lavage or decontamination with activated charcoal or tannic acid. Gastric emptying is often delayed, and the small, plentiful seeds can become trapped among the gastrointestinal folds after ingestion; thus gastric decontamination can be an important therapy.
• Physostigmine in severe toxicity given 1-2 mg IM/IV after every half hour as required. It is a physiological antidote. Pilocarpine may also be given.

Medico-legal importance:

In India, datura is used as a stupefying poison prior to robbery, kidnapping, and rape. It is also known as a rail-road poison, as it is commonly encountered during a journey. Robbers disguised as saints may offer ‘prasad’ mixed with datura seeds and rob the passengers.

Yellow oleander:

All parts of the plant are poisonous. The active principles are thevatin, and thevatoxin, which are cardiac glycosides. The nectar of the flower yields poisonous honey. Symptoms include burning sensation in the mouth, tingling of the tongue, dryness of throat, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, dilated pupils, irregular action of heart followed by drowsiness, coma, collapse, and death.

The given image shows the flowers of Cerebra thevatia.
questions.learning: Datura, Physostigmine — The clinical vignette in the question is suggestive of Datura poisoning for which the appropriate antidote is physostigmine, a reversible acetylcholine esterase antagonist.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient has a history of dilation and curettage (D&C). Subsequent evaluation shows normal levels of all hormones, including estrogen and progesterone. Based on this presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A history of dilation and curettage (D&C) followed by amenorrhea with normal hormone levels (estrogen, progesterone, FSH, LH) is diagnostic of Asherman Syndrome. This syndrome involves intrauterine adhesions or scarring that obliterates the uterine cavity. Because hormone production is normal, the ovaries are functioning correctly, but the endometrium cannot bleed because it has been replaced by fibrous tissue. PCOS (Option A) would typically show hormonal imbalances like an elevated LH:FSH ratio. Premature Ovarian Insufficiency (Option B) would present with high FSH and low estrogen. Endometriosis (Option D) causes pain and infertility but not amenorrhea with normal hormone levels. Thus, the scarred outflow tract is the only viable diagnosis given the post-surgical history and normal labs
questions.learning: A history of dilation and curettage (D&C) followed by amenorrhea with normal hormone levels (estrogen, progesterone, FSH, LH) is diagnostic of Asherman Syndrome.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A person has the false belief that he owns a lot of property and is wealthy, and that someone he knows wants to kill him to take it away. He appears depressed and physically unwell. What is seen here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Delusion of grandeur and persecution

This scenario where he has lots of property and somebody wants to kill him points towards diagnosis of delusion of grandeur and persecution.

A person has the false belief that he possesses vast property and is very rich, which represents a delusion of grandeur, characterized by an exaggerated sense of self-importance, wealth, exceptional abilities, or fame. He also believes that someone wants to kill him and take away his property, which corresponds to a delusion of persecution, the most common type of delusion. Thus, both delusions of grandeur and persecution are present in this case.

A delusion is a false, firm, fixed belief that is not in keeping with the patient’s socio-cultural and educational background.

Delusions are of two types based on their origin:

Primary: Delusions that do not occur in response to another psychopathological form such as mood disorder.
Secondary: Delusions that are secondary to other morbid psychological conditions like depressive moods and hallucinations. They are understandable when a detailed psychiatric history and examination are available.

DSM-5 criteria for diagnosis of delusional disorder:

The presence of one (or more) delusions with a duration of 1 month or longer.

* Criteria for schizophrenia have never been met.

* Functioning is not markedly impaired, and behavior is not obviously bizarre or odd.

* If manic or major depressive episodes have occurred, these have been brief relative to the duration of the delusional periods.

* Not attributable to substance abuse, another medical condition, or another mental disorder.

Other options:

* Delusion of reference means delusion in which events, objects, or other persons in one’s immediate environment have a particular and unusual significance in reference to the person experiencing the delusion.
Examples : A feeling that people on television or radio are talking about or talking directly to them
Believing that headlines or stories in newspapers are written especially for them.

* Delusion of Nihilism seen in cotard’s syndrome is a false belief that self, body parts or world do not exist.

Pearl PF1258: Types of delusions

THE TYPES OF DELUSIONS

Delusion of control

False belief that a person’s will, thoughts, or feelings are being controlled by external forces.

Delusion of grandeur or Megalomania

Exaggerated conception of one’s importance, power, or identity.

Delusion of infidelity or morbid jealousy or Othello syndrome

False belief that one’s lover is unfaithful. Sometimes called pathological jealousy.

Delusion of love or erotomania

False belief that another person is in love with them. In De Clerambault syndrome, the woman believes that a man, frequently older and of higher status, is in love with her.

Delusion of misidentification

Capgras syndrome: Belief that a familiar person has been replaced by an exact double i.e. an impostor.

Fregoli syndrome: Person holds a delusional belief that different people are in fact a single person who changes his or her appearance or is in disguise.

Nihilistic delusion

False belief that oneself, others or the world, is non-existent or about to end. When nihilistic delusion is accompanied by ideas concerning bodily function failure e.g. putrefaction of intestine etc, it is called Cotard syndrome.

Delusion of infestation

False belief that one is infested with small but visible organisms. As a monosymptomatic delusional disorder, this is called Ekbom syndrome.

Delusion of persecution

The most common delusion. False belief of being harassed or persecuted.

Delusion of poverty

The person strongly believes they are financially incapacitated.

Delusion of reference

False belief that the behavior of others has a particular and unusual significance, usually of a negative nature. The person may falsely feel that others are talking about them (e.g. the people on television are talking to or about the person).

Delusion of self-accusation

False feeling of remorse and guilt. Seen in depression with psychotic features.
questions.learning: Delusion of grandeur and persecution — This scenario where he has lots of property and somebody wants to kill him points towards diagnosis of delusion of grandeur and persecution.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presents with a history of petechiae, ecchymosis, thrombocytopenia, and large platelets on peripheral smear. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)

Correct answer is A because the findings suggest immune thrombocytopenic purpura, characterized by immune-mediated platelet destruction with compensatory release of large, young platelets from bone marrow.

Autoantibodies (IgG) against platelet GpIIb/IIIa

↓

Splenic destruction of platelets

↓

Thrombocytopenia

↓

Bone marrow compensation → ↑ megakaryocytes

↓

Large (giant) platelets in blood

PBS showing giant platelet

Lab Findings in ITP-

| Parameter | Finding

| --------- | -------

| Platelet count | ↓↓↓

| Bleeding time | ↑

| PT / aPTT | Normal

| Bone marrow | ↑ Megakaryocytes

IVIG rapidly increases platelet count by blocking Fc receptor–mediated platelet destruction in the spleen and is used when rapid platelet rise is needed.

First-line:

• Steroids (Prednisolone)

Urgent / Severe bleeding:

• IVIG
• Platelet transfusion (only if life-threatening)

Chronic/refractory:

• Splenectomy
• Rituximab

| Feature | ITP | TTP | DIC

| ------- | --- | --- | ---

| Platelets | ↓↓↓ | ↓ | ↓

| PT/aPTT | Normal | Normal | ↑

| Smear | Large platelets | Schistocytes | Schistocytes

| Cause | Autoimmune | ADAMTS13 deficiency | Consumption

| Treatment | Steroids, IVIG | Plasma exchange | Treat cause

Aspirin worsens bleeding by impairing platelet function. Methotrexate is not standard therapy for ITP. Bone marrow transplant is not indicated as marrow production is usually normal or increased.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient presents with impotence and bilateral resting pain. The following finding is seen in the legs. At which level has the pathology occurred?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aortoiliac bifurcation

The given scenario of a male patient with impotence, bilateral resting pain, and the image showing a gangrenous foot with amputated toes is suggestive of Leriche's syndrome and it indicates that the level of occlusion is at the aortoiliac bifurcation.

Peripheral arterial diseases occur mainly due to atherosclerosis or thromboembolism. Lerich's syndrome is a rare condition in which aortoiliac obstruction causes impotence and claudication (crampy pain) in the thigh or buttocks. Other features of aortoiliac arterial occlusion include absent femoral and distal pulses and a bruit over the aortoiliac region.

In general, features of chronic lower limb arterial occlusion are intermittent claudication, rest pain, ulcers, gangrene, absence of arterial pulses, bruit, and delayed capillary refilling. Rest pain occurs when limb perfusion is so severely compromised that anaerobic respiration occurs even at rest. This causes pain that increases on lying down or elevation of the foot. It reduces when the foot hangs below.

Investigations that are useful include Doppler ultrasound, duplex scanning, ankle-brachial pressure index, and digital subtraction percutaneous angiography (DSA). Through a DSA, endovascular intervention can be performed along with obtaining information on the dynamic arterial flow.

Management is by exercise, smoking cessation, control of diabetes, and weight loss if obese. Drugs such as HMG CoA reductase inhibitors and 75 mg of clopidogrel or aspirin should be given. Transluminal angioplasty and stenting are useful.

Other options:

Options A and D: Femoropopliteal occlusion can lead to claudication in the calf with a palpable femoral pulse but absent distal pulses.

Option B: Iliac obstruction causes thigh and calf claudication with a bruit over the aortoiliac region. The femoral and distal pulses are absent.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Human infection occurs through ingestion of quadrinucleate cysts in contaminated food or water. Which organism is most likely responsible for this infection?
questions.explanation: The ingestion of mature, quadrinucleate cysts via the feco-oral route is the standard mode of transmission for Entamoeba histolytica, the protozoan responsible for amoebiasis. Once ingested, these resistant cysts undergo excystation in the small intestine to release trophozoites, which can cause characteristic flask-shaped ulcers in the colon or extra-intestinal complications like liver abscesses. Giardia lamblia (A) also forms cysts, but these are typically ellipsoidal and contain four nuclei alongside distinct internal structures like axostyles. Cryptosporidium parvum (C) produces oocysts that are immediately infectious upon excretion but are not described as quadrinucleate in the same diagnostic context. Cyclospora cayetanensis (D) involves the ingestion of sporulated oocysts containing two sporocysts, each with two sporozoites. Because the term "quadrinucleate cyst" is the classic, high-yield descriptive hallmark for the infectious stage of E. histolytica in medical parasitology, it is the most accurate answer for this clinical vignette
questions.learning: The ingestion of mature, quadrinucleate cysts via the feco-oral route is the standard mode of transmission for Entamoeba histolytica, the protozoan responsible for amoebiasis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: On ocular examination, a teenage girl with a low body weight is found to have the ocular abnormality shown. According to the WHO classification, which grade does this finding correspond to?
questions.explanation: The image depicts a Bitot's spot, which is a characteristic finding of Vitamin A deficiency (Xerophthalmia). Bitot's spots are dry, foamy, triangular patches of keratinized epithelium typically located on the temporal bulbar conjunctiva. According to the World Health Organization (WHO) classification for Xerophthalmia, the specific grades are: 1. X1A: Conjunctival xerosis (dryness) 2. X1B: Bitot's spot 3. X2: Corneal xerosis 4. X3A/B: Corneal ulceration/keratomalacia Options A (1A), C (2A), and D (2B) are incorrect as they represent different stages or are not standard WHO xerophthalmia codes. The "teenage girl with low body weight" suggests chronic malnutrition, which is the primary risk factor for this deficiency. Bitot's spots are reversible with high-dose Vitamin A supplementation. Therefore, based on the pathognomonic visual finding shown in the image, WHO grade 1B is the correct classification
questions.learning: The image depicts a Bitot's spot, which is a characteristic finding of Vitamin A deficiency (Xerophthalmia). Bitot's spots are dry, foamy, triangular patches of keratinized epithelium typically located on the temporal bulbar conjunctiva.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Methylene blue is used as an antidote for?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Nitrites

Methylene blue is the antidote for methemoglobinemia, commonly caused by nitrite/nitrate poisoning.

• Nitrites oxidize hemoglobin (Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺) → form methemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen
• Leads to functional hypoxia despite normal oxygen levels

Mechanism of action of methylene blue:

• Acts as an electron donor via NADPH-dependent pathway
• Reduces methemoglobin (Fe³⁺) back to hemoglobin (Fe²⁺)
• Restores oxygen-carrying capacity

Clinical features of methemoglobinemia:

• Cyanosis not improving with oxygen
• Chocolate-brown colored blood
• Dyspnea, fatigue, confusion

Why not other options:

• Phosphorus / Aluminium phosphide: No role of methylene blue
• Mercury: Treated with chelators (e.g., BAL, DMSA)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient underwent cardiac surgery and was admitted to the ICU. He later developed ventilator-associated pneumonia and was started on empirical antibiotics. A few hours later, the patient developed acute kidney injury (AKI). Serum procalcitonin was sent. Which of the following statements regarding procalcitonin is correct?
options: It helps in determining the duration of antibiotic therapy
It helps in identifying which empirical antibiotics to be given
It can be used to confirm source of infection
It is used to differentiate bacterial from fungal cause
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It helps in determining the duration of antibiotic therapy

• Procalcitonin = precursor of calcitonin
• In health → made in thyroid C cells
• In bacterial infection → produced systemically (lungs, liver, etc.)

Think of PCT as a thermostat for bacterial inflammation.

Procalcitonin is an acute-phase reactant that rises in systemic bacterial infections and correlates with inflammatory burden. Serial procalcitonin levels are used to guide initiation and, more importantly, duration and de-escalation of antibiotic therapy.

Falling levels indicate resolution of bacterial infection and support stopping antibiotics early.

It does not identify the infecting organism, source of infection, or select specific empirical antibiotics.

| Feature | Procalcitonin | CRP

| ------- | ------------- | ---

| Specificity | More specific for bacterial | Less specific

| Rise | Rapid (6–12 hrs) | Slower

| Use | Guide antibiotics | General inflammation

| Viral infections | Low | Elevated

| Clinical use | ICU, sepsis | Broad

Clinical Correlation

In ICU:

• Sepsis monitoring
• Antibiotic stewardship
• Avoid unnecessary prolonged therapy
