questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient on long-term warfarin therapy is posted for surgery. What is the appropriate management?
options: Stop warfarin 5 days prior and switch to LMWH
Stop on the day of surgery
Stop warfarin 2 days before surgery without any bridging therapy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stop warfarin 5 days prior and switch to LMWH

Patients receiving long-term warfarin who are undergoing major surgery should have warfarin discontinued approximately 5 days before surgery to allow the INR to normalize. In patients at high risk of thromboembolism (e.g., mechanical heart valves, atrial fibrillation with high stroke risk, recent venous thromboembolism), bridging anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) is recommended until shortly before surgery and restarted postoperatively when appropriate.

• Warfarin has a long half-life (36–42 hours).
• Stopping it 5 days before surgery usually reduces the INR to a safe level.
• LMWH bridging minimizes the period without anticoagulation in high-risk patients.

Why not the other options?

• B. Continue medication: Increases the risk of significant perioperative bleeding for most major surgeries.
• C. Stop on the day of surgery: Too late; the anticoagulant effect persists for several days.
• D. Stop warfarin 2 days before surgery without bridging therapy: Insufficient time for INR normalization and leaves high-risk patients inadequately managed.
questions.learning: Stop warfarin 5 days prior and switch to LMWH Patients receiving long-term warfarin who are undergoing major surgery should have warfarin discontinued approximately 5 days before surgery to allow the INR to normalize.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following statement regarding ranula are true except
options: Bluish, translucent, cystic swelling in the floor of mouth
Marsupialisation or excision is the treatment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arises from submandibular salivary gland

The incorrect statement regarding ranula is it arises from the submandibular salivary gland. It is a mucous extravasation cyst occurring as a result of obstruction of one of the sublingual salivary glands in the floor of the mouth.

Features :

* Translucent, bluish, soft, cystic fluctuant swelling present below the tongue pushing it upwards and medially thus interfering with speech, mastication, respiration, and swallowing.

* Plunging ranula presents as asymptomatic, enlarging neck mass.

Management:

* Marsupialisation – unroofing the cyst and tacking the edges of the cyst to adjacent tissues.

* Sclerosing agents like bleomycin.

* Sublingual gland excision – recurrence rate is very low.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is the least likely risk factor for falls in an elderly person?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hearing impairment

Falls in older adults are multifactorial and are most commonly associated with impaired vision, muscle weakness, gait and balance disorders, arthritis, cognitive impairment, and medications. Although hearing impairment may contribute indirectly to reduced environmental awareness, it is not considered a major independent risk factor for falls compared with the others.

Why not the other options?

• B. Visual deficit ✓: Major risk factor due to impaired depth perception, reduced contrast sensitivity, and poor hazard detection.
• C. Arthritis ✓: Causes pain, joint stiffness, and impaired mobility, increasing fall risk.
• D. Muscle weakness ✓: One of the strongest modifiable risk factors, particularly weakness of the lower limbs.
questions.learning: Hearing impairment Falls in older adults are multifactorial and are most commonly associated with impaired vision, muscle weakness, gait and balance disorders, arthritis, cognitive impairment, and medications.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-month-old infant presents with feeding difficulties, recurrent vomiting, poor growth, jaundice, and hepatomegaly. Examination also reveals oil drop cataracts, and laboratory tests show elevated galactose in blood and urine. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible for this infant’s condition?
questions.explanation: The combination of neonatal jaundice, hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, and the pathognomonic finding of oil drop cataracts is diagnostic for classic galactosemia. This autosomal recessive metabolic disorder is caused by a profound deficiency of the enzyme Galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT). Without GALT, the infant cannot metabolize galactose (derived from lactose in milk), leading to the toxic accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the liver, brain, and lens of the eye. G6PD deficiency (Option A) results in hemolytic anemia but not cataracts. ALDH (Option C) is involved in alcohol metabolism. PKU (Option D) results from phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency and leads to intellectual disability rather than acute liver failure and cataracts. Diagnosis is confirmed by elevated galactose levels in the blood and urine. The immediate treatment is the strict, lifelong removal of lactose and galactose from the diet to prevent irreversible liver damage and developmental delay
questions.learning: The combination of neonatal jaundice, hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, and the pathognomonic finding of oil drop cataracts is diagnostic for classic galactosemia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The ligament that maintains anteversion of the uterus during pregnancy is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Round ligament

The round ligament helps maintain the anteversion of the uterus during pregnancy.

However, the anteversion in the non-pregnant uterus is maintained by both the uterosacral ligament and round ligament.

Anteflexion of uterus is at the level of internal os.

Angle of anteversion
Angle of anteflexion

Angle between the cervix and vagina
Angle between cervix and uterus

90o
120o

(Mnemonic - V for version, V for vagina)

The uterus normally lies in a position of anteversion and anteflexion.

In anteversion, the external os is directed downward and backward, so that on vaginal examination, the fingers find that the lowest part of the cervix is the anterior lip.

When the uterus is retroverted, the cervix is directed downward and forward, and the lowest part of the cervix is either the external os or its posterior lip.
questions.learning: Round ligament — The round ligament helps maintain the anteversion of the uterus during pregnancy. However, the anteversion in the non-pregnant uterus is maintained by both the uterosacral ligament and round ligament.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the use of secondary prevention in Colorectal cancer?
options: Vaccine to reduce transmission of cancer
For early diagnosis and improved prognosis and treatment
To screen for cancer before onset of disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. For early diagnosis and improved prognosis and treatment

| Level of Prevention | Aim

| ------------------- | ---

| Primary prevention | Prevent occurrence of disease

| Secondary prevention | Early detection and early treatment

| Tertiary prevention | Reduce disability and complications

Secondary prevention aims at early detection of disease after its onset but before symptoms become advanced.

In colorectal cancer, this includes screening methods like fecal occult blood testing, sigmoidoscopy, or colonoscopy to detect cancer at an early, treatable stage.

Early diagnosis through secondary prevention leads to better prognosis and more effective treatment, distinguishing it from primary prevention (risk reduction) and tertiary prevention (palliation).

Early detection allows:

| Benefit | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Early treatment | Tumor removed before spread

| Better prognosis | Higher survival rates

| Reduced mortality | Early-stage cancers are curable

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the correct order of the normal phases of wound healing?
options: Proliferative phase > Hemostatic phase > Inflammatory phase > Remodeling phase
Hemostatic phase > Inflammatory phase > Proliferative phase > Remodeling phase
Inflammatory phase > Hemostatic phase > Proliferative phase > Remodeling phase
Remodeling phase > Proliferative phase > Destructive phase > Inflammatory phase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hemostatic phase > Inflammatory phase > Proliferative phase > Remodeling phase

The correct order of the normal phases of wound healing is as follows: Hemostatic phase > Inflammatory phase > Proliferative phase > Remodeling phase.

Inflammatory phase: begins immediately after wounding and lasts 2-3 days. Bleeding is followed by vasoconstriction and thrombus formation to limit blood loss. Occasionally, the early part of inflammatory phase is called hemostatic phase.

Proliferative phase lasts from 3rd day to 3rd week consisting mainly of fibroblast activity with production of collagen and ground substance, growth of new blood vessels and re-epithelialization of the wound surface.

Remodeling phase is characterized by maturation of collagen- type 1 replacing type 3 until a ratio of 4:1 is achieved. The mature collagen leads to increased tensile strength and represents approximately 80% of the uninjured skin strength.
questions.learning: Hemostatic phase > Inflammatory phase > Proliferative phase > Remodeling phase The correct order of the normal phases of wound healing is as follows: Hemostatic phase > Inflammatory phase > Proliferative phase > Remodeling phase.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug is used to treat multiple myeloma that is known to cause reactivation of Herpes Zoster?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bortezomib

The drug used to treat multiple myeloma and that has the potential to cause reactivation of Herpes Zoster is bortezomib.

Bortezomib is an inhibitor of proteasome-mediated protein degradation. It is central to the treatment of multiple myeloma, both untreated and relapsed. Bortezomib is given intravenously or subcutaneously and dosage depends upon the disease, route of administration, and the patient’s history.  It is known to predispose patients to the reactivation of herpesvirus, including Herpes Zoster.

Adverse effects include thrombocytopenia, fatigue, peripheral neuropathy, neutropenia, anaemia, anorexia, nausea, limb pain, dizziness, etc. Other adverse events like cardiac tamponade, disseminated intravascular coagulation, toxic epidermal necrolysis, etc. have been reported.

Other options:

Option B: Lenalidomide is the drug of choice in patients with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) associated with 5q deletion, and is an immunomodulatory analogue of thalidomide. It suppresses bone marrow and is often associated with significant leukopenia.

Option C: Daratumumab is a monoclonal antibody against CD-38.

Option D: Elotuzumab is a monoclonal antibody against SLAMF7, a glycoprotein expressed in multiple myeloma cells and natural killer cells. It is used in combination with lenalidomide and dexamethasone for the treatment of multiple myeloma.
questions.learning: Bortezomib — The drug used to treat multiple myeloma and that has the potential to cause reactivation of Herpes Zoster is bortezomib. Bortezomib is an inhibitor of proteasome-mediated protein degradation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following clinical factors has the worst prognosis in a case of acute limb ischemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Paralysis

Paralysis is seen in a nonviable limb and has the worst prognosis in a case of acute limb ischemia.

The classification of acute limb ischemia is:

a)Viable (I):

* Mild pain

* No sensory or motor deficits

* Capillary refill normal

* Doppler evaluation normal

* Urgent evaluation to be done

b)Marginally threatened(IIa):

* Moderate pain

* Minimal sensory deficit( in toes) with no motor deficit

* Delayed capillary refill is seen here

* Abnormal arterial doppler

* Urgent revascularization is needed

c)Immediately threatened(IIb):

* Severe pain

* Paraesthesia and mild to moderate muscle weakness

* Delayed capillary refill

* Abnormal arterial doppler

* Emergency revascularization is needed.

d)Nonviable(III):

* Irreversible muscle and tissue damage.

* Pain is variable here due to the death of the nerves

* Profound sensory loss, paralysis, and rigor of the limbs

* Abnormal arterial and venous dopplers

* Amputation is needed here

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct about triage?
questions.explanation: Triage is the process of prioritizing patients based on the severity of their condition during mass casualty incidents. The Yellow category is for "delayed" priority, representing patients who are stable but require medical care and observation; their treatment can be safely postponed for a short time. The Red category (Option A) is for "immediate" priority—patients with life-threatening but treatable injuries, such as airway obstruction or tension pneumothorax. The Green category (Option D) is for the "walking wounded" or ambulatory patients with minor injuries. The Black category (Option C) is for the deceased or those whose injuries are so extensive that survival is unlikely even with maximal care. Efficient triage ensures the greatest good for the greatest number of people when resources are overwhelmed. Correct color-coding allows rapid visual identification of priority by responding medical teams. Knowledge of these categories is a fundamental skill in emergency and disaster medicine

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following foods is not included in the DASH diet?
questions.explanation: The DASH diet (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) is a standardized nutritional plan designed to lower blood pressure. It is specifically characterized by being low in sodium (Option C is the correct "not included" choice). The diet emphasizes foods that are rich in potassium (Option A), calcium (Option B), and magnesium (Option D). These minerals help relax blood vessels and improve cardiac health. The DASH plan encourages the consumption of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while strictly limiting salt (sodium), red meat, and added sugars. High sodium intake is a primary driver of fluid retention and elevated blood pressure. Therefore, because the fundamental goal of the diet is to reduce salt intake to either 2,300 mg or 1,500 mg per day, a "rich in sodium" diet is the definitive opposite of the DASH philosophy
questions.learning: The DASH diet (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) is a standardized nutritional plan designed to lower blood pressure. It is specifically characterized by being low in sodium (Option C is the correct "not included" choice).

• They preferentially stain areas of high nucleic acid content → suspicious for dysplasia/malignancy
• Help in targeted biopsy by highlighting abnormal epithelium

Why not other options:

• H&E: Standard histopathological stain, used after biopsy, not during procedure
• Silver nitrate: Cauterizing agent, not a diagnostic stain
• Congo red: Used for amyloidosis, not for vocal cord lesions

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A patient has bruising, petechiae, and occasional minor epistaxis without any significant impairment in his daily activities. On further workup, a diagnosis of a mild case of ITP is made. How will you manage the patient?
options: A single dose of intravenous immunoglobulin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Education, counseling and watchful expectancy

In this patients with mild ITP, the next step in management is education, counselling, and watchful expectancy.

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura or idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is an acquired disorder in which there is immune-mediated destruction of platelets. The antibodies formed in the spleen against the cell-surface antigens GpIIb/IIIa or GpIb/IX, cause increased peripheral destruction of platelets. It can be

* Asymptomatic.

* Mild symptoms- bruising and petechiae, and occasional minor epistaxis which has very little interference with daily living.

* Moderate symptoms- more severe skin and mucosal lesions, more troublesome epistaxis, and menorrhagia.

* Severe symptoms- bleeding episodes - menorrhagia, epistaxis, and melena - requiring transfusions or hospitalization, symptoms interfering seriously with quality of life.

Treatment of ITP:

* Mild to moderate bleeding symptoms- watchful expectancy, education, and counselling.

* Platelet count < 30,000 + risk factors for bleeding (antiplatelet drugs/anticoagulants or concomitant bleeding disorders)- oral glucocorticoids or intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) or IV anti-D

* Severe bleeding symptoms- IV methylprednisolone ± IVIG or IV anti-D

* Life-threatening bleeding (eg. intracranial haemorrhage)- platelet transfusion + IV methylprednisolone + IVIG or IV anti-D

The role of splenectomy in ITP should be reserved for 2 circumstances:

* The older child (≥4 yr) with severe ITP that has lasted >1 year (chronic ITP) and whose symptoms are not easily controlled with medical therapy

* When life-threatening hemorrhage (ICH) complicates acute ITP and the platelet count cannot be corrected rapidly with transfusion of platelets and administration of IVIG and corticosteroids.

Pearl PF1322: Idiopathic/Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)

It is characterized by

* Isolated thrombocytopenia—the presence of antibody against platelet membrane glycoprotein and subsequent destruction in reticuloendothelial system

* Normal bone marrow—normal or even increased number of megakaryocytes

* Absence of other causes of thrombocytopenia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
Match the following with appropriate precursors

i. Melatonin
a. Tyrosine

ii. Histamine
b. Tryptophan

iii. Norepinephrine
c. Cystine

iv. Glutathione
d. Histidine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. i-b, ii-d, iii-a, iv-c

The correct matched sequence is : i-b, ii-d, iii-a, iv-c.

i. Melatonin
b. Tryptophan

ii. Histamine
d. Histidine

iii. Norepinephrine
a. Tyrosine

iv. Glutathione
c. Cystine

i. Melatonin – b. Tryptophan

Tryptophan is an essential amino acid and the precursor for the synthesis of melatonin, produced by the pineal gland. The process begins with tryptophan being converted into serotonin, and then serotonin is further converted into melatonin.

ii. Histamine – d. Histidine

Histamine is derived from the amino acid histidine. The conversion of histidine into histamine is catalyzed by the enzyme histidine decarboxylase. Histamine is involved in local immune responses, acts as a neurotransmitter, and plays a role in regulating gastric acid secretion.

iii. Norepinephrine – a. Tyrosine

Norepinephrine (noradrenaline) is synthesized from tyrosine. Tyrosine is first converted to L-DOPA by the enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase, and then L-DOPA is converted into dopamine. Finally, dopamine is hydroxylated to form norepinephrine. Norepinephrine is a neurotransmitter involved in the sympathetic nervous system's fight-or-flight response.

iv. Glutathione – c. Cystine

Glutathione is a tripeptide composed of glutamate, cystine, and glycine. The cystine component is crucial because it contains a thiol (-SH) group, which is responsible for the antioxidant properties of glutathione.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the marked structure in the USG of liver given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Portal vein

The marked structure is the portal vein.

Normal liver parenchyma echotexture is homogeneous and more reflective than the adjacent renal cortex.

Portal veins typically have hyperechoic walls (as they are invested by the Glisson capsule), and thus appear bright, while hepatic veins do not have reflective walls.

In color doppler, the portal vein waveform is normally continuous and may vary slightly with respiration and the cardiac cycle.

Hepatic veins converge on the IVC and right atrium and have walls indistinguishable from the adjacent parenchyma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient fell from a train onto the railway tracks and injured both his legs severely. He was urgently taken to the hospital and the following procedure was done as shown in the image below. What is the rationale for performing this procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Life saving procedure

The above patient shown in the image had undergone a below-knee amputation. In the background of trauma with a severely injured, crushed or septic limb amputation is a life-saving procedure.

Major amputations can be done for,

* Dead limb -Gangrene

* Deadly limb- Wet gangrene, spreading infection (gas gangrene), malignancy

* Dead loss limb- Severe critical rest pain which cannot be revascularized, paralysis, trauma etc

Even though, the below-knee amputations provide a better fit for a prosthesis(Option A), it is not the main rationale behind this procedure.

Mangled extremity score system (MESS) is commonly used to decide whether the limb should undergo amputation. Components of the score: Shock, Ischemia, Soft tissue injury and age.

Other options:

Option C: Amputation can be used for the treatment of cancer but it does not reduce the risk of cancer.

Option D: Good cosmetic outcomes are not the indications for amputation in a trauma patient.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which among the following is not part of the Beck's cognitive theory on depression?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Introjection

Introjection is not a part of the Beck's cognitive theory of depression.

Aaron Beck's cognitive triad consists of:

• Beliefs about oneself - a pessimistic self-image
• Perceptions of the surroundings - a tendency to see the world as unfriendly and challenging,
• Thoughts about the future - anticipating pain and defeat.

The psychodynamic understanding of depression, initially defined by Sigmund Freud and later expanded by Karl Abraham, is considered the classic view of depression. This theory includes four main points: (1) disturbances in the infant-mother relationship during the oral phase (the first 10 to 18 months of life) create a predisposition to depression later in life; (2) depression can arise from the real or imagined loss of an important object; (3) introjection of the lost object serves as a defense mechanism to cope with the distress of the loss; and (4) because the lost object is associated with both love and hate, feelings of anger are turned inward toward the self.

* Hepatitis C virus

Transfusion-transmitted diseases currently not routinely tested are:

* Hepatitis A virus

* Hepatitis E virus

* Parvovirus B19

* Dengue fever virus

* Zika virus

Note: In India, malaria is also routinely tested along with HCV, HBV, HIV and syphilis before blood transfusion.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presents with tachycardia, hypertension, tongue fasciculations, excessive salivation, dilated pupils, and mild redness at the bite site. The child reports that the biting animal had an upward-curved tail. Which animal is most likely responsible for this bite?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation—tachycardia, hypertension, tongue fasciculation, and hypersalivation—represents the "autonomic storm" characteristic of Scorpion envenomation. Scorpion venom contains neurotoxins that trigger a massive release of catecholamines (sympathetic) and acetylcholine (parasympathetic). The report of an animal with a "curved tail pointing upwards" is pathognomonic for a scorpion. Dilated pupils further indicate sympathetic overactivity. Sea urchins (Option A) cause localized pain and puncture wounds. Caterpillars (Option B) typically cause dermatitis or localized stings. Shellfish poisoning (Option D) usually presents with gastrointestinal symptoms or paralytic neurotoxicity but lacks the upward-pointing tail and the intense autonomic storm. In India, the Red Scorpion (Mesobuthus tamulus) is notoriously dangerous for children, often leading to pulmonary edema if not treated with Prazosin. Therefore, both the specific physical description and the systemic neuro-autonomic symptoms point definitively to a scorpion sting

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Hepatitis B subunit vaccine contains which of the following antigen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. HbsAg

Hepatitis B subunit vaccines are composed of the HBsAg (Hepatitis B virus surface antigen).

Subunit vaccines are produced from macromolecules derived from immunogenic components of pathogens by recombinant DNA technology. They differ from inactivated whole-cell vaccines, by containing only the antigenic parts of the pathogen. These parts are necessary to elicit a protective immune response.

Hepatitis B vaccine is made by inserting the HbsAg gene into the yeast cell. This modified yeast cell produces large amounts of hepatitis B surface antigen, which is purified and harvested and used to produce the vaccine. The recombinant hepatitis B vaccine is identical to the natural hepatitis B surface antigen, but does not contain virus DNA and is unable to produce infection.
questions.learning: HbsAg Hepatitis B subunit vaccines are composed of the HBsAg (Hepatitis B virus surface antigen). Subunit vaccines are produced from macromolecules derived from immunogenic components of pathogens by recombinant DNA technology.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Mechanical nociceptors and their response to a probe with a blunt object, pinprick, and toothed forceps with serrations are recorded as an output of a force transducer coupled to the stimulator. What could be inferred from this?
options: There are no responses from the nociceptors when stimulated by blunt forceps
Pinching with toothed forceps causes stimulation of mechano-nociceptors, but no pain
Pricking with a needle does not stimulate nociceptors
Sharp pain sensation is carried by C fibres
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. There are no responses from the nociceptors when stimulated by blunt forceps

There are no responses from the nociceptors when stimulated by blunt forceps.

Mechanical nociceptors typically respond to noxious mechanical stimuli, such as sharp pressure or intense stretch. A blunt object, such as blunt forceps, may not provide a strong enough stimulus to activate these nociceptors, leading to no response.

The sharp painful sensation felt immediately upon injury is known as fast pain. The poorly localized dull aching pain is characteristic of slow pain. The nerve fibers carrying fast pain and slow pain are Aδ and C respectively.

Nociceptors are innervated by both Aδ and C fibers. Aδ fibers are myelinated and larger in diameter with a faster conduction velocity. C fibers are unmyelinated and conduct impulses at a slower rate. When nociceptors are activated by a noxious stimulus, activated Aδ fibers release glutamate and mediate fast pain. It is a rapid response that is responsible for localizing the noxious stimulus.

Other Options:

Option B: Pinching with toothed forceps causes stimulation of mechanonociceptors, but no pain: Pinching with toothed forceps typically applies more localized pressure, which can activate mechanical nociceptors. However, it may still cause a painful sensation, not just a mechanical response. It is more likely that pain is perceived, even if the response is primarily mechanical.

Option C: Pricking with a needle does not stimulate nociceptors: A needle prick is a sharp stimulus that activates nociceptors, particularly mechanical nociceptors in response to tissue damage.

Option D: Sharp pain sensation is carried by C fibers: Sharp pain (due to a needle prick) is typically carried by A-delta fibers, which transmit fast, localized pain sensations. C fibers are responsible for carrying dull, burning pain that occurs later after the initial sharp pain.
questions.learning: There are no responses from the nociceptors when stimulated by blunt forceps There are no responses from the nociceptors when stimulated by blunt forceps.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is responsible for balance and equilibrium?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Semicircular canal

The semicircular canals that are a part of the bony labyrinth are responsible for balance and equilibrium.

The semicircular canals are three loop-shaped structures filled with endolymph fluid and lined with hair cells that detect angular acceleration in three planes (horizontal, vertical, and oblique).

When the head moves, the fluid inside these canals shifts, causing the hair cells to bend. This bending generates nerve impulses that are transmitted to the brain via the vestibular nerve, informing the brain about the direction and speed of head movement. This mechanism is essential for maintaining posture, coordinating eye movements, and ensuring balance.

Other options:

Option A: The vestibule, which includes the utricle and saccule, also contributes to balance by detecting linear acceleration and the position of the head relative to gravity. However, the semicircular canals are primarily responsible for detecting rotational movements, making them key to the sensation of balance and equilibrium.

Option C: The organ of Corti is the sense organ of hearing and is situated on the basilar membrane of the cochlear duct. It detects sound vibrations and converts them into electrical signals for the auditory nerve. It is involved in hearing, not balance or equilibrium.

Option D: The cochlea is a spiral-shaped organ responsible for converting sound waves into electrical signals. It contains hair cells that detect sound vibrations and transmit them as nerve impulses to the auditory nerve, allowing us to perceive sound.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient develops a recurrent skin rash at the same site after taking NSAIDs for knee pain and reports a similar episode at the identical location six months earlier following NSAID use for back pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The description of a skin lesion that recurs at the exact same anatomical site whenever the specific causative drug is taken is the hallmark of a fixed drug eruption (FDE) (Option C). FDEs typically appear as well-circumscribed, round or oval, erythematous or dusky-red patches that may occasionally blister. Common triggers include NSAIDs (like the case described), sulfonamides, and tetracyclines. After the initial lesion heals, it often leaves a patch of gray or brown post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (Option B), which is a consequence rather than the primary diagnosis. General drug hypersensitivity (Option A) would more likely present as a widespread rash (e.g., urticaria or exanthematous eruption). Drug-induced hypermelanosis (Option D) involves generalized skin darkening rather than recurrent localized patches. The site-specific recurrence is pathognomonic for FDE, believed to be due to localized memory T-cells remaining in the skin
questions.learning: The description of a skin lesion that recurs at the exact same anatomical site whenever the specific causative drug is taken is the hallmark of a fixed drug eruption (FDE) (Option C).

options: The tachyarrhythmia is best explained by decreased density and sensitivity of myocardial β-adrenergic receptors, which paradoxically lowers the threshold for ectopic atrial activity

Increased sarcolemmal Ca²⁺-ATPase activity together with decreased phospholamban expression enhances sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium cycling, contributing to the increased chronotropy and contractility seen in this condition
Her elevated cardiac output is primarily due to increased systemic vascular resistance, which increases afterload and secondarily raises heart rate via baroreceptor-mediated reflex tachycardia
Atrial fibrillation is a rare and incidental finding in this condition, occurring no more frequently than in the general population, and should prompt a search for an alternative cardiac etiology
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increased sarcolemmal Ca²⁺-ATPase activity together with decreased phospholamban expression enhances sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium cycling, contributing to the increased chronotropy and contractility seen in this condition

• This patient's presentation, including the ophthalmopathy with periorbital edema, exophthalmos, and lid retraction, is characteristic of Graves disease-associated hyperthyroidism.
• Thyroid hormone (T3) directly alters cardiac gene expression:

• ↑ SERCA2 (Sarcoplasmic Reticulum Ca²⁺-ATPase) expression/activity
• ↓ Phospholamban (PLB) expression

• Normally, phospholamban inhibits SERCA2. Therefore:

• ↓ Phospholamban + ↑ SERCA2 → Faster reuptake of Ca²⁺ into the sarcoplasmic reticulum → Faster calcium cycling

• This results in:

• ✅ Increased contractility (positive inotropy)
• ✅ Faster relaxation (positive lusitropy)
• ✅ Increased heart rate (positive chronotropy)

• Additionally, thyroid hormone also:

• ↑ β₁-adrenergic receptor expression
• ↑ Sensitivity to catecholamines
• ↑ Cardiac output
• ↓ Systemic vascular resistance

• Hyperthyroidism is characteristically associated with tachycardia and increased cardiac output, not bradycardia, which is instead a feature of hypothyroidism.
• Atrial fibrillation is a recognized and clinically important arrhythmic complication of hyperthyroidism, related to the increased adrenergic sensitivity and metabolic demand on the heart.

questions.text: A patient presents with seizures, a cherry-red spot on the macula, and no hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory investigations reveal a deficiency of hexosaminidase. Which compound is accumulated in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. GM2 ganglioside

The clinical triad of seizures, neurodegeneration, cherry-red spot on macula, and absence of hepatosplenomegaly is characteristic of Tay–Sachs disease.

• Deficiency of hexosaminidase A
• Leads to accumulation of GM2 ganglioside in neurons

Pathophysiology:

• GM2 accumulates in lysosomes of neurons → progressive neurodegeneration
• Retina becomes pale due to lipid accumulation, while the fovea appears as a cherry-red spot
• No organomegaly (important differentiating feature)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Galactosylceramide: Accumulates in Krabbe disease
• Sphingomyelin: Accumulates in Niemann–Pick disease (with hepatosplenomegaly)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is least likely regarding Rh incompatibility in a newborn?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased urine bilirubin

Amongst the given options, increased urine bilirubin is least likely with Rh incompatibility in newborns.

Rh incompatibility leads to hemolysis in the newborn, causing the release of large amounts of hemoglobin. This hemoglobin is converted to biliverdin and then to unconjugated bilirubin.

The newborn liver has a limited capacity to convert this large amount of unconjugated bilirubin to its soluble form through glucuronide conjugation. As a result, levels of unconjugated bilirubin increase (option A). Unconjugated bilirubin, being water-insoluble and bound to albumin, is not excreted in urine.

Intestinal bacteria convert unconjugated bilirubin to urobilinogen and stercobilinogen, which are excreted in urine and stool (options B and D).
questions.learning: Increased urine bilirubin Amongst the given options, increased urine bilirubin is least likely with Rh incompatibility in newborns. Rh incompatibility leads to hemolysis in the newborn, causing the release of large amounts of hemoglobin.

Dose-related toxicity of phenytoin causes ataxia, vertigo, diplopia, and nystagmus.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following consumes the highest energy during assimilation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Proteins

Proteins consume the highest energy during assimilation.

The energy wasted in the assimilation of food is represented as diet-induced thermogenesis or specific dynamic action(SDA). Diet-induced thermogenesis (DIT) can be defined as the increase in energy expenditure above the basal metabolic rate and is expressed as a percentage.

The values for diet-induced thermogenesis are relatively higher protein and alcohol consumption and lower at a high-fat consumption, the hierarchy for it, being in the sequence of alcohol> protein> fat> carbohydrate. The value of DIT for protein is 30%, the lipid is 15% and carbohydrate is 5%. Hence, taking into account the loss of energy as DIT, additional 10% calories should be provided in a mixed diet.
questions.learning: Proteins Proteins consume the highest energy during assimilation. The energy wasted in the assimilation of food is represented as diet-induced thermogenesis or specific dynamic action(SDA).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man undergoes semen analysis as part of an infertility evaluation. According to the WHO 2021 (6th edition) reference values, what is the lower reference limit for total sperm motility (progressive + non-progressive)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 42%

According to the WHO Laboratory Manual for the Examination and Processing of Human Semen (6th edition, 2021), the lower reference limit for total sperm motility (progressive + non-progressive) is 42%, while progressive motility alone should be ≥30%.

Why not the other options?

• A. 42%: Correct. Current WHO 2021 lower reference limit for total motility.
• B. 40%: WHO 2010 (5th edition) lower reference limit; no longer current.
• C. 30%: Refers to progressive motility, not total motility.
• D. 50%: WHO 1999 (4th edition) lower reference limit; outdated.

High-Yield WHO 2021 Semen Reference Values

| Parameter | Lower Reference Limit

| --------- | ---------------------

| Semen volume | 1.4 mL

| Sperm concentration | 16 million/mL

| Total sperm number | 39 million/ejaculate

| Total motility | 42%

| Progressive motility | 30%

| Vitality (live sperm) | 54%

| Normal morphology | 4%
questions.learning: 42% According to the WHO Laboratory Manual for the Examination and Processing of Human Semen (6th edition, 2021), the lower reference limit for total sperm motility (progressive + non-progressive) is 42%, while progressive motility alone should be ≥30%.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is true about macular opacity?
options: Only the pupillary margin is visible
Iris and pupillary margins are not visible
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Only the pupillary margin is visible

Among the given options, ‘only the pupillary margin is visible’ is the true statement regarding macular opacity. Macular opacity is a type of corneal opacity.

Corneal macular opacity refers to a moderate to dense opacity in the cornea. In such cases, light transmission through the cornea is partially obstructed. This limits the visibility of deeper structures like the iris and its fine details(options A & C). However, because the pupillary margin contrasts with its surrounding structures and lies directly behind the corneal opacity and the obstruction selectively allows the pupillary margin to be visible(options B & D).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following features is characteristic and specific to kwashiorkor?
questions.explanation: Pitting edema is the hallmark and most characteristic feature specific to kwashiorkor, distinguishing it from marasmus and other forms of protein-energy malnutrition. Kwashiorkor results primarily from severe protein deficiency despite relatively adequate caloric intake. The profound hypoalbuminemia that results causes a dramatic fall in plasma oncotic pressure, leading to fluid shift from the intravascular compartment into the interstitial spaces, producing characteristic bilateral pitting edema, classically starting in the lower limbs and advancing upward. This edema can sometimes mask the underlying weight loss, giving a deceptively "well-nourished" appearance. Why other options are wrong: (B) Weight loss is incorrect because weight loss is a common feature of both marasmus and kwashiorkor. It is not specific to kwashiorkor alone. In fact, edema in kwashiorkor may even conceal true weight loss, making this feature less reliable as a distinguishing characteristic. (C) Flag sign is incorrect because although flag sign — alternating bands of pigmented and depigmented hair — does occur in kwashiorkor, it is not specific to it. It can also appear in other nutritional deficiency states and is considered a supportive rather than pathognomonic feature. (D) Muscle wasting is incorrect because muscle wasting is the hallmark feature of marasmus, not kwashiorkor. In marasmus, severe caloric deprivation causes the body to catabolize muscle proteins for energy, leading to extreme muscle wasting and a "skin and bones" appearance
questions.learning: Pitting edema is the hallmark and most characteristic feature specific to kwashiorkor, distinguishing it from marasmus and other forms of protein-energy malnutrition.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: If DNA is damaged in the cell cycle, which gene causes cell cycle arrest?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. p53

If the DNA is damaged in the cell cycle, the p53 gene causes arrest of the cell cycle in G1 phase to provide time for DNA repair. In case the DNA damage could not be repaired, p53 triggers apoptosis.

In conditions where there is mutation in p53 gene, the cells with damaged DNA continue to replicate and thus may undergo neoplastic transformation.
questions.learning: p53 If the DNA is damaged in the cell cycle, the p53 gene causes arrest of the cell cycle in G1 phase to provide time for DNA repair. In case the DNA damage could not be repaired, p53 triggers apoptosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An AIDS-positive patient presents with fever, vomiting, and signs of meningitis. Which investigation is most useful for the rapid diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis?
options: Urine lateral flow assay for cryptococcal antigen
questions.explanation: The urine lateral flow assay (LFA) for cryptococcal antigen is the preferred test for rapid bedside diagnosis, especially in resource-limited settings. It is highly sensitive and specific, often detecting the antigen even before clinical symptoms of meningitis develop in AIDS patients. While India ink preparation (Option A) can detect the capsulated yeast Cryptococcus neoformans in CSF, it has relatively low sensitivity compared to antigen tests. Blood culture (Option B) can identify disseminated infection but takes several days to yield results. CSF culture (Option C) remains the gold standard for definitive diagnosis but is time-consuming, typically requiring three to seven days for fungal growth. Therefore, for immediate clinical decision-making in an acute presentation of meningismus, the urine LFA provides the fastest reliable results
questions.learning: The urine lateral flow assay (LFA) for cryptococcal antigen is the preferred test for rapid bedside diagnosis, especially in resource-limited settings.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Ligamentum flavum has high levels of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Elastin fibres

Ligamentum flavum has high levels of elastin fibres.

The ligamenta flava are a series of ligaments that connect the ventral parts of the laminae of adjacent vertebrae. They predominantly contain elastic tissue and form part of the posterior surface of the vertebral canal. The high content of elastin allows it to be stretched by 80% without damage. The ligamentum flava resist separation of the laminae in flexion and assist in extension back to the anatomical position.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Identify the marked tarsal bone shown in the image given below?
questions.explanation: The foot X-ray highlights the Navicular bone (Option C). The navicular is a boat-shaped tarsal bone located on the medial side of the foot, situated between the talus proximally and the three cuneiform bones distally. The Talus (Option D) is the large bone that sits on top of the calcaneus and articulates with the tibia and fibula to form the ankle joint. The Calcaneus (Option A) is the largest tarsal bone and forms the heel. The Cuboid (Option B) is located on the lateral side of the foot, articulating with the calcaneus. The navicular bone is critical for maintaining the medial longitudinal arch of the foot. It is also the site of the rare pediatric condition known as Köhler disease (avascular necrosis). Precise identification of the tarsal bones is essential for diagnosing fractures and congenital foot deformities. Thus, the medial, boat-shaped bone is the navicular
questions.learning: The foot X-ray highlights the Navicular bone (Option C). The navicular is a boat-shaped tarsal bone located on the medial side of the foot, situated between the talus proximally and the three cuneiform bones distally.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
A patient presented with tendon xanthomas. His lipid profile showed serum cholesterol levels to be 283 mg/dL and serum LDL to be 202 mg/dL. He was started on lovastatin. What is the likely diagnosis?

LDL - Low density lipoprotein
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Familial hypercholesterolemia

The clinical presentation with tendon xanthomas and elevated serum LDL (low-density lipoprotein) and elevated serum cholesterol points to a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia (FH).

Familial hypercholesterolemia  (type IIa hyperlipoproteinemia) is an inherited disorder due to defects in LDL receptors. This defect causes a decrease in the uptake of LDL and cholesterol. As a result, the blood levels of both LDL and cholesterol are elevated. Such patients are at increased risk to develop atherosclerosis and coronary artery disease.

Features of FH:

• Painful polyarthritis and tendinitis are common.
• Physical findings seen are corneal arcus and tendon xanthomas over Achilles tendon and the dorsum of hands. Xanthomas are tumorous masses produced by foamy cell clusters (lipid-laden macrophages) found in the connective tissue of the skin and in tendons.

Diagnosis is done clinically based on hypercholesterolemia with

• LDL > 190 mg/dl,
• Family history of hypercholesterolemia and/or
• Premature coronary artery disease.

Treatment includes lifestyle changes, restriction of a fatty diet, and pharmacotherapy with statins in heterozygous FH patients.

Recent drugs for specific treatment of homozygous FH are:

• Lomitapide, a microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) inhibitor, and
• Mipomersen, an antisense oligonucleotide against apoB.

The image below shows Achilles tendon xanthoma and a plain lateral radiograph of both ankles showing bilateral symmetrical swellings (arrows) superior to the calcaneum respectively.

Other options

Option B: Tangier’s disease is a hypolipoproteinemia caused by a mutation of the ABCA1 gene. Enlarged orange tonsils are pathognomonic. Low HDL levels are seen. There is an increased risk for atherosclerosis.

The image below shows enlarged yellow-orange colored tonsils in Tangier's disease.

Option C: Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) deficiency causes type I hyperlipoproteinemia due to defects in LPL or apo C-II. Eruptive xanthomas are seen. Chylomicrons and VLDL are elevated. LDL and HDL are low. There is no risk for coronary disease.

Option D: Familial hyperchylomicronemia syndrome is caused due to either LPL deficiency, ApoC-II deficiency, ApoA-V deficiency, or GPIHBP1 mutation. Clinically, patients present with recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain due to acute pancreatitis. The retinal blood vessels may be opalescent and are called lipemia retinalis. Increased levels of triglycerides (mostly >1000 mg/dL) is seen. The risk of premature coronary heart disease is low.
questions.learning: Familial hypercholesterolemia — The clinical presentation with tendon xanthomas and elevated serum LDL (low-density lipoprotein) and elevated serum cholesterol points to a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia (FH).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 22-year-old pregnant lady presented with a fever and was started on antibiotics. The fever did not subside. On further investigation, she was diagnosed to have septic pelvic thrombophlebitis. Which among the following is the next course of treatment for her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Antibiotics+Heparin

Antibiotics plus heparin is the next course of treatment for septic pelvic thrombophlebitis.

Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis (SPT) refers to the pelvic infection with thrombosis of one/both ovarian veins. The pathogenesis of this disease is due to the spreading uterine infection (secondary to trauma of delivery or surgery) combined with the hypercoagulable state of the pregnancy (thrombus formation).

The patients usually present with constant lower abdominal pain and occasionally with a palpable tender sausage-shaped mass (most diagnostic finding, but rare).

SPT is usually suspected when the fever fails to respond to antibiotic therapy. It can be confirmed by computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the abdomen and pelvis. Patients are treated with a combination of heparin and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Anticoagulation is done to prevent further thrombosis and reduce the spread of septic emboli.

Note: The use of anticoagulation is controversial as not all clinicians favor it. A small randomized study did not demonstrate a benefit, but the majority accept short-term anticoagulation as a part of the treatment regimen.
questions.learning: Antibiotics+Heparin Antibiotics plus heparin is the next course of treatment for septic pelvic thrombophlebitis. Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis (SPT) refers to the pelvic infection with thrombosis of one/both ovarian veins.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Cytochrome C oxidase present in ETC can be blocked by all except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nitric Oxide

Nitric Oxide cannot block cytochrome C oxidase present in ETC.

Nitric Oxide: While NO can modulate ETC activity and inhibit respiration temporarily, it does not universally block Complex IV like the other inhibitors. (Option C)

Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) in the electron transport chain (ETC) is the terminal enzyme that facilitates the transfer of electrons to molecular oxygen, reducing it to water. Various inhibitors can block this process, leading to impaired oxidative phosphorylation and ATP synthesis:

Carbon monoxide: CO binds strongly to the heme iron of cytochrome c oxidase in its reduced (ferrous, Fe²⁺) state. This prevents oxygen from binding and accepting electrons, halting the production of water and the proton gradient. Poisoning with CO can lead to severe hypoxia at the cellular level, even in the presence of normal oxygen levels. (Option A)

Cyanide: Cyanide binds irreversibly to the ferric (Fe³⁺) iron in the heme group of cytochrome c oxidase. It completely blocks electron transfer to oxygen, making it a potent inhibitor. Cyanide poisoning results in rapid cellular asphyxiation and is life-threatening. (Option B)

Hydrogen Sulfide: Inhibits Complex IV at high concentrations by binding to its heme groups, similar to cyanide. Its inhibition is dose-dependent, but it remains a strong inhibitor at high levels. (Option D)
questions.learning: Nitric Oxide Nitric Oxide cannot block cytochrome C oxidase present in ETC. Nitric Oxide: While NO can modulate ETC activity and inhibit respiration temporarily, it does not universally block Complex IV like the other inhibitors.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Match the features seen due to compression of the following structures in case of thyroid swelling.

1. Trachea
a. Hoarseness

2. Esophagus
b. Horner's Syndrome

3. Sympathetic chain
c. Dyspnea

4. Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve
d. Dysphagia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1-c, 2-d, 3-b, 4-a

The features seen due to compression of the surrounding structures in case of thyroid swelling are as follows:

1. Trachea
c. Dyspnea

2. Esophagus
d. Dysphagia

3. Sympathetic chain
b. Horner's Syndrome

4. Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve
a. Hoarseness

The normal thyroid gland is impalpable. Thyroid swellings may be uniform enlargement of the gland, isolated solitary nodules, or multinodular goiter. Large thyroid swelling may compress the surrounding structures and present as pressure symptoms.

• Compression of the trachea can cause respiratory symptoms like dyspnea and stridor.
• Pressure on the esophagus causes dysphagia.
• Compression of the sympathetic chain leads to Horner's syndrome.
• Unilateral paralysis of the recurrent laryngeal nerve produces hoarseness. Vocal cord paralysis from RLN compression is extremely rare and should raise concern for malignant change.
questions.learning: 1-c, 2-d, 3-b, 4-a The features seen due to compression of the surrounding structures in case of thyroid swelling are as follows: 1. Hoarseness The normal thyroid gland is impalpable.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: When evaluating a new diagnostic test for a rare disease, which factor has the greatest influence on the positive predictive value (PPV) of the test?
questions.explanation: The Positive Predictive Value (PPV) is the probability that an individual with a positive test result truly has the disease. While PPV is mathematically related to sensitivity (Option A) and specificity (Option C), it is most profoundly influenced by the prevalence of the disease in the population being tested. In a rare disease with very low prevalence, even a highly specific test will yield more false positives than true positives, significantly lowering the PPV. Conversely, as prevalence increases, the PPV rises because a positive result becomes more likely to be a true positive. Specificity (Option C) also significantly affects PPV, but prevalence is the population-level factor that determines the clinical utility of the test result. Relative risk (Option D) is a measure of association between exposure and disease, not a metric for test accuracy. Therefore, prevalence is the most critical variable affecting the probability of disease given a positive result

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure passing through the foramen marked.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Abducens nerve

The marked foramen is the superior orbital fissure and the abducens nerve passes through it.

The abducens nerve is the 6th cranial nerve and arises from the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction. It runs through the Dorello's canal which is present at the medial most end of the petrous ridge and then enters the cavernous sinus where it lies lateral to the internal carotid artery. It enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure within the common tendinous ring and supplies the lateral rectus.

Other options:

Spinal accessory nerve passes through the foramen magnum along with the medulla oblongata and the verterbral arteries

Ophthalmic artery passes through the optic canal along with the optic nerve.

Middle meningeal artery and vein pass through the foramen spinosum along with the meningeal branch of mandibular nerve.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 19-year-old presented to the psychiatry OPD. He has a charming persona and is well-composed and behaved in front of interviewers. His mother complains of him getting into fights and bunking classes, drinking alcohol and getting involved in police cases. What kind of personality disorder does he have?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Antisocial

The patient most likely has antisocial personality disorder. Although the patient seems charming and well-composed, he is aggressive and clearly exhibits disregard for social norms, and shows no remorse for his actions. These findings are characteristic of antisocial personality disorder.

Antisocial Personality Disorder is characterized by a long-term pattern of manipulation, exploitation, or violation of others' rights. Individuals with antisocial personality disorder tend to show no regard for right or wrong and often disregard the feelings, rights, and safety of others.

Other options:

Option A: Paranoid personality disorder is characterized by unwarranted suspicion, hypersensitivity, jealousy, envy, rigidity, excessive self-importance, and a tendency to blame and ascribe evil motives to others.

Option C: Narcissistic personality disorder is marked by a heightened sense of self-importance. Individuals with this personality disorder display a lack of empathy and grandiose feelings. This is to mask their fragile self-esteem and vulnerability.

Option D: Individuals with schizotypal personality disorder appear strange to surrounding people. They have ideas of reference, odd or magical thinking, inappropriate or constricted affect, and suspiciousness. It is most commonly associated with depression in nearly half of the patients.
questions.learning: Antisocial — The patient most likely has antisocial personality disorder. Although the patient seems charming and well-composed, he is aggressive and clearly exhibits disregard for social norms, and shows no remorse for his actions.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 39-year-old man sustains significant chest trauma from a road traffic accident. After chest tube insertion, there is an acute blood loss of approximately 1800 mL within an hour. What is the most appropriate immediate step in managing this patient?
options: Conservative management for the next 6 hours
questions.explanation: In a patient with a massive hemothorax following chest trauma, the indications for an Emergency Thoracotomy are very specific. The most appropriate immediate step is surgery if there is an initial chest tube drainage of (as in this case with 1800 ml) OR a continuous drainage of per hour for 2 to 4 consecutive hours. Such massive blood loss suggests a major injury to a hilar vessel, the heart, or an intercostal artery that cannot be managed conservatively. Continuing resuscitation (Option C) alone without surgical control of the bleeding is insufficient. Options A and D (conservative management or waiting) are life-threatening delays in the face of active, high-volume hemorrhage. The goal of emergency thoracotomy is to control the source of bleeding, evacuate clots, and repair major structural damage. This is a critical trauma skill. Rapid assessment and immediate decision-making are necessary to prevent exsanguination and hypovolemic shock in these high-stakes trauma scenarios

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Laryngeal crepitus is absent in all of the following except
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Parapharyngeal abscess

Laryngeal crepitus is absent in all of the following except parapharyngeal abscess.

Moving the larynx back and forth while pressing it against the spine demonstrates laryngeal crepitus. When absent, it is a clinical sign of a mass in the retrolaryngeal space or hypopharynx, probably due to a laryngeal trauma or malignancy. It is absent in cases where the larynx is fixed suggesting posterior extension of malignancy into the prevertebral fascia.

In parapharyngeal abscess, the maximal swelling is behind the posterior faucial pillar and there may be little or no oedema of the soft palate. This condition is usually unilateral and occurs on one side of the neck.

Any condition behind the cricoid e.g. postcricoid malignancy or in front of the vertebra e.g. prevertebral or retropharyngeal abscess (hypo pharyngeal abscess) will lead to absent laryngeal crepitus.
questions.learning: Parapharyngeal abscess Laryngeal crepitus is absent in all of the following except parapharyngeal abscess. Moving the larynx back and forth while pressing it against the spine demonstrates laryngeal crepitus.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The biological method for Mosquito Larva control is done by?
questions.explanation: Biological control of mosquitoes involves using natural predators or organisms to reduce the mosquito population. The most common and effective biological method for larva control is the introduction of larvivorous fish, specifically the Gambusia affinis (mosquito fish) or Guppy fish, into stagnant water sources. These fish feed avidly on mosquito larvae, significantly reducing the number of adults that emerge. Spraying insecticides (Option A) is a chemical control method. Distributing bed nets (Option B) and using repellents (Option D) are personal protective measures that prevent bites but do not control the larval population. Biological control is environmentally friendly, sustainable, and highly effective for managing mosquito-borne diseases like malaria and dengue in permanent or semi-permanent water bodies. It is a key component of Integrated Vector Management (IVM) strategies, which aim to reduce reliance on chemical insecticides and prevent the development of resistance in mosquito populations

questions.text: A 62-year-old man develops sudden massive blood loss following trauma. His mean arterial pressure falls to 35 mmHg. Within seconds, he develops marked sympathetic activation with intense peripheral vasoconstriction and a sharp rise in heart rate. This powerful pressure response is mediated by which of the following mechanisms?
options: Direct ischemia of the vasomotor center
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Direct ischemia of the vasomotor center

When mean arterial pressure (MAP) falls to very low levels (<40 mmHg), the brainstem experiences ischemia, leading to activation of the central nervous system ischemic response.

Mechanism:

• Reduced cerebral perfusion causes CO₂ accumulation and decreased O₂ in the medullary vasomotor center.
• This strongly stimulates the sympathetic nervous system, producing:
• Intense peripheral vasoconstriction
• Marked increase in heart rate
• Rapid rise in blood pressure
• This response is one of the most powerful short-term mechanisms for restoring blood pressure during severe shock.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A person is planning to move from Nigeria to the USA. He is advised to have a vaccine certificate that is valid. Which vaccine certificate will be validated by the US Embassy for VISA purposes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 17D vaccine

The International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005) mandate that travellers from endemic countries (such as Nigeria) must produce a valid yellow fever vaccination certificate when entering countries like the USA.

The strain used for the yellow fever vaccination is the 17D vaccine. The 17D vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine, administered subcutaneously.  It is valid for a lifetime beginning 10 days after vaccination.  The incubation period of yellow fever is 3–6 days. Unvaccinated people are required to remain quarantined for 6 days (maximum period of incubation).
